citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a finite list $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ in a real or complex inner product space ([[def-inner-product-space]]), its **Gram matrix** is

$$G(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1}):=(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)_{i,j<r}\in M_r(\mathbb F),$$

using the square matrix space [[def-matrix-space]]. Its **Gram determinant** is the determinant ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) $\det G(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$. For the empty list, the Gram matrix is the unique $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is $1$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

For every finite list $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ in a real or complex inner product space, its Gram determinant is a nonnegative real number. It is positive if and only if the list is linearly independent, and it is zero if and only if the list is linearly dependent. The empty Gram determinant is $1$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ have compact support. If $f$ is Riemann integrable on one closed rectangle whose interior contains its support, then it is integrable on every such rectangle, and all the resulting integrals are equal. This includes the empty-support case.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The boundary is closed and bounded, hence compact by F1. Consider the family of all available local one-sided graph neighborhoods and all smaller ambient chart neighborhoods whose compact closures lie inside such neighborhoods. This family covers $S$; compactness retains finitely many smaller neighborhoods and their corresponding charts, without selecting a chart separately for every point. The partition is constructed explicitly in the next two steps. Each graph chart is a homeomorphism onto its image, has rank two, and has $C^1$ transitions: on an overlap the inverse of the second graph chart is its rigid-coordinate projection onto the two base coordinates.

Consider all rational centers $a\in\mathbb Q^3$ and positive rational radii $r<R$ for which $\overline B_R(a)$ lies inside one original chart neighborhood $O_j$. Assign each pair to the least such index $j$. Their inner balls $B_r(a)$ cover $S$, since every point has a small ball inside one chart neighborhood, and rational centers and radii can be chosen with a strict margin around that point. F1 retains finitely many inner balls covering $S$. For each retained pair put $s_l=(r_l+R_l)/2$ and $$b_l(x)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{s_l^2-|x-a_l|^2}{s_l^2-r_l^2}\right).$$ By F2 each $b_l$ is smooth, between zero and one, equals one on $\overline B_{r_l}(a_l)$ and has support in $\overline B_{s_l}(a_l)\Subset O_{j(l)}$. This is a finite explicit selection from one covering family, with no countable-choice premise.

For graph charts $X:U_X\to S\cap O_X$ and $Y:U_Y\to S\cap O_Y$, put $E=S\cap O_X\cap O_Y$, $V=X^{-1}(E)$ and $W=Y^{-1}(E)$. These parameter domains are open, and $T=Y^{-1}\circ X:V\to W$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with $X=Y\circ T$. F4 gives $DX=(DY\circ T)DT$ and hence $J_X=(J_Y\circ T)|\det DT|$, with $J_X=\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$; rank two makes both Gram densities positive. Let $w:S\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with compact support $C\subset E$. The function $p(z)=w(Y(z))J_Y(z)$ on $W$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^2$, is continuous with support contained in the compact set $Y^{-1}(C)\subset W=T(V)$, so it is Riemann integrable by F5. Apply F3 with $n=2$ and this $T,p$. Its pulled-back integrand on $V$ is $w(X(y))J_X(y)$, so the two zero-extended coordinate integrals agree.

Put $s=\sum_l b_l$ and $\theta=\sigma(4s-1)$. Then $s\ge1$ on $S$ and $\theta=1$ on the neighborhood $\{s>1/2\}$ of $S$. For $s>0$ define $c_l=\theta b_l/s$, and extend it by zero on $s=0$. Since $\theta=0$ where $s\le1/4$, this extension is smooth. Each $c_l$ is nonnegative with compact support inside $O_{j(l)}$. Put $\chi_j=\sum_{l:j(l)=j}c_l$, using zero for an empty index set. Then each support is a finite union of compact subsets of $O_j$, and $\sum_j\chi_j=\theta=1$ near $S$.

For each $j$, $S\cap\operatorname{supp}\chi_j$ is compact and contained in $S\cap O_j$. Its inverse under $X_j$ is compact inside $U_j$. Thus $g_j$ vanishes outside a compact subset of $U_j$, its extension by zero is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, and F5 makes its integral finite and independent of the containing rectangle.

Given two chart partitions $\chi_j$ and $\eta_k$, insert $\sum_k\eta_k=1$ in each integral of the first sum. The support on $S$ of each $\chi_j\eta_k$ is compact inside both chart neighborhoods, so step 2.2 transfers this continuous overlap integrand to the second chart. Finite linearity in F5 and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ recover exactly the second sum, proving chart and partition independence.

The graph derivative has columns $(e_i,\partial_i h)$, so its Gram matrix has entries $G_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\partial_i h\,\partial_j h$ for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$, and $\det G=(1+(\partial_1h)^2)(1+(\partial_2h)^2)-(\partial_1h)^2(\partial_2h)^2=1+|Dh|^2$. The vector $(-Dh,1)$ is perpendicular to both tangent columns and points out of the subgraph. On overlaps both graph descriptions have the same tangent plane; of its two unit normals the exterior side selects the same one. For the upper-side region the outward normal is the negative of the displayed subgraph normal. Rigid coordinate maps transport the chosen exterior-side vector, including orientation-reversing maps, by their orthogonal linear part; the exterior-side criterion still gives agreement on overlaps. The graph formula is continuous. Componentwise finite linearity and the continuous dot product give all vector, tensor and flux assertions.

For the conditional agreement assertion only, assume Countable Choice. By step 4.1 each zero-extended $g_j$ is continuous and compactly supported in $\mathbb R^2$, hence bounded and Borel on a containing nondegenerate closed rectangle and Riemann integrable there. Apply F6 with $n=2$ to this rectangle. Its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree, and it vanishes outside the rectangle. Equality term by term in the finite chart sum gives equality of the continuous-field surface integrals; step 5.1 already makes the Riemann sum independent of the chosen charts and partition. This imports no Countable Choice premise into the preceding construction or independence proof, and asserts no extension to arbitrary measurable surface fields.

citations.quote:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open region, let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be a family of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ with $J(t,a):=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Here $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous; a diffeomorphism is a bijection with an inverse of the stated regularity. Write $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, $F=D_a\chi$, $L=D_xu$, and $\theta=\operatorname{tr}L=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Here $D_a\chi$ and $D_xu$ are matrices of coordinate partial derivatives. The joint inverse $A$ has domain $\Omega=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$.

A compact Jordan set $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ means a compact set whose boundary, for every $\varepsilon>0$, is coverable by finitely many axis-parallel boxes with total volume less than $\varepsilon$, where a box's volume is the product of its side lengths. Integrals over such sets are Riemann integrals, defined by extending the integrand by zero to a containing rectangle. Let $K\subset U$ be any compact Jordan set and let $q,\rho\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Then $A$ is jointly $C^2$, and for every $a\in U$ and $t\in I$,

$$\partial_tF(t,a)=L(t,\chi(t,a))F(t,a),\qquad \partial_tJ(t,a)=J(t,a)\theta(t,\chi(t,a)),\qquad J(t,a)=J(0,a)\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\theta(s,\chi(s,a))\,ds\right).$$

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, equivalently $\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\!\cdot(\rho u)=0$, holds on $\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\subset U$, and if and only if $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho(0,\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\in U$ and $t\in I$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^1$ reference domain, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be an orientation-preserving family of diffeomorphisms on an open neighborhood $U\supseteq\overline B$, with $\chi(0,a)=a$ and $J(t,a)=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Set $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let the current density $\rho\in C^1$ be positive on the swept material region, and define $\rho_0(a)=\rho(0,a)$. Assume the adopted single-component mass balance with no sources or diffusion relative to $u$, on every bounded $C^1$ material subregion. Then this integral material-mass balance is equivalent, under these smoothness hypotheses, to $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$. It also forces $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho_0(a)$. Consequently, for positive density, $D_t\rho=0$ throughout the material region if and only if $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there. This is a conditional deduction within the adopted smooth model; it asserts no result for vacuum, shocks, weak solutions, or empirical applicability.

derivations.claim: The motion $\chi_t$ is a smooth diffeomorphism on $\mathcal O$ with $F=\begin{pmatrix}1&\gamma t&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $J=1$; it preserves the slab because it leaves $y$ unchanged. Its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,\chi_t(X,Y,Z))=\partial_t\chi_t(X,Y,Z)=(\gamma Y,0,0)$, which agrees with the stated field since $y=Y$. The initial density is positive on $B_R$ because $|Y|<R$ and $\varepsilon<1$.

The current field $\rho(t,x,y,z)=\rho_*(1+\varepsilon y/(2R))$ is positive throughout $\mathcal O$, nonconstant in $y$, and satisfies $\rho(t,\chi_t(X,Y,Z))J=\rho_0(X,Y,Z)$. Direct differentiation gives $\partial_t\rho=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_x(\gamma y)=0$, and $u\cdot\nabla\rho=0$, hence $D_t\rho=0$ by [F1] and the local continuity equation. The material mass balance follows from [F2].

The same field has $\partial_y\rho=\rho_*\varepsilon/(2R)\ne0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,-\gamma)\ne0$ by the curl convention [F1]. It is thus an incompressible, mass-conserving motion with nonuniform density and nonzero vorticity, refuting both asserted implications. The example is purely kinematic and is not claimed to solve a momentum equation.

Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. For $r=1,2$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be such that every slice $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ is a bijection with $C^2$ inverse and $J(t,a):=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$, where $D_a\chi$ is the matrix of reference-coordinate partial derivatives. Write $H(t,a):=(t,\chi(t,a))$ and $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. The map $H$ is injective and its derivative is block triangular with determinant $J>0$, so the inverse function theorem gives local $C^1$ inverses; injectivity makes them agree on overlaps. Hence $\Omega$ is open and the joint inverse $A(t,x):=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$ is $C^1$. Define $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, which is $C^1$. For any $C^1$ vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, let $D_xf$ be its matrix of spatial coordinate partial derivatives and define $D_tf:=\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$. Set $L:=D_xu$, $D:=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $W:=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}L$, and $a_m:=D_tu$. Here $\operatorname{tr}M:=\sum_iM_{ii}$ for a square matrix $M$, $I_3$ denotes the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and

$$SO(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

Let $Q\in C^2(I,SO(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, hold time fixed, and change spatial coordinates by $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$. This map preserves Euclidean distances and orientation because $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$ and $\det Q=1$; the coordinate change does not assert that the observer is inertial. Set $\chi^*(t,a):=Q(t)\chi(t,a)+c(t)$ and $\Omega^*:=\{(t,x^*):t\in I,\ x^*=\chi^*(t,a)\text{ for some }a\in U\}$. Define the transformed velocity, material derivative, rate tensors and acceleration from $\chi^*$ by the same formulas on $\Omega^*$; in particular, $D_t^*f=\partial_tf+(D_{x^*}f)u^*$ and $a_m^*:=D_t^*u^*$. For corresponding points $x=\chi(t,a)$ and $x^*=\chi^*(t,a)$, the transformed fields satisfy

$$u^*(t,x^*)=Q'(t)x+Q(t)u(t,x)+c'(t),\qquad L^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)L(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},$$

$$D^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)D(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad W^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)W(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \theta^*(t,x^*)=\theta(t,x).$$

Thus $D$ transforms objectively, meaning its transformed tensor components obey $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ under every such $Q,c$; $W$ acquires the observer spin $Q'Q^{\mathsf T}$ and is not objective under general time-dependent rotations. If $a_m:=D_tu$ is the material acceleration, then

$$a_m^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)a_m(t,x)+2Q'(t)u(t,x)+Q''(t)x+c''(t).$$

When $Q'=0$ and $c''=0$, the acceleration formula reduces to $a_m^*=Qa_m$. These are mathematical kinematic identities and assert no force law or balance equation.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Work on $I=\mathbb R$ and $U=\mathbb R^3$. By [F3], define $R(t)=\exp(t\Omega)$ and $Q(t)=R(-t)$. They are $C^\infty$, $Q'=-\Omega Q=-Q\Omega$, and $RQ=QR=I_3$. Transpose the convergent series term by term: transposition is continuous in operator norm since each entry obeys $|N_{ij}|\le\|N\|_{\rm op}$ and [F3] gives $\|N^T\|_{\rm op}\le3\|N\|_{\rm op}$. As $\Omega^T=-\Omega$, this yields $R^T=Q$. Thus $R,Q$ are orthogonal; their continuous determinants lie in $\{-1,1\}$ and equal $1$ at zero, so connectedness of $\mathbb R$ makes them $1$ everywhere. Define $\chi(t,a)=R(t)a$. This is $C^2$, each slice is a bijection of $U$ onto $\mathbb R^3$ with $C^2$ inverse $x\mapsto Q(t)x$, $J=\det R=1>0$, and $\chi(0,a)=a$. Moreover $\partial_t\chi=\Omega R(t)a=u(t,\chi(t,a))$, so this motion induces the stated velocity and satisfies every motion hypothesis of [F2]. By [F1], $L=\Omega$ and $\tau=\mu\Omega\ne0$.
Take the rigid observer $x^*=Q(t)x$, $c=0$. By [F2], its velocity is $u^*=Qu+Q'x=Q\Omega x-\Omega Qx=0$, because $Q\Omega=\Omega Q$. Thus $L^*=0$ and the same candidate law gives $\tau^*=0$.

Objectivity from [F1] would instead require $\tau^*=Q\tau Q^T=\mu Q\Omega Q^T=\mu\Omega\ne0$, since $Q$ commutes with $\Omega$. This contradicts step 2.1, so the candidate $\tau=\mu L$ is not objective. The example tests a tensor law and makes no claim that it satisfies a separate angular-momentum or empirical admissibility condition.

citations.quote: Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.
A bounded real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable if and only if its discontinuity set is null.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case
$$\int_Q1_E=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Put $S=\partial V$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F4]. At each $p\in S$, the local graph condition gives rigid coordinates and an open planar set on which $S$ is the graph of a $C^1$ function. Choose a small closed nondegenerate rectangle inside that planar set so its graph lies within the boundary chart and covers a neighborhood of $p$ in $S$. Compactness gives finitely many such graph patches covering $S$. Each patch has content zero by [F1]. A rigid image of a cube of side $\ell$ lies in an axis-parallel cube of side $\sqrt3\ell$, so rigid coordinate changes enlarge the total covering volume by at most $3\sqrt3$. Thus each patch has content zero in the original coordinates.

Parameterize a local graph patch at $p\in S$ by $\gamma(y)=(y,h(y))$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$; its derivative has rank two because its first two coordinates are $y$. Differentiate $\phi^{-1}\circ\phi=\mathrm{id}$ and use [F11] to see that $D\phi$ is invertible. Thus $D(\phi\circ\gamma)$ has rank two. Choose rigid target coordinates so the first two coordinates of this derivative are invertible. The inverse function theorem [F10] gives a local $C^1$ inverse for those two coordinates, so the third coordinate expresses $\phi(S)$ locally as a $C^1$ graph. The homeomorphism $\phi$ maps the local one-sided region $V$ to one side of that image graph. Hence $\phi(V)$ has locally $C^1$ graph boundary.
By [F2], the finite union of the source graph patches in step 1.1 shows that $S$ has content zero.

The compact image $\phi(S)$ has a finite cover by the local graph patches from step 1.2. By [F1] each patch has content zero in its rigid coordinates, and the cube-cover comparison in step 1.1 transfers that property to the original coordinates. Therefore $\phi(S)$ has content zero. It is closed and bounded by compactness and [F4], so its boundary is a subset of that content-zero set and [F3] makes $\phi(S)$ Jordan measurable.

The Jordan boundary criterion [F3] makes the bounded open set $V$ Jordan measurable by step 2.1. The closure $\overline V$ is closed and bounded, and $\partial\overline V\subseteq S$, so [F2]–[F4] make it compact Jordan. The compact image $\phi(\overline V)$ is bounded by [F5], and its boundary is contained in $\phi(S)$; [F2] and [F3] make it Jordan measurable. The open image $\phi(V)$ is bounded as a subset of $\phi(\overline V)$, and its boundary is $\phi(S)$; [F3] makes it Jordan measurable.

The function $f$ is bounded by some $M\ge0$ on the compact set $\phi(\overline V)$ by [F5]. In a common containing rectangle, its zero extensions from $\phi(V)$ and $\phi(\overline V)$ differ only on $\phi(S)$, which has content zero by step 2.2. Their bounded difference $g$ has discontinuities only on that content-zero set, so [F6] makes it integrable. Moreover $|g|\le M1_{\phi(S)}$. By [F7], $\int 1_{\phi(S)}=\operatorname{cont}(\phi(S))=0$; monotonicity and the absolute-value estimate [F8] imply $|\int g|\le\int|g|\le M\int1_{\phi(S)}=0$. The zero-extension definition [F9] therefore gives equal integrals:
$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its indicator $1_E$ is Riemann integrable on a fixed nondegenerate bounding
rectangle $Q$. In that case
$$\int_Q1_E=\operatorname{cont}(E).$$

At each sphere point $p$, choose rigid coordinates centered at $a_0$ with the third axis parallel to $p-a_0$. Near $p$, the sphere is the graph $z=\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$ over a disk about $y=0$ (reversing the third axis if needed), and $V$ lies on one side; hence $V$ is a bounded $C^1$ subdomain. Choose a nondegenerate closed cube $Q\subset V$. By [F1] the integral over $V$ exists; monotonicity [F2] and the cube-content formula [F3] give $\int_V1\,dx\ge\int_Q1\,dx=\operatorname{vol}(Q)>0$, hence $\int_Vh\,dx\ge c\int_V1\,dx>0$. If instead $h(a_0)<0$, the same ball construction gives $h\le-c$ on $V$ and $\int_Vh\,dx\le-c\int_V1\,dx<0$, contradicting either stated integral hypothesis.

The zero-integral case therefore has neither positive nor negative values, so $h=0$ throughout $\Omega$. The nonnegative-integral case has no negative values, so $h\ge0$ throughout $\Omega$. These are the two asserted conclusions.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,

On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations

same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws

5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,

continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

derivations.claim: Divide $\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s=1$ by $\cosh^2s>0$ to get $1-\operatorname{sech}^2s=\tanh^2s$. Let $f(s)=s-\tanh s$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f'(s)=\tanh^2s\ge0$. If $s>0$, apply [F3] on $[0,s]$ to obtain $f(s)-f(0)=f'(c)s\ge0$ for some $c\in(0,s)$; at $s=0$ equality holds. Thus $s-\tanh s\ge0$.

Let $g(s)=s^3/3-f(s)$. By step 1.1 and monotonicity in [F2], $s-\tanh s\ge0$ and $s+\tanh s\ge0$ for $s\ge0$. Hence $g(0)=0$ and $g'(s)=s^2-\tanh^2s=(s-\tanh s)(s+\tanh s)\ge0$. For $s>0$, [F3] on $[0,s]$ gives $g(s)-g(0)=g'(c)s\ge0$ for some $c\in(0,s)$; at $s=0$ equality holds. Therefore $s-\tanh s\le s^3/3$.

The definitions [F1] and reciprocal identity [F5] give $1-\tanh s=2e^{-s}/(e^s+e^{-s})$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^s>0$ and using [F4] gives $1-\tanh s=2/(e^{2s}+1)$. This is nonnegative, and $e^{2s}+1\ge e^{2s}>0$, so $2/(e^{2s}+1)\le2e^{-2s}$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both claimed bounds.

At the included endpoint s=0 the proof states equality in steps 1.1–2.1 and the deep bound in step 3.1.
For each fixed s>0, steps 1.1–2.1 use one Mean Value Theorem witness on [0,s]; no simultaneous choice function is used.

A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\oint_\gamma u^{[t]}\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\int_S u^{[t]}\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\in S$ is $\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma^{[t]}n_S\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

For all $a,b,c\in\mathbb R^3$, the Euclidean cross product satisfies

$$a\times(b\times c)=b\langle a,c\rangle-c\langle a,b\rangle.$$
