Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\oint_\gamma u^{[t]}\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\int_S u^{[t]}\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\in S$ is $\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma^{[t]}n_S\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

For $z\in\mathbb C$, let $E(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n/n!$ be the complex exponential and set $s_{\mathbb C}(z)=(E(iz)-E(-iz))/(2i)$ and $c_{\mathbb C}(z)=(E(iz)+E(-iz))/2$, where $i^2=-1$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, define the real-valued functions $S(t)=\operatorname{Re}(s_{\mathbb C}(t))$ and $C(t)=\operatorname{Re}(c_{\mathbb C}(t))$, with $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)=x$. These are the real restrictions of the complex sine and cosine; on real inputs they agree with the usual real sine and cosine.

For $t\in\mathbb R$, define $S(t)=\operatorname{Re}((E(it)-E(-it))/(2i))$ and $C(t)=\operatorname{Re}((E(it)+E(-it))/2)$, where $E(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}z^n/n!$ and $\operatorname{Re}(x+iy)=x$. Then $S$ and $C$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and satisfy $S'(t)=C(t)$ and $C'(t)=-S(t)$ for every real $t$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For the incompressible branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Write $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ for the corresponding fields with the same stated regularity. Set $u(t,x)=Uu^*(T,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p^*(T,X)$, where $p_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is constant. Then the original system is equivalent under this invertible change of variables to

$$\partial_Tu^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

For the barotropic branch, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives with $P'(\rho_0)=c^2>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time and first and second spatial partial derivatives, let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial partial derivatives, and let any potential $V$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. $$\partial_T\rho^*+\operatorname{div}_X(\rho^*u^*)=0,\qquad \partial_Tu^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\operatorname{Ma}^{-2}(\rho^*)^{-1}\nabla_Xp^*-\nabla_XV^*.$$

Write $\theta=kx-\omega t$. A surface elevation is the scalar field $\eta(t,x,y)$, and a velocity potential is a scalar field $\phi(t,x,y,z)$. Define the finite-depth linear potential-wave problem by

$$\Delta\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \phi_z(t,x,y,-h)=0,$$

$$\eta_t(t,x,y)=\phi_z(t,x,y,0),\qquad \phi_t(t,x,y,0)+g\eta(t,x,y)=0,$$

$$\eta(t,x,y)=aC(\theta),\qquad \phi(t,x,y,z)=\frac{ag}{\omega}\frac{\cosh(k(z+h))}{\cosh(kh)}S(\theta)$$

are fields that are $C^2$ in the spatial variables and $C^1$ in time, with the displayed derivatives extending to $z=-h$ and $z=0$, and they satisfy this system exactly. Define the shallow and deep comparison frequencies by $\omega_{\rm sh}=k\sqrt{gh}$ and $\omega_{\rm deep}=\sqrt{gk}$. They obey

$$0\le\frac{\omega_{\rm sh}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\rm sh}^2}\le\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\qquad 0\le1-\frac{\omega}{\omega_{\rm sh}}\le\frac{(kh)^2}{3},\qquad 0\le\frac{\omega_{\rm deep}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\rm deep}^2}\le2e^{-2kh}.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\oint_\gamma u^{[t]}\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\int_S u^{[t]}\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\in S$ is $\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma^{[t]}n_S\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\oint_\gamma u^{[t]}\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\int_S u^{[t]}\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\in S$ is $\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma^{[t]}n_S\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Let $I_3$ denote the $3	imes3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $ho_0^{-1}

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. For each fixed $t\in I$, set $p^{[t]}(x)=p(t,x)$ and $\sigma_E^{[t]}(x)=-p^{[t]}(x)I_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant at time $t$ to be $\int_S\sigma_E^{[t]}n_S\,dS=-\int_Sp^{[t]} n_S\,dS$. For time-independent fields the resultant is independent of $t$, and the section superscripts may be omitted. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. For a steady velocity field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$ with $u(x)$ denoting its time-independent spatial value. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$ and an interior parameter point, whose tangent plane is defined by [[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]], put
$$E=\langle\varphi_u,\varphi_u\rangle,\qquad F=\langle\varphi_u,\varphi_v\rangle,\qquad G=\langle\varphi_v,\varphi_v\rangle.$$
The matrix $G_\varphi=\begin{pmatrix}E&F\\F&G\end{pmatrix}$ is the **Gram matrix** of the parameter tangents, and the quadratic form $E\,du^2+2F\,du\,dv+G\,dv^2$ is the **first fundamental form** ([[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]]).

The surface area density is $J_\varphi=\sqrt{\det G_\varphi}$, where $G_\varphi$ is the Gram matrix of $\varphi_u$ and $\varphi_v$. The determinant is nonnegative for all parameter points and positive in the interior because the two tangents are independent there ([[thm-gram-determinant-detects-linear-independence]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a regular surface patch and let $q$ be a continuous real-valued function on $\varphi[D]$. For a continuous scalar field $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS:=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$, and $\operatorname{Area}(S):=\int_DJ_\varphi$.

Here $S$ denotes the patch with its chosen parametrization. Both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan region $D$ by continuity ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]). Boundary values are included in the parameter integral but may be changed on the content-zero boundary without changing its value.

Since $(U\cdot x)/r^3=-U\cdot\nabla(1/r)$, commuting smooth derivatives gives $\Delta((U\cdot x)/r^3)=0$. Also $\Delta(U\cdot x)=0$, so $\Delta\phi=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}u=\Delta\phi=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ by equality of the mixed second partials of $\phi$. Direct differentiation yields $u=U+\frac{a^3}{2r^3}\bigl(U-3(U\cdot n)n\bigr)$. This gives uniform $u\to U$ at infinity. The displayed formulas extend smoothly to $D$ since their denominators are powers of $r>0$. Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

Substituting the pipe parameters into [F1] gives $w(r)=1-r^2$, which as a Cartesian radial field is $1-y^2-z^2$, smooth on the full disk and zero at $r=1$. Polar integration gives $2\pi\int_0^1r(1-r^2)\,dr=\pi/2$. The parameter values are positive where required, so the exact-solution and restricted-uniqueness conclusions of [F1] apply to both displayed fields.

Let $D=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0\}$, let $\rho_0>0$, $p_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\kappa\ne0$. On $D$ define

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. Both $\operatorname{div}u_v=0$ and $\Delta u_v=0$ on $D$, and the pointwise identity

$$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Separately, for $\Omega_0\ne0$ set $u_s=(-\Omega_0y,\Omega_0x,0)$ and $p_s=p_0+\rho_0\Omega_0^2r^2/2$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This smooth steady field is divergence-free and satisfies the same constant-density equation for every $\nu>0$. For this steady field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $\gamma:J\to\mathbb R^3$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $\gamma'(s)=u_s(\gamma(s))$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. For a steady velocity field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$ with $u(x)$ denoting its time-independent spatial value. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and on $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ define $n=x/r$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. Then $u,p$ are smooth in the exterior and up to $r=a$, $u\to U$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction at infinity, and $u\cdot n=0$ on $r=a$. The pair solves $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the steady formal constant-density incompressible Euler system. Its boundary condition is impermeable slip/no-through: $u$ is generally nonzero tangent to the sphere, so this is not a no-slip solution. For the formal Euler stress $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from the center into the exterior, the exact resultant is

$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$

The theorem concerns only this explicit inviscid mathematical model; it asserts neither a viscous zero-drag result nor an observed force. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U,u$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_\infty$ in pascals.

On $r=1$, $|u|^2=(9/4)(1-n_x^2)$, so $p=\frac12(1-\frac94(1-n_x^2))=-5/8+(9/8)n_x^2$. This is even under $n\mapsto-n$; spherical area is invariant and $n$ changes sign, hence $\int_{|x|=1}pn\,dS=0$. Therefore $\int\sigma_En\,dS=-\int pn\,dS=0$, as claimed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation at time $t$ is $\oint_\gamma u^{[t]}\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable at time $t$ is $\int_S u^{[t]}\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction at $(t,x)$ for $x\in S$ is $\sigma^{[t]}(x)n_S(x)$ and the formal resultant force at time $t$ is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma^{[t]}n_S\,dS$. When time is fixed, $u(x)$ and $\sigma(x)$ may denote these spatial sections; for time-independent fields this notation is independent of the chosen time. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For $x,t\in\mathbb R$, assume the fields are independent of a third spatial coordinate. Let $H_+=[0,\infty)$ and $H_-=(-\infty,0]$. The real-valued interface displacement is a $C^\infty$ map $\eta:\mathbb R_x\times\mathbb R_t\to\mathbb R$, and the real-valued scalar potentials are maps $\phi_\pm:\mathbb R_x\times H_\pm\times\mathbb R_t\to\mathbb R$. Each $\phi_\pm$ is $C^\infty$ on the open half-domain; $\phi_\pm$ and their first partial derivatives $\partial_x\phi_\pm$, $\partial_y\phi_\pm$, and $\partial_t\phi_\pm$ admit continuous one-sided traces at $y=0$, locally in $(x,t)$. On the open half-domains use ordinary pointwise Euclidean derivatives in $(x,y)$ and set $\Delta=\partial_{xx}+\partial_{yy}$. Let $U_+,U_-\in\mathbb R$ be constant horizontal base velocities, and let the two half-planes $y>0$ and $y<0$ have the same constant density $\rho_0>0$. The potentials satisfy $\Delta\phi_\pm=0$ and, for every fixed $(x,t)$, $\phi_\pm$, $\partial_x\phi_\pm$, $\partial_y\phi_\pm$, and $\partial_t\phi_\pm$ tend to zero as $y\to+\infty$ and $y\to-\infty$ respectively. The stipulated linear interface equations, interpreted by one-sided traces at $y=0$, are $(\partial_t+U_\pm\partial_x)\eta=\partial_y\phi_\pm$ and continuity of the defined pressure perturbations $p'_\pm(x,t)=-\rho_0[\partial_t\phi_\pm+U_\pm\partial_x\phi_\pm]_{y=0^\pm}$. Gravity and surface tension are absent. Complexify this real linear system for the following normal-mode calculation.

For every real $k>0$, every nonzero complex amplitude $H$, and every $A_+,A_-,\lambda\in\mathbb C$, consider a mode of the form $\eta=H e^{ikx+\lambda t}$, $\phi_+=A_+e^{-ky}e^{ikx+\lambda t}$, $\phi_-=A_-e^{ky}e^{ikx+\lambda t}$. Set $\overline U=(U_++U_-)/2$ and $\Delta U=U_+-U_-$. The mode equations require

$$\lambda=-ik\overline U\pm \frac{k|\Delta U|}{2}.$$

If $\Delta U\ne0$, one root has positive real part $k|\Delta U|/2$, and its real or imaginary part gives a real exponentially growing solution of the stated linear system.

For the $2\pi$-periodic interface, require the fields to be periodic in $x$ and set $\mathbb T_{2\pi}=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$. For a complex-valued trigonometric polynomial $\eta$ on this torus, define $\widehat\eta_j=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\eta(x)e^{-ijx}\,dx$ and, for $m\ge0$, $\|\eta\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}(1+j^2)^m|\widehat\eta_j|^2$. Let $H^m(\mathbb T_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$ be the completion of the complex-valued trigonometric polynomials in this norm; real-valued fields are viewed as elements of its real subspace. If $\Delta U\ne0$, then for every fixed $t>0$ this exact mode family has bounded initial $H^m$ norm but unbounded evolved $H^m$ norm as its integer wavenumber $k\to\infty$. Thus no uniform estimate of the form $\|\eta(t)\|_{H^m}\le C_t\|\eta(0)\|_{H^m}$ holds for this family. This is a linear interface-model conclusion, not a theorem of nonlinear turbulent transition, viscous shear-layer behavior, or physical instability in a particular experiment.

derivations.claim: The $x$-dependence of each potential is a sine or cosine and its $y$-dependence is $e^{-y}$ above or $e^y$ below, so $\partial_{xx}\phi_\pm=-\phi_\pm$ and $\partial_{yy}\phi_\pm=\phi_\pm$. Hence $\Delta\phi_\pm=0$, and the exponential factors give the required decay.
At $y=0$, $(\partial_t+\partial_x)\phi_+=2e^t\sin x$ and $(\partial_t-\partial_x)\phi_-=2e^t\sin x$. Therefore $p'_+=p'_-=-2e^t\sin x$, so pressure continuity holds.
At $y=0$, $(\partial_t+\partial_x)\eta=e^t(\cos x-\sin x)=\partial_y\phi_+$, while $(\partial_t-\partial_x)\eta=e^t(\cos x+\sin x)=\partial_y\phi_-$. Thus both kinematic conditions hold.
Here $k=1$, $\overline U=0$, and $\Delta U=2$. The growing branch in [F1] has $\lambda=1$, agreeing with the explicit factor $e^t$ in $\eta$; this is one exact linear-model example only.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$. For an integer $r\ge1$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region whose boundary is, near each boundary point and in coordinates $y=Qx+c$ for some $Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and $c\in\mathbb R^3$ with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$, the graph of a $C^1$ function; let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset U$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi:I\times U\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ such that, for every $t\in I$, the map $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open set $\chi_t(U)$ with a $C^2$ inverse and with $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$ for all $a\in U$. The coordinate $a$ labels a reference point and $x=\chi(t,a)$ is its current position; $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$ is the swept open set and $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$ is the current image of $B$.

For $(t,x)\in\Omega$, define the inverse label $A(t,x)$ by $\chi(t,A(t,x))=x$, and put $F(t,a):=D_a\chi(t,a)$ and $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$. The joint map $H(t,a):=(t,\chi(t,a))$ is injective and has block-triangular derivative with determinant $J(t,a)>0$. The Euclidean inverse function theorem therefore gives local $C^1$ inverses; they agree on overlaps because the label is unique, so $A$ is globally $C^1$ on $\Omega$. Define the Eulerian velocity field $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$; an Eulerian field is a function of time and current position. Thus $u$ is $C^1$.

For any $C^1$ scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, its material derivative is $D_tf:=\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$, componentwise; it is the derivative along the curves $t\mapsto\chi(t,a)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$.
The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Write $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, $F=D_a\chi$, $L=D_xu$, and $\theta=\operatorname{tr}L=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. derivations.claim: By [A2] and [F2], $P$ and $P^{-1}$ preserve the Lebesgue sigma-algebra and measure. Pullback by $P$ bijects nonnegative simple minorants and preserves their level-set measures, so the nonnegative integral is preserved by its defining supremum; applying positive and negative parts gives the same conclusion for the integrable tested scalar products in [F1]. Thus the time-first coordinates and the spatial-first weak definition give the same test integrals. For a test $\phi$ supported in $\mathcal O$, apply the product rule to the space-time current $(U^\pm,F_1^\pm,F_2^\pm,F_3^\pm)$ separately on $\mathcal O^-$ and $\mathcal O^+$. Coordinatewise integration by parts in $t,x_1,x_2,x_3$ gives $\int_{\mathcal O}(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi)=-\int_{\mathcal O^-}W^-\cdot\phi-\int_{\mathcal O^+}W^+\cdot\phi-\int_{J\times D}K_{\rm graph}\cdot\phi(t,x',h(t,x'))\,dx'\,dt$, where $W^\pm=\partial_tU^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xF^\pm-S^\pm$ and $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]$. Compact support removes all outer-boundary terms; the remaining graph term is the difference of the two side conormal fluxes.

The unnormalised space-time conormal from minus to plus is $(-\partial_th,-\nabla_{x'}h,1)$. Its contraction with the jump current equals $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]=\lambda([F]n-V_n[U])$. Since $\lambda>0$, the graph coefficient vanishes exactly when $[F]n-V_n[U]=0$, and has the same sign as the scalar entropy jump coefficient.

If the weak identity holds, choose tests supported wholly inside either side in step 1.1. Each continuous component of $W^\pm$ must vanish: a nonzero value would have a fixed strict sign on a small ball and contradict the identity for a nonnegative $C^1$ bump there. With these bulk terms zero, step 1.1 gives zero integral of $K_{\rm graph}$ against every trace of a test. Any compactly supported $C^1$ graph test $\zeta(t,x')$ extends to the patch as $\phi(t,x',x_3)=\zeta(t,x')\eta(x_3-h(t,x'))$, where $\eta$ is a $C^1$ cutoff with $\eta(0)=1$ and sufficiently small support. Such a uniform tube lies in $\mathcal O$ because the graph over $\operatorname{supp}\zeta$ is compact in this open patch. A nonzero component of continuous $K_{\rm graph}$ would have a fixed sign on a small graph patch and contradict the identity. Hence $W^\pm=0$ and $K_{\rm graph}=0$. Conversely, these equalities make the weak integral zero by step 1.1, and step 1.2 gives the stated jump condition.

For the scalar inequality, step 1.1 gives the weak integral as the negative of the bulk integrals of $g^\pm=\partial_tH^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xG^\pm-R^\pm$ and the negative graph integral with coefficient $K_H=[G_3]-\partial_th[H]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[G_{1,2}]$. If both bulk residuals and $K_H$ are nonnegative, the weak integral is nonpositive for every nonnegative test. Conversely, a negative bulk residual at a point admits a nonnegative bump supported on that side and violates the weak inequality. If $K_H<0$ at a graph point, continuity gives a smaller graph patch where $K_H$ is bounded above by a negative constant. Choose a nonnegative test with fixed positive trace on that patch and support in a tube of width $\varepsilon$ about the graph. The negative interface contribution to the weak integral is positive and independent of $\varepsilon$, while the bounded bulk terms have magnitude $O(\varepsilon)$; for small enough $\varepsilon$ the weak integral is positive, a contradiction. Hence both the side inequalities and $K_H\ge0$ are necessary. Step 1.2 shows $K_H=\lambda([G]\cdot n-V_n[H])$, so the stated jump sign is equivalent.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. The pointwise continuity equation $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, equivalently $\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\!\cdot(\rho u)=0$, holds on $\Omega$ if and only if $M_K$ is constant on $I$ for every compact Jordan $K\subset U$, and if and only if $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho(0,\chi(0,a))J(0,a)$ for all $a\in U$ and $t\in I$. > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Fix an admissible $V$ and let $K=\overline V$. By [F4], $K$ is compact Jordan and its open-region integrals equal the corresponding closure integrals. Apply [F3] componentwise to $f=\rho u$; the derivative of its material integral is
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr)\,dx.$$
Pointwise mass continuity and the product rule give
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)=\rho D_tu.$$

Substitute the first balance in [A1] into step 1.1 and apply [F5] to $\sigma$, using countable choice from [F6]. This yields
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\rho D_tu-\rho b-\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
The integrand is continuous because $b$ is continuous and the other fields are $C^1$. Every sufficiently small open ball $Q\Subset\Omega_t$ is such a material region: its inverse image under $\chi_t$ is a bounded $C^1$ region compactly contained in $B$. If a component of the continuous integrand were nonzero at a point, it would have a strict fixed sign on a smaller ball and its integral there could not vanish. Thus $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$ pointwise on $\mathcal O_B$.

For each component $i$,
$$\partial_t(\rho u_i)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(\rho u_i u_j) =\rho(\partial_tu_i+u\cdot\nabla_xu_i)+u_i\bigl(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)\bigr).$$
The last term is zero by [F2]. Substituting step 2.1 and moving $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ to the flux gives the conservative momentum equation.

Apply [F3] to $\rho(x\times u)$ and use $D_tx=u$ and $u\times u=0$. The transport derivative is $\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho D_tu)\,dx$. Substitute step 2.1 and compare with the angular balance in [A1]; applying [F5] to the moment-stress flux gives
$$\int_{P_t}\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)\,dx=0.$$
This residual is continuous, so the fixed-sign-ball argument of step 2.1 makes it zero pointwise. With $\epsilon_{ikl}$ the alternating symbol and $M_{ij}=\sum_{k,l}\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\sigma_{lj}$, direct differentiation gives
$$\bigl(\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)-x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma\bigr)_i =\sum_{j,l}\epsilon_{ijl}\sigma_{lj}.$$
For $i=1,2,3$ these equations are respectively $\sigma_{32}=\sigma_{23}$, $\sigma_{13}=\sigma_{31}$, and $\sigma_{21}=\sigma_{12}$, hence $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$.

If $\sigma$ is symmetric, the component identity in step 3.2 gives $\operatorname{div}_x(x\times\sigma)=x\times\operatorname{div}_x\sigma$. The product rule and $u\times u=0$ give
$$\partial_t(\rho x\times u)+\operatorname{div}_x\bigl(\rho(x\times u)\otimes u\bigr) =x\times\bigl(\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u)\bigr).$$
Use step 3.1 and the stress-divergence identity, then integrate over $P_t$. The transport formula [F3] and divergence theorem [F5] recover the angular-momentum integral balance in [A1].

Dot $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$ from step 2.1 with $u$. The component product rule gives $u\cdot\operatorname{div}\sigma=\operatorname{div}(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)-\sigma:D_xu$. Since $\sigma$ is symmetric, its contraction with the skew part of $D_xu$ is zero, so $\sigma:D_xu=\sigma:D$. Also $D_tk=u\cdot D_tu$. Combining these identities with [F2] yields
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho ku-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D.$$

Apply [F3] to $\rho E$ in the total-energy balance [A1]. Rewrite $(\sigma n)\cdot u=(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)\cdot n$ and apply [F5] to $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and $q$. The integral of the continuous residual
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho Eu-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)-\rho b\cdot u-\rho r$$
is zero on every $P_t$. The fixed-sign-ball argument from step 2.1 proves that this residual vanishes pointwise. Conversely, integrating this local equation and using [F3] and [F5] recovers the material total-energy balance.

Subtract the kinetic equation in step 4.2 from the total-energy equation in step 3.3 and use $E=e+k$. The body-work terms cancel and leave $\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho eu+q)=\sigma:D+\rho r$. Expanding the mass-transport term using [F2] gives $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}_xq+\rho r$. Conversely, adding this internal-energy equation to the kinetic equation in step 4.2 recovers the total-energy equation in step 3.3.

Adopt the mathematical Countable Choice convention: every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. Use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, measurable maps, almost-everywhere equality and Lebesgue integrals of the conservative weak-form definition. This convention specifies the mathematical weak branch.

Work in a classical Cartesian inertial frame with SI units on a fixed open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and time interval $(0,T_f)$, where $T_f>0$ is measured in seconds. Write $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for functions whose absolute value is integrable on every compact subset. Let all fields be measurable functions of $(t,x)$ on $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. Space-time integrals use the restriction of $\lambda_4$ to $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$, and initial integrals use the restriction of $\lambda_3$ to $\Omega$; both restrictions use their trace sigma-algebras. The displayed iterated notation uses the completed-product convention, with section integrals for almost every time, as in the conservative weak-form definition. Require $T>0$ almost everywhere wherever $q/T$ or $r/T$ is used. Let $\rho\ge0$ be mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $u$ velocity in metres per second, $\sigma$ Cauchy stress in pascals, $b$ body acceleration in metres per second squared, $e$ specific internal energy in joules per kilogram, $q$ outward-positive conductive heat flux in watts per square metre, $r$ specific heat supply in watts per kilogram, $T>0$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $s$ specific entropy in joules per kilogram kelvin. Set $E:=e+|u|^2/2$, use $t=\sigma n$ for traction and rowwise matrix divergence, and define the test-gradient by $(\nabla\psi)_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}\psi_i$ and the Frobenius product by $A:B:=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

A test function is a $C^1$ function on $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$, compactly supported in space-time and vanishing near $T_f$; it may be nonzero at $t=0$. Let scalar test functions be $\phi,\eta,\zeta$ and vector test function be $\psi$. Adopt as a separate weak-branch model assumption that the displayed conservative variables, fluxes and sources below belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and satisfy the following identities for every indicated test function. Initial conservative data $\rho_0,m_0,\mathcal E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ represent initial mass, momentum, total-energy and entropy densities; the initial terms specify distributional data and do not assert a strong trace.

Mass balance, for every scalar $\phi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\cdot\nabla\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Momentum balance, for every vector $\psi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma):\nabla\psi+\rho b\cdot\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\cdot\psi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Total-energy balance, for every scalar $\eta$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho E\,\partial_t\eta+(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)\cdot\nabla\eta+(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\eta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\mathcal E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Physical entropy inequality, for every nonnegative scalar $\zeta\ge0$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+(\rho s u+q/T)\cdot\nabla\zeta+(\rho r/T)\zeta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$

Every conservative density, product, flux and source displayed in these tests is required to be locally integrable up to $t=0$, including $\rho u\otimes u$, $\rho E u$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$, $q/T$ and $\rho r/T$: its absolute value has finite integral on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using its values for $t>0$. This condition assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Interior test functions impose no boundary condition; walls, thermal exchange, periodic identifications and stronger initial trace conditions are separate data. This weak mass/momentum/energy adoption and the physical entropy inequality are not inferred for arbitrary discontinuous or vacuum states from the smooth balance postulate. The source term and the sign of the entropy inequality use the outward-positive heat-flux convention above.

Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L_n,\lambda_n)$, where $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\mathcal L_E:=\{E\cap B:B\in\mathcal L_n\}$ and the measure $\lambda_E(A):=\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\lambda_E$-null set. Nonnegative integrals are suprema of nonnegative simple minorants; signed real integrals are the difference of the positive- and negative-part integrals when those parts are finite. Finite-dimensional integrals are taken componentwise.

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $D:=\Omega\times[0,T)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ in spatial-first coordinates $(x,t)$. Both $D$ and $\Omega$ are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. Spatial integrals use $\lambda_\Omega$ from $\lambda_3$, and space-time integrals use $\lambda_D$ from $\lambda_4$. For a finite coordinate array $v$, set $\|v\|_1:=\sum_i|v_i|$, summing all entries for a matrix. A measurable field $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is locally integrable when $\int_K\|f\|_1\,d\lambda_E<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq E$. Fields on $D$ are identified up to $\lambda_D$-almost-everywhere equality, and initial fields on $\Omega$ up to $\lambda_\Omega$-almost-everywhere equality. The slice $\Omega\times\{0\}$ is contained in a Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb R^4$; values of a space-time representative on that slice do not determine the separately prescribed initial field.

In the displayed weak identities, $\int_0^T\int_\Omega f\,dx\,dt$ denotes the joint integral of the zero extension of $f$ from $D$ with respect to $\lambda_4$. Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant), and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities, where $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Suppose that for every nonempty bounded open $V$ with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side and every $t\in I$,
$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$
Then the pointwise continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0$$
holds throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$. The larger set $\mathcal O$ is only the ambient regularity domain; no balance outside $\chi_t(B)$ is assumed or concluded. This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

Assume countable choice: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $C_0\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U_C$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline{C_0}$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous, and set $C(t)=X_t(C_0)$. Let $g$ be a scalar $C^1$ field on an open neighborhood of $\{(t,x):x\in\overline{C(t)},\,t\in I\}$. $$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C(t)}g(t,x)\,dx =\int_{C(t)}\partial_tg(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial C(t)}g(t,x)\,w(t,x)\cdot n(t,x)\,dS_x.$$
For vector-valued $g$, the identity holds componentwise. No condition equating $w$ with a fluid velocity is required.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. $$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
