By [F4], the set $\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$; then $n\mapsto g(A_n)$ chooses an element of each $A_n$. Thus the countable-choice hypothesis $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ required by [F3] and [F5] follows from the stated Axiom of Choice.

The postulate [A1] already supplies a matrix $\sigma(t,x)$ with $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ for every unit normal. If another matrix $\widetilde{\sigma}(t,x)$ had this property, setting $n=e_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ would give $\widetilde{\sigma}(t,x)e_i=\sigma(t,x)e_i$ for all three standard basis vectors. The matrices have the same columns and are equal, so the adopted representation is unique at every event.

Apply [F2] to the material mass equality in [A1]. Its hypotheses hold by the $C^2$ motion and positive $C^1$ density in the Statement, so $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on $\mathcal O_B$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. $$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. The translated fields $\widetilde f$ are defined on the chart's swept open set, with positive $C^1$ reference density $\rho_0(a)=\rho(t_0,a)$ on $\overline B$. Apply [F3] componentwise to $\widetilde\rho\widetilde u$, with boundary velocity $\widetilde u$, and [F4] rowwise to $\widetilde\rho\widetilde u\otimes\widetilde u$ and $\widetilde\sigma$. The adopted material momentum equation gives $\int_{P_s}R\,dx=0$, where $R:=\partial_s(\widetilde\rho\widetilde u)+\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\rho\widetilde u\otimes\widetilde u-\widetilde\sigma)-\widetilde\rho\widetilde b$ is continuous. At $s=0$, all small balls $V$ about $x_0$ with compact closure in $B$ are admissible and $P_0=V$. A nonzero component of $R(0,x_0)$ would have a fixed strict sign on such a ball and a nonzero integral, a contradiction. Consequently local momentum holds at $(t_0,x_0)$; arbitrariness gives $\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b$ throughout $\mathcal O$, in particular near every control closure.

By [F3], the time derivative of the mass in $C(t)$ equals $\int_{C(t)}\partial_t\rho+\int_{\partial C(t)}\rho w\cdot n$. Substitute continuity from step 1.2 and apply [F4] to $\rho u$. The result is $-\int_{\partial C(t)}\rho(u-w)\cdot n\,dS$, the first formula.

Apply [F3] componentwise to $\rho u$ and substitute the momentum equation from step 2.1. Apply [F4] to each row of $\rho u\otimes u-\sigma$. The formulas contain $w$ only through $w\cdot n$. If $w\cdot n=u\cdot n$, both relative-flux integrands vanish pointwise.

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant) and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Use SI units in a classical Cartesian inertial frame with absolute time; inertial changes have form $t^*=t+t_0$, $x^*=Qx+ct+d$, where $SO(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\det Q=1\}$, $c$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $d$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities in kilograms per cubic metre, let $u\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^3)$ be the velocity induced by this motion, so $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$ for every $(t,a)\in I\times U$, measured in metres per second, and let $b\in C^0(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^3)$ be body acceleration in metres per second squared. Let $\sigma\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$ be Cauchy stress in pascals, with traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ for every outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. For every nonempty bounded open reference region $V$ whose closure is compact in $B$ and whose $C^1$ boundary is locally a graph with the region on one side, put $P_t=\chi_t(V)$. Adopt on each $P_t$ the material mass, linear-momentum and angular-momentum balances:

$$\int_{P_t}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Here $dS$ is Euclidean surface measure, with chart density $\sqrt{\det(DY^{\mathsf T}DY)}$. The angular momentum equation is about a fixed inertial origin; the model has no surface couples or intrinsic spin.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The adopted traction representation is pointwise unique. The local momentum and stress-symmetry conclusions below hold on the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$; the larger $\mathcal O$ supplies ambient regularity only. With $D_tu:=\partial_tu+(D_xu)u$ and rowwise divergence $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$, the local momentum equation is

$$\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma,$$

equivalently

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b,$$

where $(u\otimes u)_{ij}=u_i u_j$. The angular momentum balance with no couples implies $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$. Conversely, in this same smooth positive-density setting, the local momentum equation with symmetric $\sigma$ implies the angular momentum balance. The model postulate adopts the traction representation; this theorem establishes its local balance consequences and uniqueness.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant), and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities, where $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Suppose that for every nonempty bounded open $V$ with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side and every $t\in I$,
$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$
Then the pointwise continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0$$
holds throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$. The larger set $\mathcal O$ is only the ambient regularity domain; no balance outside $\chi_t(B)$ is assumed or concluded. This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Assume countable choice: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $C_0\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U_C$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline{C_0}$. Let $X\in C^2(I\times U_C;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices onto open images (bijections with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant). Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous, and set $C(t)=X_t(C_0)$. Let $g$ be a scalar $C^1$ field on an open neighborhood of $\{(t,x):x\in\overline{C(t)},\,t\in I\}$. Define the boundary velocity by $w(t,X(t,\xi))=\partial_tX(t,\xi)$ and let $n$ be the outward Euclidean unit normal on $\partial C(t)$. Use Euclidean surface measure, whose chart density is $\sqrt{\det(DY^{\mathsf T}DY)}$. Then
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C(t)}g(t,x)\,dx =\int_{C(t)}\partial_tg(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial C(t)}g(t,x)\,w(t,x)\cdot n(t,x)\,dS_x.$$
For vector-valued $g$, the identity holds componentwise. No condition equating $w$ with a fluid velocity is required.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

derivations.claim: For any countable family of nonempty sets, [F4] provides a choice function on the set of its distinct members; composing with the sequence chooses from each indexed member. Hence the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis used by [F3] and [F6] follows from the stated Axiom of Choice.

Apply [F2] to the material mass balance: the Statement supplies the normalized motion, its induced velocity and both positive $C^1$ densities. This gives continuity on $\mathcal O_B$. The same fields and material mass, linear- and angular-momentum balances meet [F1], giving local momentum and symmetric stress there.

Fix an admissible $V$ and put $P_t=\chi_t(V)$. By [F7], it is a bounded $C^1$ region whose swept closure lies in the ambient field domain. Apply [F6] to $\rho E$ with material boundary velocity $u$, and [F3] to $\rho Eu$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and $q$. Since $(\sigma n)\cdot u=(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)\cdot n$, the adopted total-energy balance gives zero integral over every $P_t$ of the continuous residual $R:=\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho Eu-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)-\rho b\cdot u-\rho r$. For fixed $t$, every sufficiently small ball $Q\Subset\Omega_t$ is such an image, since $V=\chi_t^{-1}(Q)$ is admissible by [F7]. A nonzero value of a continuous $R$ has fixed strict sign on a smaller ball and would have nonzero integral, a contradiction. Thus $R=0$ throughout $\mathcal O_B$, proving the stated local total-energy equation and its outward heat-flux sign.

Put $k=|u|^2/2$. Taking the dot product of $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$ from step 2.1 with $u$ and applying the chain rule yields $\rho D_tk=\rho b\cdot u+u\cdot\operatorname{div}\sigma$.

Under [A3], continuity and the chain rule give $\partial_t(\rho\Phi)+\operatorname{div}(\rho\Phi u)=\rho D_t\Phi=\rho u\cdot\nabla\Phi$. Adding this identity to the total-energy equation in step 2.2 cancels the body-power source $\rho b\cdot u$ and, since $r=0$, gives the conservative equation for $\rho(E+\Phi)$.

By the product rule, $u\cdot\operatorname{div}\sigma=\operatorname{div}(\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)-\sigma:D_xu$. Since $\sigma$ is symmetric and its contraction with the skew part of $D_xu$ is zero, $\sigma:D_xu=\sigma:D$. The continuity equation from step 2.1 gives $\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}(\rho k u)=\rho D_tk$. Substitution of step 3.1 therefore gives the kinetic-energy balance.

Subtract the kinetic balance in step 4.1 from the total-energy balance in step 2.2. The identical body-power terms cancel, and the stress-work fluxes cancel, leaving $\partial_t(\rho e)+\operatorname{div}(\rho e u+q)=\sigma:D+\rho r$. Expanding the mass transport term with the continuity equation from step 2.1 gives $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$.

The $C^1$ fields permit differentiation under each fixed-domain integral. For a fixed bounded $C^1$ region $C$ with closure inside the fluid region, apply [F3] to the potential-energy equation from step 3.2. The boundary flux $(\rho(E+\Phi)u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)\cdot n$ vanishes under no-slip $u=0$ and insulation $q\cdot n=0$. For a periodic cell, the coverage hypothesis $Q\subset\Omega_t$ ensures that the local equation holds on all of $Q$ at every time. Use the fundamental rectangle $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j]$ and put $G=\rho(E+\Phi)u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q$. Every component of $G$ is $C^1$ and periodic. For each $j$, the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus gives
$$\int_Q\partial_{x_j}G_j\,dx=\int_{\prod_{k\ne j}[0,L_k]}\bigl(G_j(x_1,\ldots,L_j,\ldots,x_3)-G_j(x_1,\ldots,0,\ldots,x_3)\bigr)\,dx_{\widehat j}=0,$$
where $dx_{\widehat j}$ is the product volume measure in the two coordinates other than $x_j$.
Thus $\int_Q\operatorname{div}G\,dx=0$, and integrating the local equation from step 3.2 gives $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Q\rho(E+\Phi)\,dx=0$. The periodicity follows from [A2] and [A3].

Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L_n,\lambda_n)$, where $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\mathcal L_E:=\{E\cap B:B\in\mathcal L_n\}$ and the measure $\lambda_E(A):=\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\lambda_E$-null set. Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ be a motion with orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant) and $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Use SI units in a classical Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O;(0,\infty))$ be positive densities, and let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, $e:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$, $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, and $\sigma:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be $C^1$, with $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$ for every $(t,a)\in I\times U$; let $b:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $r:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Their units are respectively kilograms per cubic metre, metres per second, joules per kilogram, watts per square metre, pascals, metres per second squared, and watts per kilogram. Define $k:=|u|^2/2$, $E:=e+k$, $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{ij}$, $D:=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $D_t:=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla_x$, and $A:B:=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Use rowwise divergence $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$ and vector divergence $\operatorname{div}q=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j$. For every nonempty bounded open $V$ whose closure is compact in $B$ and whose $C^1$ boundary is locally a graph with the region on one side, put $P_t=\chi_t(V)$ and let $n$ be its outward Euclidean unit normal. Use Euclidean surface measure $dS$ with chart density $\sqrt{\det(DY^{\mathsf T}DY)}$.

Adopt, on each such material region,

$$\int_{P_t}\rho\,dx=\int_V\rho_0\,da,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma n\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times\sigma n\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\bigl(u\cdot\sigma n-q\cdot n\bigr)\,dS.$$

The angular-momentum balance is about a fixed inertial origin; assume no surface couples or intrinsic spin. Assume also the Axiom of Choice. On the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, angular momentum gives $\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T}$, and the local total-energy balance is

$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r.$$

It splits into the kinetic and internal-energy balances

$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}(\rho k u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D,$$

$$\rho D_t e=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r.$$

Thus the boundary power flux is $-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$ and the outward heat flux is $q$. If additionally $b=-\nabla_x\Phi$ for a time-independent $C^1$ scalar potential $\Phi$ defined on an open spatial set containing every $\Omega_t$, measured in joules per kilogram, and $r=0$, then

$$\partial_t\bigl(\rho(E+\Phi)\bigr)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho(E+\Phi)u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q\bigr)=0.$$

Consequently $\int_C\rho(E+\Phi)\,dx$ is constant on any bounded fixed $C^1$ region $C$ with closure contained in the fluid region throughout $I$, with no-slip $u=0$ and insulation $q\cdot n=0$, or on a periodic cell $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j]$ with side lengths $L_j>0$ metres, $Q\subset\Omega_t$ for every $t\in I$, and opposite faces identified by translations when all fields and $\Phi$ are periodic. All local equations above are asserted on $\mathcal O_B$; the larger $\mathcal O$ supplies ambient regularity only. These are deductions for any solution with the stated regularity; the theorem does not assert that a solution exists.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ and define $q_D(x)=x^TDx$ on $S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x^Tx=1\}$. The sphere is nonempty, closed because $x\mapsto x^Tx$ is continuous, and bounded because each $|x_i|\le1$ there. The function $q_D$ is continuous because it is a finite sum of coordinate products. By [F1], $q_D$ has a maximum at some $e\in S^2$.

Let $X=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2,d_3)$. The proper half-turns $Q_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, $Q_2=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1)$, and $Q_3=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ each leave $X$ fixed. Equivariance gives $L(X)=Q_iL(X)Q_i^T$ for each $i$; because $L(X)$ is symmetric, these three equalities force every off-diagonal entry to vanish.

Let $y\in S^2$ satisfy $e^Ty=0$ and put $c(t)=(e+ty)/\sqrt{1+t^2}$. Then $c(t)^Tc(t)=1$ and differentiating at $0$ gives $c'(0)=y$. The differentiable function $t\mapsto q_D(c(t))$ has a maximum at $0$, so its derivative there is $0$: its right difference quotients are nonpositive and its left difference quotients are nonnegative. Differentiating gives $0=y^TDe+e^TDy=2y^TDe$, since $D^T=D$. By scaling, this holds for every $y\perp e$, so $De$ is a scalar multiple of $e$.

Let $E_{jj}$ be the diagonal matrix with a $1$ in position $(j,j)$ and $0$ elsewhere, and let the $j$th column of a matrix $M$ be the diagonal vector $(L(E_{jj})_{11},L(E_{jj})_{22},L(E_{jj})_{33})^T$. Linearity and step 1.2 give $\operatorname{diag}L(X)=M(d_1,d_2,d_3)^T$, where $\operatorname{diag}A=(A_{11},A_{22},A_{33})^T$. A permutation matrix $P$ permutes the coordinate basis; if $\det P=-1$, then $-P\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ and $(-P)X(-P)^T=PXP^T$. Equivariance says $\operatorname{diag}L(PXP^T)=\operatorname{diag}(PL(X)P^T)$, hence $MPd=PMd$ for every vector $d$ and $MP=PM$. Equivalently $M_{ij}=M_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}$ for every permutation $\pi$, so its diagonal entries have a common value $c$ and its off-diagonal entries have a common value $d_0$. Thus $L(X)=(c-d_0)X+d_0(\operatorname{tr}X)I$.

If $z\perp e$, then $e^TDz=(De)^Tz=0$, so $e^\perp$ is invariant under $D$, and the restriction of $D$ to this two-dimensional plane is symmetric. Its unit circle is a nonempty closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^3$; repeating the argument of steps 1.1 and 2.1 on this invariant plane gives a unit eigenvector in $e^\perp$. The remaining one-dimensional orthogonal complement is invariant and consists of eigenvectors. Hence $D$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Only finitely many vectors are chosen in this construction; no arbitrary choice principle is used.

By step 3.1 write an arbitrary $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ as $D=OXO^T$ with $O$ orthogonal and $X$ diagonal. If $\det O=-1$, change the sign of one eigenvector; this changes $\det O$ to $1$ and leaves $OXO^T$ unchanged. We may therefore take $O\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Equivariance and step 2.2 yield $L(D)=(c-d_0)D+d_0(\operatorname{tr}D)I$.

Set $2\mu=c-d_0$ and $\lambda=d_0$. Conversely, for any real $\lambda,\mu$, the map $D\mapsto2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I$ is linear and equivariant: $QIQ^T=I$, and $\operatorname{tr}(QDQ^T)=\sum_{j,k=1}^3D_{jk}\sum_{i=1}^3Q_{ij}Q_{ik}=\sum_{j=1}^3D_{jj}=\operatorname{tr}D$ because the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal. If two coefficient pairs give the same map, evaluation at $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)$ makes their $2\mu$ coefficients equal, and evaluation at $I$ then makes their $\lambda$ coefficients equal. This proves existence, converse, and uniqueness.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Let $\operatorname{Sym}(3)=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$, let $I$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and define
$$\operatorname{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I,\ \det Q=1\}.$$
An orthogonal matrix is one with $Q^TQ=I$; define $O(3)$ by this condition without the determinant restriction. For $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ set $\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3D_{ii}$. Suppose $L:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ is real-linear, meaning $L(aD+bE)=aL(D)+bL(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and satisfies
$$L(QDQ^T)=QL(D)Q^T\qquad(Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3),\ D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Then there are unique $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$L(D)=2\mu D+\lambda(\operatorname{tr}D)I\qquad(D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)).$$
Conversely, each map of this form is real-linear and satisfies the displayed equivariance. Linearity and rotational equivariance are hypotheses of this mathematical classification; it does not assert that a material response is linear or isotropic.

A smooth positive-density barotropic Euler solution is a pair of fields $ho\in C^2(\Omega,(0,\infty))$ and $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying
$$ \partial_tho+\operatorname{div}(ho u)=0,\qquad ho igl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u igr)+
abla P(ho)=0. $$
Here $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$, $
abla$ is the spatial gradient, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u$ is the material acceleration. The constitutive stress is $\sigma=-P(ho)I_3$ under the tension-positive traction convention. Thus “barotropic” means that pressure is a specified function of density alone, and “Euler” here means that the viscous stress is absent. No sign of $P'(ho)$ is built into the definition; a positive acoustic response is a separate hypothesis where used. In SI interpretation, $ho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $P$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $P'(ho)$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. The model gives equations for a smooth solution and asserts no existence theorem.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

boundaries.evidence: Nonempty Omega is absent from the Definition. With Omega=empty the velocity, pressure and stress maps are empty, so the differential identities, rho=rho0 and div u=0 are vacuous; rho0>0 and nu=mu/rho0 remain well-defined constants. Thus the row should record this harmless formal empty-domain case rather than invent a nonempty hypothesis.

template_review.reason: The current Definition still requires only open Omega, not nonempty Omega. Its new SI units for u,p do not exclude empty maps. On empty Omega all stress, divergence and momentum identities are vacuous, while rho_0>0 and nu=mu/rho_0 are defined constants; the checked disposition remains valid.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open, with coordinates $(v,s)$, and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two (write $e\in C^2(U)$). The pair $(U,e)$ is a **simple-fluid state relation** for the purposes of this mathematical library. At $(v,s)\in U$, $v$ is the specific-volume coordinate, $s$ the specific-entropy coordinate, and $e(v,s)$ the specific-energy value. Define
$$T(v,s):=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s):=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho:=\frac1v.$$
In these partial derivatives the other state coordinate is held fixed. Write $e_{vv},e_{vs},e_{sv},e_{ss}$ for the corresponding second partial derivatives, set
$$H_e:=\begin{pmatrix}e_{vv}&e_{vs}\\ e_{sv}&e_{ss}\end{pmatrix},$$
and define the coordinate-Hessian determinant
$$J_e:=e_{vv}e_{ss}-e_{vs}e_{sv}.$$
The **local thermal-chart hypothesis** at a state is $T>0$ and $e_{ss}>0$; it is a pointwise hypothesis and does not assert a global inverse. The conditions $e_{vv}>0$ and $J_e>0$, when required, are separate pointwise response restrictions. The definition itself imposes no sign condition on $e_{vv}$ or $J_e$ and no invertibility or convexity condition on all of $U$.

Under the physical SI interpretation only, $v$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ has units $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ has units $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ has units $\mathrm K$, $p$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. This is a mathematical definition of a state relation and makes no claim that an actual material obeys it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subset I	imes\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)	o\mathbb R$ be a continuously differentiable pressure function. A smooth positive-density barotropic Euler solution is a pair of fields $ho\in C^2(\Omega,(0,\infty))$ and $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying
$$ \partial_tho+\operatorname{div}(ho u)=0,\qquad ho igl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u igr)+
abla P(ho)=0. $$
Here $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$, $
abla$ is the spatial gradient, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u$ is the material acceleration. The constitutive stress is $\sigma=-P(ho)I_3$ under the tension-positive traction convention. Thus “barotropic” means that pressure is a specified function of density alone, and “Euler” here means that the viscous stress is absent. No sign of $P'(ho)$ is built into the definition; a positive acoustic response is a separate hypothesis where used. In SI interpretation, $ho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $P$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $P'(ho)$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. The model gives equations for a smooth solution and asserts no existence theorem.

Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in U$ with $T_b=e_s(v_b,s_b)>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$ and $p=-e_v$, and use the local chart $s=s(v,T)$ from the unique branch satisfying $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$. Define
$$c_v:=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial T}e(v,s(v,T))\right|_{v=v_b,T=T_b}, \qquad c_s^2:=v_b^2 e_{vv}(v_b,s_b).$$
Because $U$ is open, choose an open interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$ such that $(1/\rho,s_b)\in U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$, and define $P:J_\rho\to\mathbb R$ by $P(\rho):=p(1/\rho,s_b)=-e_v(1/\rho,s_b)$. Then $P\in C^1(J_\rho)$ and the chain rule gives $P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b)=c_s^2$. This is the local isentropic pressure-response coefficient; its sign is not assumed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval. On $I\times\mathbb R^3$, let $\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to J_\rho$ and $u:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous partial derivatives through order two. Use the Euclidean dot product $x\cdot y:=\sum_{i=1}^3x_i y_i$ and norm $|x|:=\sqrt{x\cdot x}$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Use $\nabla h=(\partial_{x_i}h)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u_i$. Consider the mathematical barotropic system
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \rho\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nabla P(\rho)=0.$$
Here $\Delta r:=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i x_i}r$. For $r:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with continuous partial derivatives through order two, the pointwise first variation about $(\rho_b,0)$ is defined by differentiating at $\varepsilon=0$ after substituting $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon r$ and $u=\varepsilon w$, with $\varepsilon$ sufficiently close to zero locally at each point so the perturbed density lies in $J_\rho$. It is
$$r_t+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b w_t+c_s^2\nabla r=0, \qquad r_{tt}=c_s^2\Delta r.$$
If $c_s^2>0$, then with $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$, for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $A\in\mathbb R$ the following are plane-wave solutions:
$$r=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad \omega=c_s|k|.$$
If $c_s^2<0$, then for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$ and every $A\in\mathbb R$, set $a=\sqrt{-c_s^2}|k|>0$. The fields
$$r=Ae^{at}\cos(k\cdot x),\qquad w=-\frac{aA}{\rho_b|k|^2}k e^{at}\sin(k\cdot x)$$
solve the same linearized system and have exponential time factor $e^{at}$; for $A\ne0$, their amplitudes grow exponentially. These are exact statements about the linearized mathematical system; they provide no finite-amplitude error or lifespan estimate and make no empirical claim about a material.

derivations.claim: Since $P(\rho)=p(1/\rho,s_b)$ and $p=-e_v$, the chain rule at fixed $s_b$ gives $P'(\rho_b)=p_v(v_b,s_b)(-1/\rho_b^2)=(-e_{vv})(-v_b^2)=v_b^2e_{vv}$. This is $c_s^2$ by definition.

Substitute $\rho_\varepsilon=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$ and $u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon w$ into the model equations from [L1]. The order-$\varepsilon$ continuity term is $\partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w$. The convective term in momentum is order $\varepsilon^2$, while differentiability of $P$ gives $\nabla P(\rho_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho+o(\varepsilon)$. Dividing by $\varepsilon$ and taking the derivative at zero yields the stated first-variation system.

Differentiate the first equation of the first-variation system in time. Take the divergence of the second equation; because $\rho_b$ and $P'(\rho_b)=c_s^2$ are constant, substitution gives $\partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho$.
