Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. For $(v,s)\in U$, $v$ is the specific-volume coordinate, $s$ the specific-entropy coordinate, and $e(v,s)$ the specific-energy value; set $T=e_s(v,s)$ and $p=-e_v(v,s)$, with each state partial derivative holding the other coordinate fixed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, meaning that near every boundary point it is the graph of a continuously differentiable function after a rigid coordinate change. Let $N\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset N$, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times N,\mathbb R^3)$, where $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. For each $t\in I$, assume $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $N$ onto an open set with a $C^2$ inverse and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Define $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, and $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$; this swept set $\Omega$ is open. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, set $D_tf:=\partial_tf+\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}f$ componentwise. For each nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $V$ with $\overline V\subset B$, set $P_t:=\chi_t(V)$; here a $C^1$ domain is locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph.

Let $\rho,v,s,T,p,q,r,b$ be fields on $\Omega$ with continuous first partial derivatives, with $\rho>0$, $(v,s)\in U$, $v=1/\rho$, $T=e_s(v,s)>0$, and $p=-e_v(v,s)$. Let $e$ on $\Omega$ denote the composition $e(v,s)$. Let $\sigma$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ stress matrix field, let $\tau$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ matrix field, and suppose $\sigma=-pI+\tau$, where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity. For a scalar field $h$, define $(\nabla h)_i:=\partial_{x_i}h$; define $L:=\nabla u$ by $L_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D:=(L+L^T)/2$, and $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Define $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ for matrices, $\operatorname{div}q:=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}q_i$, and $\operatorname{div}(q/T)$ componentwise. Put $a_m:=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, $k:=|u|^2/2$, and $E:=e+k$. The fields $u,q,b$ are vector-valued and $r$ is scalar-valued.

Assume there is a contact traction $t_c(t,y,n)\in\mathbb R^3$ depending on a surface only through its point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\in S^2$, continuous in $(y,n)$ and uniformly bounded near each point. Assume its local force balance $\int_{\partial P}t_c(t,y,\nu_P(y))\,dS_y+\int_P\rho(t,y)(b(t,y)-a_m(t,y))\,dy=0$ for every nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $P$ whose closure is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Surface integrals use Euclidean surface measure with chart area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. Suppose the unique Cauchy stress supplied by this contact balance satisfies $t_c(t,y,n)=\sigma(t,y)n$ and has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the contact result alone does not imply that regularity.

Assume the pointwise continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and, for every such material subdomain $V$ and every $t\in I$, the integral balances
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal, $\times$ is the ordinary vector cross product, and all fields are continuous up to the swept closures. The angular-momentum balance gives $\sigma=\sigma^T$, and the local internal-energy equation supplied by these hypotheses is $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$. Define the entropy residual $\mathcal G:=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. Then
$$\mathcal G=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}.$$
At any state with $e_{ss}>0$, a unique local $C^1$ branch $s(v,T)$ satisfies $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$; the local Helmholtz function $a(v,T):=e(v,s(v,T))-Ts(v,T)$ then satisfies $a_T=-s$ and $a_v=-p$. The entropy identity does not assert $\mathcal G\ge0$ and makes no empirical claim. In the physical SI interpretation, $\rho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $v$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $e,k,E$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p,\sigma,\tau,t_c$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the entropy formula along a material trajectory. The chain rule gives $D_ts=(c_v/T)D_tT-(R/\rho)D_t\rho$. The continuity equation in [L1] is $D_t\rho+\rho\theta=0$, so $D_t\rho=-\rho\theta$. Hence $\rho T D_ts=\rho c_vD_tT+\rho RT\theta=\rho c_vD_tT+p\theta$.

The local internal-energy equation from [L1] and $\sigma=-pI_3+\tau$ give $\rho D_te=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$, since $I_3:D=\theta$. With $e=c_vT$, this is the stated full temperature balance.
If $\tau=q=r=0$, the temperature equation gives $D_tT=-(R/c_v)T\theta$. Substitution in the differentiated entropy formula of step 1.1 yields $D_ts=-(R\theta)+(R\theta)=0$.

On a trajectory with entropy value $s_0$, solve the entropy formula for $T/T_{\mathrm{ref}}=\exp((s_0-s_{\mathrm{ref}})/c_v)(\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{ref}})^{R/c_v}$. Using $p=\rho RT$, collect powers of $\rho$ to obtain $p=K(s_0)\rho^{1+R/c_v}$ with the displayed positive $K(s_0)$. Its dependence on $s_0$ shows that different entropy levels can have different coefficients.

Assume the complete smooth material, state, contact and mass/momentum/angular-momentum/total-energy balance hypotheses of the mathematical Gibbs-entropy identity, including $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stated in Facts & Assumptions. Let $R>0$ be a specific gas constant and $c_v>0$ a constant specific heat at constant volume, both in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. Choose reference values $T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$ in $\mathrm K$, $\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and $s_{\mathrm{ref}}$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. On $v>0,\ s\in\mathbb R$, adopt
$$ T(v,s)=T_{\mathrm{ref}}\exp\!\left(\frac{s-s_{\mathrm{ref}}}{c_v}\right) \left(\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{ref}}v}\right)^{R/c_v},\qquad e(v,s)=c_vT(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=\frac{R\,T(v,s)}{v}. $$
These formulas give $T=e_s>0$, $p=-e_v$, and $e\in C^2((0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$; equivalently, with $\rho=1/v$, $s=s_{\mathrm{ref}}+c_v\ln(T/T_{\mathrm{ref}})-R\ln(\rho/\rho_{\mathrm{ref}})$ and $p=\rho RT$. The logarithms have dimensionless arguments.

For a smooth solution, define $\theta=\operatorname{div}u$, $\sigma=-pI_3+\tau$, and the local entropy residual $\mathcal G=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. The temperature balance is
$$ \rho c_vD_tT=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r. $$
On the additional adiabatic, inviscid, unsourced branch $\tau=0,\ q=0,\ r=0$, one has $D_ts=0$. Along any trajectory on which the entropy value is $s_0$, the pressure law is
$$ p=K(s_0)\rho^\gamma,\qquad \gamma=1+\frac{R}{c_v},\qquad K(s_0)=RT_{\mathrm{ref}}\exp\!\left(\frac{s_0-s_{\mathrm{ref}}}{c_v}\right) \rho_{\mathrm{ref}}^{-R/c_v}>0. $$
The factor $K(s_0)$ can differ between trajectories with different entropy values. The gas closure is an adopted model, and the adiabatic conclusion does not apply when viscous work, heat conduction, or heat supply is present.

$$ \rho c_vD_tT=-p\theta+\tau:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r. $$
On the additional adiabatic, inviscid, unsourced branch $\tau=0,\ q=0,\ r=0$, one has $D_ts=0$. Along any trajectory on which the entropy value is $s_0$, the pressure law is
$$ p=K(s_0)\rho^\gamma,\qquad \gamma=1+\frac{R}{c_v},\qquad K(s_0)=RT_{\mathrm{ref}}\exp\!\left(\frac{s_0-s_{\mathrm{ref}}}{c_v}\right) \rho_{\mathrm{ref}}^{-R/c_v}>0. $$
The factor $K(s_0)$ can differ between trajectories with different entropy values. The gas closure is an adopted model, and the adiabatic conclusion does not apply when viscous work, heat conduction, or heat supply is present.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Let $V\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $V$ lying locally on one side of that graph. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline V\subset U$. Let $\phi:U\to\phi(U)$ be a bijection onto an open image with $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ both $C^1$, and let $f:\phi(U)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator is Riemann integrable by the zero-extension convention; a set has content zero when it has finite cube covers of arbitrarily small total volume. Then $V$ and $\phi(V)$ are bounded open sets with locally $C^1$ graph boundaries, their compact closures are Jordan measurable, $\partial V$ and $\phi(\partial V)$ have content zero, and

$$\int_{\phi(V)}f(x)\,dx=\int_{\phi(\overline V)}f(x)\,dx.$$

Thus a balance integral over an open $C^1$ material region agrees with the compact-Jordan integral on its closure after a $C^1$ diffeomorphic motion.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

The pointwise model equation in [A1] holds on the same fixed spatial region used in the energy integral (or on its periodic lift). Dot $\rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma$ with $u$. The component product rule gives $u_i\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}(\sigma_{ij}u_i)-\sigma_{ij}\partial_{x_j}u_i$, while $D_t(|u|^2/2)=u\cdot D_tu$. Since $\rho_0$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, this yields
$$ \partial_t\left(\frac{\rho_0|u|^2}{2}\right) +\operatorname{div}\left(\frac{\rho_0|u|^2}{2}u-\sigma^Tu\right) =-\sigma:\nabla u. $$

Fix $t$ and put $e=\rho_0|u|^2/2$ and $F=eu-\sigma^Tu$. In the periodic case, [F2] integrates each $\partial_jF_j$ first in $x_j$; opposite endpoint values agree, so $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=0$. In the bounded-domain case, $F$ is $C^1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$ and vanishes on $\partial\Omega$. Here is a direct zero-flux argument requiring no additional choice axiom. Use a finite cubic mesh of side $h$ in a fixed containing box and let $P_h$ be the union of the closed mesh cubes contained in $\Omega$. Let $B_h$ be the union of mesh cubes at distance at most $4\sqrt3h$ from $\partial\Omega$. Since this compact boundary has content zero by [F1], $\operatorname{vol}(B_h)\to0$: for any finite open box cover of the boundary, all sufficiently small $B_h$ lie in that cover, and such covers have arbitrarily small total volume. Also $\Omega\setminus P_h\subseteq B_h$. Applying [F2] on each cube of $P_h$ and cancelling common faces expresses $\int_{P_h}\operatorname{div}F$ as the sum of the exposed face integrals. Each exposed face is within $2\sqrt3h$ of the boundary. The derivative of $F$ is bounded by a constant $M$ on a compact neighborhood of that boundary, so the segment mean-value estimate [F3] and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ give $|F|\le2\sqrt3Mh$ on these faces for sufficiently small $h$. Their number is at most six times the number of cubes in $B_h$. Thus [F4] bounds the absolute sum of face integrals by $12\sqrt3M\operatorname{vol}(B_h)\to0$. The omitted volume integral is bounded by $\sup_{\overline\Omega}|\operatorname{div}F|\operatorname{vol}(B_h)\to0$. Hence $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=0$ also in this case.

On every compact time interval, $e$ and $e_t$ are continuous on its product with $\overline\Omega$. For fixed $t$ and small nonzero $k$, the mean-value estimate gives
$$\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}\left|\frac{e(t+k,x)-e(t,x)}{k}-e_t(t,x)\right|\le\sup_{\substack{|s-t|\le|k|\\x\in\overline\Omega}}|e_t(s,x)-e_t(t,x)|\longrightarrow0,$$
by [F3]. Every spatial integral exists by [F1] or rectangular continuity. Multiplying the displayed uniform error by the finite volume and using [F4] proves $E_k'(t)=\int_\Omega e_t(t,x)\,dx$; the same estimate without the quotient proves continuity of this derivative. Integrating step 1.1 spatially and applying step 2.1 therefore gives $E_k'(t)=-\int_\Omega\sigma:\nabla u\,dx$.

Using the Frobenius contraction and $|D|^2=D:D$ defined in the Statement, write $
abla u=D+W$, where $W=(
abla u-
abla u^T)/2$ is skew-symmetric. A symmetric matrix is Frobenius-orthogonal to a skew-symmetric matrix, so $D:W=0$. The stress law gives $\sigma:
abla u=(-pI_3+2\mu D):(D+W)=-p\,\operatorname{div}u+2\mu|D|^2=2\mu|D|^2$. Thus $ rac{d}{dt}E_k=-2\mu\int_\Omega|D|^2\,dx$. The spatial dissipation integral is continuous in time by the same uniform-continuity estimate as step 3.1. Applying [F2] in time from $t_1$ to $t_2$ proves the stated energy equality and nonincrease because $\mu\ge0$.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval containing $0$. Use SI units: time is measured in seconds, spatial coordinates and lengths in metres, $\rho_0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mu$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. A bounded $C^1$ domain means a bounded open set locally on one side of a continuously differentiable boundary graph. The fixed spatial region $\Omega$ is either a nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ or one rectangular period cell $[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$ with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres. In the bounded-domain case, let $\mathcal O\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open and contain $I\times\overline\Omega$, and suppose $u\in C^2(\mathcal O,\mathbb R^3)$ and $p\in C^1(\mathcal O,\mathbb R)$. In the periodic case, take $u$ and $p$ on $I\times\mathbb R^3$, periodic with their derivatives on opposite faces of the stated cell. In either case suppose the smooth fields satisfy on the stated spacetime domain the pointwise constant-density incompressible Newtonian model equations
$$ \rho=\rho_0>0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $\mu\ge0$ is constant, the body force is zero, $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^T)/2$, $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, and $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is the rowwise divergence. In the bounded-domain case impose the no-slip condition $u=0$ on $I\times\partial\Omega$; in the periodic case the model equations hold on the periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$.

For matrices $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ define the Frobenius contraction $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ and the squared norm $|D|^2:=D:D=\sum_{i,j=1}^3D_{ij}^2$. Let $E_k(t)=\frac{\rho_0}{2}\int_\Omega |u(t,x)|^2\,dx$, using one period cell in the periodic case. For every $t_1<t_2$ in $I$,
$$ E_k(t_2)+2\mu\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\int_\Omega |D(t,x)|^2\,dx\,dt=E_k(t_1). $$
Thus $E_k$ is nonincreasing; strict decay is not claimed when $D$ vanishes. The theorem is conditional on an actual smooth solution and supplies no existence or long-time regularity result.

Use SI units: time is measured in seconds, spatial coordinates and lengths in metres, $\rho_0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mu$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. A bounded $C^1$ domain means a bounded open set locally on one side of a continuously differentiable boundary graph. The fixed spatial region $\Omega$ is either a nonempty bounded $C^1$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ or one rectangular period cell $[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$ with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres. In the bounded-domain case, let $\mathcal O\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open and contain $I\times\overline\Omega$, and suppose $u\in C^2(\mathcal O,\mathbb R^3)$ and $p\in C^1(\mathcal O,\mathbb R)$. In the periodic case, take $u$ and $p$ on $I\times\mathbb R^3$, periodic with their derivatives on opposite faces of the stated cell. In either case suppose the smooth fields satisfy on the stated spacetime domain the pointwise constant-density incompressible Newtonian model equations
$$ \rho=\rho_0>0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $\mu\ge0$ is constant, the body force is zero, $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^T)/2$, $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, and $\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is the rowwise divergence. In the bounded-domain case impose the no-slip condition $u=0$ on $I\times\partial\Omega$; in the periodic case the model equations hold on the periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$.

For matrices $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ define the Frobenius contraction $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ and the squared norm $|D|^2:=D:D=\sum_{i,j=1}^3D_{ij}^2$. Let $E_k(t)=\frac{\rho_0}{2}\int_\Omega |u(t,x)|^2\,dx$, using one period cell in the periodic case. For every $t_1<t_2$ in $I$,
$$ E_k(t_2)+2\mu\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\int_\Omega |D(t,x)|^2\,dx\,dt=E_k(t_1). $$
Thus $E_k$ is nonincreasing; strict decay is not claimed when $D$ vanishes. The theorem is conditional on an actual smooth solution and supplies no existence or long-time regularity result.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires t_1<t_2 in the open interval I; it claims no value at an interval endpoint.

Let $\operatorname{Sym}(3)=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and let $I_3$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $D\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ set $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, and $|D_0|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^3(D_0)_{ij}^2$. For $\mu\ge0$, $\zeta\in\mathbb R$, $K\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $g\in\mathbb R^3$, and $T>0$, define the pointwise Newtonian/Fourier residual
$$\mathcal G(D,g,T)=\frac{2\mu|D_0|^2+\zeta\theta^2}{T}+\frac{g^T\operatorname{sym}(K)g}{T^2},\qquad \operatorname{sym}(K)=\frac{K+K^T}{2}.$$
Here $g$ is the temperature-gradient value; in SI units $D$ is in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $g$ in $\mathrm{K\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathcal G$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$. The false assertion is that $\mathcal G(D,g,T)\ge0$ for every such $D,g,T$ whenever $\mu\ge0$, independently of the value of $\zeta$.

boundaries.reason: The Counterexample fixes T>0 and theta nonzero, so the witness has nonempty local data.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open domain for the model fields. Let $e\in C^2(\mathcal U)$ be the local specific-energy relation on an open $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with state coordinates $(v,s)$, $T=e_s$, and $p=-e_v$; each state partial derivative holds the other coordinate fixed. Fix $(v_b,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ with $T_b>0$ and $e_{ss}(v_b,s_b)>0$, set $\rho_b=1/v_b$, and take a barotropic pressure law $P\in C^1((0,\infty))$ that agrees with $p(1/\rho,s_b)$ on an open density interval $J_\rho\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\rho_b$, with $(1/\rho,s_b)\in\mathcal U$ for every $\rho\in J_\rho$. This is the fixed-entropy restriction of the adopted local state relation. The smooth barotropic Euler model is linearized about the uniform rest state $(\rho,u)=(\rho_b,0)$. For $C^2$ perturbation fields $\delta\rho:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $w:I\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the first variation at $\varepsilon=0$ after $\rho=\rho_b+\varepsilon\delta\rho$, $u=\varepsilon w$ is
$$ \partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_b\operatorname{div}w=0,\qquad \rho_b\partial_tw+P'(\rho_b)\nabla\delta\rho=0,\qquad \partial_{tt}\delta\rho=c_s^2\Delta\delta\rho, \quad c_s^2=P'(\rho_b)=v_b^2e_{vv}(v_b,s_b). $$
The sign of $c_s^2$ is not assumed in the base model. If $c_s^2>0$, define $c_s=\sqrt{c_s^2}$. For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb R^3$, with $\omega=c_s|k|$, the fields
$$ \delta\rho=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t),\qquad w=\frac{\omega A}{\rho_b|k|^2}k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t) $$
solve the first-variation system for every real amplitude $A$. They are exact solutions of the linearized equations, not finite-amplitude approximations with an automatic error or lifespan bound. No empirical value of $c_s$ is asserted.

In SI units, $t$ is in seconds, $x$ in metres, $\rho_b,\delta\rho,A$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u,w,c_s$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $k$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $\omega$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $c_s^2$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. Use Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval of absolute time in seconds and $E$ is an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space measured in metres. A Newtonian Cartesian inertial chart is the event map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for every $t\in I$. Write $x$ for its spatial event coordinate; no assumption $0\in I$ is needed for this chart formula. Write $I_3$ for the $3\times3$ identity matrix and set $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Inertial-chart changes have the form $t'=t+t_0$, $x'=Qx+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is constant. A frame in this statement means such an adapted chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Fix one such chart and a nonempty open spatial coordinate region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. All derivatives below are Cartesian derivatives in this fixed chart; the positive coordinate rescaling defined below is not a change of observer.

For a scalar field $f$, $\nabla_x f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$.

For a vector field $u=(u_i)$, define $D_xu,D:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\operatorname{div}_xu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $\Delta_xu,D_tu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ by $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\operatorname{div}_xu=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $(\Delta_xu)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u$. The fields $D$ and $\operatorname{div}_xu$ have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Fix constants $\rho_0>0$, $\mu>0$, $U>0$, $L>0$, and $c>0$, and define $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, $\operatorname{Re}=UL/\nu$, and $\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$. In SI units, $[u]=[U]=[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[x]=[L]=\mathrm m$, $[\rho]=[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=[P(\rho)]=[p_{\mathrm{ref}}]=[\sigma]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\Theta]=[X]=[\operatorname{Re}]=[\operatorname{Ma}]=1$; thus the two ratios are dimensionless.

Define the dimensionless coordinates and their domains by
$$\Theta=\frac{Ut}{L},\qquad X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad I^*=\left\{\frac{Ut}{L}:t\in I\right\},\qquad \Omega^*=\left\{\frac{x}{L}:x\in\Omega\right\}.$$
The map $\Phi:I\times\Omega\to I^*\times\Omega^*$, $\Phi(t,x)=(Ut/L,x/L)$, is bijective with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)=(L\Theta/U,LX)$. The corresponding $X$-derivatives are defined by the same component formulas.

In the first, force-free branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time partial derivatives and continuous first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let the pressure field $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with continuous first spatial partial derivatives. Let the density field $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ be the constant $\rho_0$. Assume $\operatorname{div}_xu=0$ and the selected incompressible Newtonian equations
$$\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}_x\sigma,\qquad (\operatorname{div}_x\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij},$$
where $\sigma:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is stress, $p$ is the constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure, and the tension-positive stress convention identifies $\sigma n$ as traction on an outward unit normal $n$. Define $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{1}{U}u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr),\qquad p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{p\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},$$
for a constant reference pressure $p_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb R$. The scaled fields are dimensionless, $[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*]=1$, and have respectively the same stated velocity and spatial-pressure regularity. Equivalently, $u(t,x)=Uu^*(\Theta,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)$. The governing equations become exactly
$$\partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{inc}}^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

In the separate, unforced barotropic Euler branch, let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ and $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous partial derivatives through total order two, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have continuous derivatives through order two, with pressure measured in pascals. Set the potential $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ to the zero function. Assume
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0,\qquad \rho D_tu+\nabla_xP(\rho)=0,$$
and assume at the chosen reference density that $P'(\rho_0)=c^2>0$, where $[P'(\rho_0)]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Define $\rho^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to(0,\infty)$, $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$, and $p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$\rho^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{\rho\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{\rho_0},\qquad u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{U},\qquad p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{P\bigl(\rho_0\rho^*(\Theta,X)\bigr)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$
These scaled fields are dimensionless, $[\rho^*]=[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*]=1$, and have continuous partial derivatives through order two. The exact transformed mass and momentum equations are
$$\partial_\Theta\rho^*+\operatorname{div}_X(\rho^*u^*)=0,\qquad \partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\operatorname{Ma}^{-2}(\rho^*)^{-1}\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{bar}}^*.$$

Initial values are data on a slice $t=t_0\in I$; boundary values are data on a chosen subset $\Gamma\subseteq I\times\partial\Omega$ wherever the relevant traces exist. Extend $\Phi$ to $I\times\mathbb R^3$ by the same coordinate formula and put $S^*=\Phi(S)$ for any such initial or boundary data set $S$. If $g_u:S\to\mathbb R^3$, $g_p:S\to\mathbb R$, $g_\rho:S\to(0,\infty)$, and $g_P:S\to\mathbb R$ are prescribed velocity, incompressible pressure-multiplier, density, and barotropic-pressure data, respectively, define $g_u^*:S^*\to\mathbb R^3$, $g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*:S^*\to\mathbb R$, $g_\rho^*:S^*\to(0,\infty)$, and $g_{P,\mathrm{bar}}^*:S^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$g_u^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_u(t,x)}{U},\qquad g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_p(t,x)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},\qquad g_\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_\rho(t,x)}{\rho_0},\qquad g_{P,\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_P(t,x)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$
Here $g_p$ and $g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*$ apply to the incompressible branch, while $g_\rho$ and $g_P$ apply to the barotropic branch; a prescribed wall-velocity field uses the same velocity map. The spatial dilation takes each boundary trace portion to its image and preserves its outward Euclidean unit normal wherever that normal exists. For momentum density $m:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, with units $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, define $m^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ by
$$m^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{m(t,x)}{\rho_0U}=\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))u^*(\Phi(t,x)),$$
where $\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=1$ in the constant-density branch. Thus $m^*$ is dimensionless. Whenever the integrals exist, total momentum on corresponding spatial regions $A\subseteq\Omega$ and $A^*=A/L$ satisfies
$$\int_A \rho u\,dx=\rho_0UL^3\int_{A^*}\rho^*u^*\,dX.$$
The total momentum has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, as does its scale factor $\rho_0UL^3$.
Because $\Phi$ and each field-value scaling are invertible, these formulas carry any already-compatible initial or boundary data to the corresponding scaled data; they assert no compatibility or solvability beyond the selected model and its separate data assumptions. Thermal evolution and heat-flux scaling are not part of this calculation. The coefficient identities do not assert an incompressible or inviscid limit, an error bound, uniqueness, identical solutions for different geometries or rescaled data, or a turbulence threshold. They are conditional predictions of the adopted model formulations and are not experimental observations or proof that either model describes a material.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

derivations.claim: In both fields velocity has only an axial component independent of the axial coordinate; hence $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=0$. The plane momentum equation reduces to $\mu v''=-G$, and the pipe equation to $\mu(w''+r^{-1}w')=-G$ for $r>0$.

Integrating the plane equation twice gives $v(y)=-Gy^2/(2\mu)+C_1y+C_0$. The wall values determine $C_0=V_0$ and $C_1=(V_1-V_0)/h+Gh/(2\mu)$, yielding the stated profile uniquely. Its integral gives $Q_{\rm ch}$; differentiation and $\sigma_{xy}=\mu v'$ give both wall shear values.

Multiplication of the pipe equation by $r$ gives $(rw')'=-Gr/\mu$. Integration yields $w=-Gr^2/(4\mu)+C\log r+D$ on $r>0$. Full-disk $C^2$ regularity forces $C=0$, and $w(a)=0$ fixes $D=Ga^2/(4\mu)$, proving uniqueness within this ansatz. Integration with area element $2\pi r\,dr$ gives $Q_{\rm pipe}$; differentiation gives $\sigma_{rx}=-Gr/2$.

Time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish, so each field solves the stationary Navier–Stokes and corresponding steady Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice, without a limiting or small-parameter hypothesis. This says nothing about finite-device behavior or empirical validity. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. $$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$

This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by
