Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For any $\ell\in(0,R)$ and $z_0\in(-H,H)$, the closed material loop $X:\mathbb R\times[0,2\pi]\to D$ is
$$X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$

It satisfies $X(t,0)=X(t,2\pi)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$. Its circulation is
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}u(t,X(t,\theta))\cdot\partial_\theta X(t,\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2.$$

Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. For every fixed $t\in I$, define the spatial sections $u^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, $u^{[t]}(x)=u(t,x)$, and $\sigma^{[t]}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\sigma^{[t]}(x)=\sigma(t,x)$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For any $\ell\in(0,R)$ and $z_0\in(-H,H)$, the closed material loop $X:\mathbb R\times[0,2\pi]\to D$ is
$$X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$

It satisfies $X(t,0)=X(t,2\pi)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$. Its circulation is
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}u(t,X(t,\theta))\cdot\partial_\theta X(t,\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2.$$

Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

The equation is defined for symmetric matrix fields, while $w$ is evaluated only where $C$ is positive definite. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. derivations.claim: If $D\ne0$, then $\tau:D=2\eta(\dot\gamma)(D:D)=\eta(\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma^2\ge0$; if $D=0$, then $\tau=0$ and the contraction is $0$.

For finite $\dot\gamma$, the Carreau base $1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2$ is finite and at least $1$. By [F2], its real power is the exponential of a finite real number, hence is finite and positive by [F6]; the parameter inequalities then make both summands nonnegative.

If $\lambda>0$, the base $y=1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2$ increases from $1$ to $+\infty$ as $\dot\gamma$ runs from $0$ to $+\infty$. Put $q=(n-1)/2$. If $q>0$, [F2], [F3], [F5] and [F6] show $y\mapsto y^q$ is strictly increasing; for every $M>0$, $y>M^{1/q}$ implies $y^q>M$ by strict monotonicity and [F4], so $y^q\to+\infty$. If $q<0$, put $p=-q>0$; [F2] and [F6] give $y^q=1/y^p$, and for every $\rho>0$, $y>\rho^{-1/p}$ implies $0<y^q<\rho$, so $y^q\to0$. If $q=0$, [F2] and [F6] give $y^0>0$, while [F4] gives $y^0=y^0y^0$, hence $y^0=1$. Consequently the Carreau factor decreases to $0$, is constantly $1$, or increases without bound for $0<n<1$, $n=1$, or $n>1$, respectively. Since $\eta_0-\eta_\infty>0$, adding $\eta_\infty$ gives the stated limits and monotonicities. If $\lambda=0$ or $\eta_0=\eta_\infty$, direct substitution gives a constant.

Since $\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2>0$ and is finite, [F2] and [F6] show that its real power is finite and positive; multiplication by $m>0$ proves the regularized viscosity claim. For $\dot\gamma>0$, the unregularized law has $|\tau|=2m\dot\gamma^{n-1}|D|=\sqrt2m\dot\gamma^n$. For $n>0$, [F2], [F3], [F5] and positivity from [F6] make $x\mapsto x^n$ strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$; given $\rho>0$, choose $\delta=\rho^{1/n}>0$. If $0<\dot\gamma<\delta$, then $\dot\gamma^n<\delta^n=\rho$ by [F4]. Thus $\dot\gamma^n\to0$ as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, so the zero extension of $\tau$ is continuous. If $0<n<1$, put $p=1-n>0$. By [F2] and [F6], $\dot\gamma^{-p}=1/\dot\gamma^p$. For any $M>0$, choose $\delta=(m/M)^{1/p}>0$. When $0<\dot\gamma<\delta$, monotonicity gives $\dot\gamma^p<\delta^p=m/M$, so $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{-p}>M$. Hence $\eta_U\to+\infty$ as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$.

By [F1], $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. Orthogonality gives $(QDQ^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}(QDQ^{\mathsf T})=QD^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T}$, so cyclicity of the finite matrix trace yields $D^*:D^*=\operatorname{tr}(QD^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(D^{\mathsf T}DQ^{\mathsf T}Q)=D:D$. Thus $\dot\gamma^*=\dot\gamma$. Consequently $\tau^*=2\eta(\dot\gamma^*)D^*=Q(2\eta(\dot\gamma)D)Q^{\mathsf T}=Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$; the zero-rate extension obeys the same identity.

derivations.claim: The norm is convex by the triangle inequality and positive homogeneity. For $0\le s\le1$, $|sD+(1-s)E|^2\le(s|D|+(1-s)|E|)^2\le s|D|^2+(1-s)|E|^2$, the second inequality following from $s(1-s)(|D|-|E|)^2\ge0$. Thus $\Phi$ is convex; it is finite everywhere and $\Phi\ge0$, so the supporting-inequality set defined in the Statement is well-defined.

Let $D\ne0$. For every $E\in\mathcal S_0$, expansion of $|E-D|^2\ge0$ gives $|E|^2\ge|D|^2+2D:(E-D)$, while Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|E|\ge|D|+(D/|D|):(E-D)$. Multiplying by $\mu_p$ and $\tau_y$ and adding shows $\Phi(E)\ge\Phi(D)+(2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|):(E-D)$, so the stated nonzero graph value belongs to the set defined in the Statement.

If $\xi$ belongs to the set defined as $\partial\Phi(D)$ with $D\ne0$, apply its supporting inequality to $E=D+hH$. For $h>0$ division by $h$ gives $\xi:H\le(\Phi(D+hH)-\Phi(D))/h$; for $h<0$ the reversed inequality gives $\xi:H\ge(\Phi(D+hH)-\Phi(D))/h$. The identity $(|D+hH|-|D|)/h=(2D:H+h|H|^2)/(|D+hH|+|D|)\to(D:H)/|D|$ and the quadratic expansion in step 1.2 show that both limits equal $(2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|):H$. Since this holds for every $H\in\mathcal S_0$, nondegeneracy of the Frobenius product gives $\xi=2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|$.

At $D=0$, the supporting inequality is $\mu_p|E|^2+\tau_y|E|\ge\xi:E$ for every $E$. If $|\xi|\le\tau_y$, Cauchy–Schwarz proves it. Conversely, if $|\xi|>\tau_y$, choose $E=t\xi/|\xi|$; the inequality would imply $|\xi|\le\mu_pt+\tau_y$ for every $t>0$, which fails for sufficiently small $t$ when $\mu_p>0$, and fails for every $t>0$ when $\mu_p=0$. Hence $\partial\Phi(0)$ is exactly the stated stress ball, proving $\mathcal B=\partial\Phi$ also at zero.

For $\tau_i\in\partial\Phi(D_i)$, the defining inequality gives $\Phi(D_2)\ge\Phi(D_1)+\tau_1:(D_2-D_1)$ and $\Phi(D_1)\ge\Phi(D_2)+\tau_2:(D_1-D_2)$. Adding and cancelling the potential values yields $(\tau_1-\tau_2):(D_1-D_2)\ge0$.
If $D\ne0$, then $\tau:D=2\mu_p|D|^2+\tau_y|D|\ge0$; if $D=0$, then $\tau:D=0$ for every point of the stress ball.

Conjugation by $Q\in SO(3)$ preserves symmetry, trace, Frobenius norm, and the Frobenius product. Substituting $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ into each nonzero formula therefore gives $Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$; at $D=0$, the full ball maps onto itself because $|Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}|=|\tau|$. This proves the stated rotation-equivariance.

risk_review.notes: Read Statement, A1 and all seven proof steps against the earlier reviewed defining graph. Convexity follows from triangle inequality and the squared-norm identity; the supporting inequalities give membership off zero and the full closed stress ball at zero. For the converse at zero, E=t xi/|xi| violates the inequality for sufficiently small positive t, including mu_p=0 separately. At nonzero D the two signs of h identify every directional pairing and hence the unique stress. Adding the two supporting inequalities proves monotonicity; power is nonnegative including zero and both coefficients zero. Orthogonal conjugation maps the entire zero-rate ball onto itself. All variables lie in the five-dimensional trace-free symmetric space, finite choices only; no existence, empirical or PDE claims. No diagrams or statement links. No repair needed.

Use SI units and an oriented Euclidean three-space with Cartesian coordinates. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ denote the real $3\times3$ matrices and $I_3$ the identity matrix. Write $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$. The generalized Newtonian branch is incompressible, so $\theta=0$ and $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. Define the shear-rate scalar $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$, with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and let $\eta(\dot\gamma)$ be a finite nonnegative viscosity with units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. The deviatoric stress is $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, in $\mathrm{Pa}$; no pressure term is included.

For $a>0$ and $r\in\mathbb R$, use the positive-base real power $a^r:=\exp(r\log_{\mathrm{nat}}a)$, where $\log_{\mathrm{nat}}$ denotes the natural logarithm. The formulas apply this power to positive numerical values in the fixed SI units, with the resulting unit exponents carried by the listed parameter units. This is the convention in the viscosity formulas below; the unregularized form is evaluated only when $\dot\gamma>0$. The integral logarithm $\log$ used in the conformation branch is defined separately there.

Two named viscosity choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda\ge0$ in $\mathrm{s}$, and dimensionless $n>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n>0$. For comparison, the unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$. When $0<n<1$, this viscosity diverges as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, although the extended stress may remain continuous.

For the Bingham branch use the Frobenius norm just defined, $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and yield parameter $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Its set-valued deviatoric stress graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)=\begin{cases}\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\\{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0.\end{cases}
$$

The value at rest is therefore a whole stress ball when $\tau_y>0$. The chosen Frobenius normalization fixes the numerical convention for $\tau_y$; a source using a differently normalized second invariant requires a corresponding parameter conversion.

For the conformation branch, set $\mathrm{Sym}(3)=\{M\in M_3(\mathbb R):M=M^{\mathsf T}\}$ and
$$\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)=\{M\in\mathrm{Sym}(3):v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\}.$$
On the swept open set $\Omega=\{(t,x)\in I\times\mathbb R^3:x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)\}$ from the smooth-motion definition, let the dimensionless conformation field be $C\in C^1(\Omega;\mathrm{Sym}(3))$. Thus $C$ is a $C^1$ matrix-valued field, and $D_tC=\partial_tC+u\cdot\nabla C$ is defined componentwise. The ambient state space for the evolution equation is $\mathrm{Sym}(3)$; the stored-energy function below is defined only on the admissible subset $\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)$, and this definition does not assume that a solution remains in that subset along a trajectory.

For each $C\in\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)$, the finite-dimensional real spectral theorem supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis $v_1,v_2,v_3$ with $Cv_i=c_iv_i$. Positive definiteness gives $c_i=v_i^{\mathsf T}Cv_i>0$ for each unit eigenvector $v_i$, and determinant multiplicativity then gives $\det C=c_1c_2c_3>0$. Define $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ by $\log r=\int_1^r ds/s$. Let $G>0$ be a modulus in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ a relaxation time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. On an incompressible motion, meaning $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}L=0$, adopt the conformation equation and stress and storage definitions

$$D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T}=-(C-I_3)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I_3),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).$$

Here both sides of the conformation equation have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are polymer and solvent stresses in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The equation is defined for symmetric matrix fields, while $w$ is evaluated only where $C$ is positive definite. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. They assert neither empirical validity for a particular material nor existence of a solution to a fluid partial differential equation.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

Let $A:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ solve the variational equation

$$A'(t)=C(t)A(t),\qquad A(t_0)=I_n,$$

on an interval $I$, where $C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ is continuous. Then every
matrix $A(t)$ is invertible. Equivalently, a fundamental matrix of the
variational equation is invertible at every time on its interval of definition.

Let $A$ be invertible. Then the inversion map is real Fr\'echet differentiable
at $A$, and for every direction $H$,

$$D\operatorname{inv}(A)[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For all $x,y>0$,

$$L(xy)=L(x)+L(y).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. For $r=1,2$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be such that every slice $\chi_t:U\to\chi_t(U)$ is a bijection with $C^2$ inverse and $J(t,a):=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$, where $D_a\chi$ is the matrix of reference-coordinate partial derivatives. Write $H(t,a):=(t,\chi(t,a))$ and $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. The map $H$ is injective and its derivative is block triangular with determinant $J>0$, so the inverse function theorem gives local $C^1$ inverses; injectivity makes them agree on overlaps. Hence $\Omega$ is open and the joint inverse $A(t,x):=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$ is $C^1$. Define $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, which is $C^1$. For any $C^1$ vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, let $D_xf$ be its matrix of spatial coordinate partial derivatives and define $D_tf:=\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$. Set $L:=D_xu$, $D:=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $W:=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}L$, and $a_m:=D_tu$. Here $\operatorname{tr}M:=\sum_iM_{ii}$ for a square matrix $M$, $I_3$ denotes the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and

$$SO(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

Let $Q\in C^2(I,SO(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, hold time fixed, and change spatial coordinates by $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$. This map preserves Euclidean distances and orientation because $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$ and $\det Q=1$; the coordinate change does not assert that the observer is inertial. Set $\chi^*(t,a):=Q(t)\chi(t,a)+c(t)$ and $\Omega^*:=\{(t,x^*):t\in I,\ x^*=\chi^*(t,a)\text{ for some }a\in U\}$. Define the transformed velocity, material derivative, rate tensors and acceleration from $\chi^*$ by the same formulas on $\Omega^*$; in particular, $D_t^*f=\partial_tf+(D_{x^*}f)u^*$ and $a_m^*:=D_t^*u^*$. For corresponding points $x=\chi(t,a)$ and $x^*=\chi^*(t,a)$, the transformed fields satisfy

$$u^*(t,x^*)=Q'(t)x+Q(t)u(t,x)+c'(t),\qquad L^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)L(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},$$

$$D^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)D(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad W^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)W(t,x)Q(t)^{\mathsf T}+Q'(t)Q(t)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \theta^*(t,x^*)=\theta(t,x).$$

Thus $D$ transforms objectively, meaning its transformed tensor components obey $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ under every such $Q,c$; $W$ acquires the observer spin $Q'Q^{\mathsf T}$ and is not objective under general time-dependent rotations. If $a_m:=D_tu$ is the material acceleration, then

$$a_m^*(t,x^*)=Q(t)a_m(t,x)+2Q'(t)u(t,x)+Q''(t)x+c''(t).$$

When $Q'=0$ and $c''=0$, the acceleration formula reduces to $a_m^*=Qa_m$. These are mathematical kinematic identities and assert no force law or balance equation.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Since $u$ and $x$ are $C^1$, $L(t)=\nabla u(t,x(t))$ is continuous on the compact interval $[0,T]$. Applying [F1] gives a unique $C^1$ solution $Z'=LZ$, $Z(0)=I_3$ on all of $[0,T]$; by [F2], each $Z(t)$ is invertible.

Set $x^*(t)=Q(t)x(t)+c(t)$, and on the open set $\{(t,y):t\in J,\ Q(t)^{\mathsf T}(y-c(t))\in\Omega\}$ define $u^*(t,y)=Q'(t)z+Q(t)u(t,z)+c'(t)$, where $z=Q(t)^{\mathsf T}(y-c(t))$. These are $C^1$ maps, and product differentiation gives $(x^*)'=u^*(t,x^*)$. At fixed time the chain rule gives $\nabla_yu^*=(Q'+Q\nabla u)Q^{\mathsf T}$, which along $x^*$ is precisely the stated $L^*$. Differentiating $QQ^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ shows that $Q'Q^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric, so $D^*:=(L^*+(L^*)^{\mathsf T})/2=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. The path $C^*=QCQ^{\mathsf T}$ satisfies $(C^*)'=QC'Q^{\mathsf T}+Q'CQ^{\mathsf T}+QC(Q')^{\mathsf T}$. Substitution cancels the observer-derivative terms and gives $(C^*)'-L^*C^*-C^*(L^*)^{\mathsf T}=Q(C'-LC-CL^{\mathsf T})Q^{\mathsf T}=-(C^*-I_3)/\lambda$. Thus the trajectory equation is covariant at the stated regularity.
By [F3] and the chain rule along $Z$, $(Z^{-1})'=-Z^{-1}Z'Z^{-1}=-Z^{-1}L$; transposing gives $(Z^{-\mathsf T})'=-L^{\mathsf T}Z^{-\mathsf T}$.

Define $Y(t)=e^{t/\lambda}Z(t)^{-1}C(t)Z(t)^{-\mathsf T}$. Product differentiation using [F4], then substitution of the equation for $C'$ and the identities in step 2.1, cancels the $LC$ and $CL^{\mathsf T}$ terms and yields $Y'(t)=\frac1\lambda e^{t/\lambda}Z(t)^{-1}Z(t)^{-\mathsf T}$.

Fix a nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$ and set $f_v(t)=v^{\mathsf T}Y(t)v$. This function is $C^1$ on $[0,T]$ and step 3.1 gives $f_v'(t)=e^{t/\lambda}|Z(t)^{-\mathsf T}v|^2/\lambda>0$. For $t>0$, [F11] on $[0,t]$ gives $f_v(t)>f_v(0)=v^{\mathsf T}C_0v>0$; the same positivity at $t=0$ is the initial hypothesis. As $Y$ is symmetric and $v$ was arbitrary, $Y(t)$ is positive definite for every $t\in[0,T]$. The identity $C=e^{-t/\lambda}ZYZ^{\mathsf T}$ and invertibility of $Z$ then give $v^{\mathsf T}Cv=e^{-t/\lambda}(Z^{\mathsf T}v)^{\mathsf T}Y(Z^{\mathsf T}v)>0$ for every nonzero $v$.

By step 4.1, $C(t)$ is positive definite for every $t\in[0,T]$. Fix such a time and write $C=C(t)$. By [F6], write $C=U\operatorname{diag}(c_1,c_2,c_3)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $c_i>0$. Determinant multiplicativity and $UU^{\mathsf T}=I_3$ give $\det C=c_1c_2c_3$; finite-sum trace cyclicity gives $\operatorname{tr}C=\sum_i c_i$; hence [F7] gives $\log\det C=\sum_i\log c_i$. For each $c>0$, [F5] gives $\log c=\int_1^c dt/t$: if $c>1$, then $\log c<c-1$ because $1/t<1$ on the interior of $[1,c]$; if $0<c<1$, then $\log c=-\int_c^1dt/t<-(1-c)=c-1$ because $1/t>1$ on the interior of $[c,1]$; at $c=1$ the integral is zero. Thus $c-\log c-1\ge0$, with equality exactly at $c=1$, so $w(C)=\frac G2\sum_i(c_i-\log c_i-1)\ge0$, with equality exactly when all $c_i=1$, that is, $C=I_3$.

By step 4.1, $C(t)$ is positive definite for every $t\in[0,T]$. Fix such a time and write $C=C(t)$. By [F6], write $C=U\operatorname{diag}(c_1,c_2,c_3)U^{\mathsf T}$ with $c_i>0$. The unique positive square root and inverse square root in [F8] are $U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{c_i})U^{\mathsf T}$ and $U\operatorname{diag}(c_i^{-1/2})U^{\mathsf T}$, respectively. Thus $C^{-1}=U\operatorname{diag}(c_i^{-1})U^{\mathsf T}$ and $\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6=\sum_{i=1}^3(c_i+c_i^{-1}-2)=\sum_{i=1}^3(\sqrt{c_i}-c_i^{-1/2})^2\ge0$.

Since $C$ is positive definite by step 4.1 and $\det C>0$ by step 5.1, Jacobi's formula and the derivative of logarithm in [F5] give $\frac{d}{dt}w(C)=\frac G2\operatorname{tr}((I_3-C^{-1})C')$. Substituting [A1] and multiplying out gives
$\operatorname{tr}((I_3-C^{-1})(LC+CL^{\mathsf T}))=\operatorname{tr}(LC)+\operatorname{tr}(CL^{\mathsf T})-\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}LC)-\operatorname{tr}(L^{\mathsf T})$.
The finite-sum identity $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ and $C^{\mathsf T}=C$ give $\operatorname{tr}(CL^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}(LC)$, $\operatorname{tr}(C^{-1}LC)=\operatorname{tr}L$, and $\operatorname{tr}(L^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{tr}L$. Also $(C-I_3):D=\operatorname{tr}((C-I_3)L)=\operatorname{tr}(LC)-\operatorname{tr}L$, since the contraction of a symmetric matrix with the skew part of $L$ is zero. Therefore the displayed linear term is $2(C-I_3):D$. Direct multiplication gives $(I_3-C^{-1})(C-I_3)=C+C^{-1}-2I_3$, so its trace is $\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6$. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}w=G(C-I_3):D-\frac{G}{2\lambda}(\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6)$.

From [A1], $(\tau_s+\tau_p):D=2\eta_sD:D+G(C-I_3):D$. Subtracting the derivative in step 6.1 gives the identity in the Statement; it is nonnegative by $\eta_s\ge0$, $D:D\ge0$, and step 5.2. Since $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ and $C^*=QCQ^{\mathsf T}$, the stress definitions give $\tau_s^*=Q\tau_sQ^{\mathsf T}$ and $\tau_p^*=Q\tau_pQ^{\mathsf T}$; trace and determinant invariance give $w(C^*)=w(C)$.

citations.quote: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Its swept open region is $\Omega=\{(t,x):x\in\chi_t(U)\}$, its inverse label is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$. A branch is incompressible when $\theta=0$, so $D$ is symmetric and trace-free. Write $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$ for the Frobenius contraction and $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$ for its norm. Define $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D=D^{\mathsf T},\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)=\{C\in M_3(\mathbb R):C=C^{\mathsf T},z^{\mathsf T}Cz>0\text{ for every }z\ne0\}$. A rigid observer change is $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$ with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$, $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, and $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. A second-order tensor transforms as $S^*=QSQ^{\mathsf T}$; a constitutive response is objective when it obeys this rule at corresponding events.

For a generalized Newtonian branch, define

$$
\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2},\qquad \tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D,
$$

where $\eta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is finite and continuous.

Here $\tau_y$ is, by definition, the radius of the Frobenius stress ball at rest; other invariant normalizations require a corresponding parameter conversion. The graph is single-valued for $D\ne0$ and set-valued at rest.

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be the real $3\times3$ matrices. For $M=(M_{ij})\in M_3(\mathbb R)$, define its trace by $\operatorname{tr}M=\sum_{i=1}^3M_{ii}$, and let $I_3$ be the $3\times3$ identity matrix, with diagonal entries $1$ and all other entries $0$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A material motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ whose slices $\chi_t(a)=\chi(t,a)$ are orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphisms onto their images, with $\chi(0,a)=a$. Its swept open region is $\Omega=\{(t,x):x\in\chi_t(U)\}$, its inverse label is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$. A branch is incompressible when $\theta=0$, so $D$ is symmetric and trace-free. Write $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$ for the Frobenius contraction and $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$ for its norm. Define $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D=D^{\mathsf T},\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)=\{C\in M_3(\mathbb R):C=C^{\mathsf T},z^{\mathsf T}Cz>0\text{ for every }z\ne0\}$. A rigid observer change is $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$ with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$, $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, and $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. A second-order tensor transforms as $S^*=QSQ^{\mathsf T}$; a constitutive response is objective when it obeys this rule at corresponding events.

For the generalized Newtonian and Bingham branches, require $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ throughout $\Omega$, so $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. In these branches, $\tau$ is a symmetric deviatoric extra stress, meaning $\operatorname{tr}\tau=0$; the total tension-positive Cauchy stress may additionally contain an isotropic pressure. In the conformation branch, $\tau_p$ and $\tau_s$ denote the polymer and solvent stresses separately and the pressure is a Lagrange multiplier. Stress is measured in Pa, $D$ and shear rate in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and a rate of stress power per volume in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$.

For a generalized Newtonian branch, define

$$
\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2},\qquad \tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D,
$$

where $\eta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is finite and continuous. Two permitted scalar choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda_C\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n_C-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda_C\ge0$ in seconds, and dimensionless $n_C>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n_R-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}^{n_R}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n_R>0$. The unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n_R-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$, so for $0<n_R<1$ the viscosity diverges at zero rate even though the extended stress can be continuous.

For the Bingham branch, let $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$ and $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Adopt $\tau\in\mathcal B(D)$, where the set-valued graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)= \begin{cases} \{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\ \{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0, \end{cases}
$$

where $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is the space of trace-free symmetric $3\times3$ real matrices. Here $\tau_y$ is, by definition, the radius of the Frobenius stress ball at rest; other invariant normalizations require a corresponding parameter conversion. The graph is single-valued for $D\ne0$ and set-valued at rest.

For an isothermal conformation branch, let $K=[t_0,t_1]\subset I$ be a compact interval with $t_0<t_1$. A pathline on $K$ is a continuously differentiable curve $x:K\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $(t,x(t))\in\Omega$ and $x'(t)=u(t,x(t))$ for every $t\in K$; derivatives at the endpoints are one-sided. Along this pathline, the material derivative of $C$ is its ordinary derivative, $D_tC(t,x(t)):=\frac{d}{dt}C(t)$. Set $L(t)=\nabla u(t,x(t))$ and $D(t)=(L(t)+L(t)^{\mathsf T})/2$. Let $G>0$ be a modulus in Pa, $\lambda>0$ a relaxation time in seconds, $\eta_s\ge0$ a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and $T_0>0$ a fixed temperature in K. $$
\frac{dC}{dt}=LC+CL^{\mathsf T}-(C-I_3)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I_3),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).

The polymer and solvent stresses $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are measured in Pa, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The determinant is positive because $C$ is symmetric positive definite. These are selected model equations on the stated smooth incompressible regime; they assert no empirical applicability to a particular material, fitted parameter values, PDE solution existence, or universal validity.

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection $\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]], [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give $m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so $m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure $m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures, and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them on the entire Borel sigma-algebra ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on $\mathbb T^n$ ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for

integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],

In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $R>0$, and let $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^d$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Define $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ componentwise: $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_d)$ belongs to it exactly when each $v_i$ belongs to the scalar $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ defined in the earlier integer-order Sobolev-space definition. Its weak derivatives are $\partial_jv_i$, its gradient is the matrix $
abla v=(\partial_jv_i)_{i,j=1}^d$, and its norm is
$$\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)}^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\left(\|v_i\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{j=1}^d\|\partial_jv_i\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2ight)=\int_\Omega\left(|v|^2+|
abla v|_F^2ight)\,dx,$$
where $v\cdot w=\sum_i v_iw_i$, $|v|^2=\sum_i|v_i|^2$, $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$, and $|A|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2$. Define $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ as the closure of the $d$-tuples of compactly supported smooth real functions in this norm. Define $\operatorname{div}v=0$ distributionally to mean $\int_\Omega v\cdot
abla\phi=0$ for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and set $V=\{v\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d):\operatorname{div}v=0\}$. Equip $V$ with the inherited $H^1$ inner product $\int_\Omega(v\cdot w+
abla v:
abla w)$. The phrase no-slip here means membership in this closure; no trace characterization on arbitrary $\Omega$ is part of the definition.

Assume full AC. Let $d\ge2$, let $R>0$, let $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^d$ be nonempty bounded open, let $\mu>0$, and let $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$. There is a unique $u\in V$ such that $$\mu\int_\Omega
abla u:
abla v=\int_\Omega f\cdot v\qquad(v\in V),$$ where $V$ is the distributionally divergence-free subspace of $H_0^1$ defined above. It satisfies $\|
abla u\|_2\le2R\|f\|_2/\mu$. This is a projected variational velocity result; it asserts no pressure, $L^2$ pressure regularity, or classical boundary regularity.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. Write $D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $D_0(\Omega)=\{h\in D(\Omega):\int_\Omega h=0\}$. For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

Assume full AC. Let $d\ge2$, $R>0$, and let $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^d$ be bounded and open. For every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le2R\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le2R\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$
Here $H_0^1$ is the closure of compactly supported smooth fields in the Sobolev norm.

abla u:
abla\psi\,dx.$$
It satisfies $|\langle T,\psiangle|\le(\|f\|_2+\mu\|

For each fixed compact support $K$, $\|\psi\|_{H^1}\le C_K p_{K,1}(\psi)$ componentwise, so $T$ is continuous on every $\mathcal D_K$ and hence belongs to $D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ with the stated inductive-limit topology. The variational identity shows that $T$ annihilates every compactly supported smooth divergence-free vector field, since each lies in $V$.

Each interval contains a central compact subinterval. Affinely rescale $b(s)=e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ on $|s|<1$, extended by zero. Every derivative is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$, and the exponential tends to zero faster than every such power; thus the extension is smooth. Normalize its positive finite integral to fix interval bumps $\theta_i$, independently of all input tests and support sets, and set $\theta(x)=\prod_{i=1}^d\theta_i(x_i)$. Then $\theta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega\theta\,dx=1$.

Their product contains every output support: the first primitive vanishes before this interval and after it because its full first-coordinate integral is zero, and the other components have this support by induction. For $p_m$ the supremum of derivatives of order at most $m$, $p_m(H)\le(b_1-a_1)p_m(h)$. Differentiating the displayed formula bounds each output derivative by a fixed bump-derivative constant times $p_m(h)$, a finite-integral length times that bound, or $p_m(\mathscr R'H)$. The one-dimensional primitive has $p_m(\mathscr Rh)\le\max(1,b_1-a_1)p_m(h)$; induction therefore gives $p_m(\mathscr Rh)\le C_{\Omega,m}p_m(h)$. All operations are linear. The one-dimensional primitive starts the induction, proving $\|\mathscr Rh\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|h\|_{H^1}$ with a constant independent of the input support. Also $\|\phi_0\|_{H^1}\le(1+|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\theta\|_{H^1})\|\phi\|_{H^1}$, since $|\int_\Omega\phi|\le|\Omega|^{1/2}\|\phi\|_2$. Therefore
$|\langle p,\phi\rangle|\le C_\Omega(\|f\|_2+\mu\|\nabla u\|_2)\|\phi\|_{H^1}$. The resulting extension is a bounded linear functional on $H_0^1$, so $p\in H^{-1}$.

For compactly supported smooth vector $\psi$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}\psi\,dx=0$. $\langle

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

**Choice context.** The finite coefficient arrays and weighted coefficient completion below are defined without Countable Choice. In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Under Countable Choice, if $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ have normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$ and $\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}$. Give $C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$ the Fr'echet topology generated by $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\phi\|_\infty$, for $m\in\mathbb N_0$, where the derivatives are those of the smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^d$. A periodic distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on this test space, extended complex-linearly to complex-valued tests. For such a distribution $S$, define $\widehat S(k)=\langle S,e^{-ik\cdot x}angle$ for $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$ and define its mean to be $\widehat S(0)=\langle S,1angle$. For an integrable function $g$, the pairing is $\langle g,\phiangle=\int_{Q_d}g\phi\,d\mu$. Define distributional derivatives by $\langle\partial_jS,\phiangle=-\langle S,\partial_j\phiangle$. abla)v_i=\sum_jv_j\partial_jv_i$. In particular, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means $-\int_{Q_d}u\cdot
abla\phi\,d\mu=0$ for every real test function $\phi$. Equality of periodic distributions means equality on every such test function. Assume Countable Choice. $$P(u\cdot

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every Cauchy sequence of reals converges to a real ([[def-real-limit]]).

More carefully, this is a statement about the *axioms*: in a complete ordered
field, that is in an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), every Cauchy sequence converges. The proof
below uses nothing about $\mathbb{R}$ except that property, through
[[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]].

**This library already knows the conclusion by a different route.**
It is proved on the Cauchy-construction page, where
$\mathbb{R}$ is built out of Cauchy sequences of rationals and completeness is
read off the construction. That proof is about a particular construction; this
one is about the axioms, and it is what tells us the statement holds in *any*
complete ordered field, however it was obtained.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

derivations.claim: Write each component as a finite sum $F_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha$. On any bounded coordinate box, for each exponent $q\ge1$ the identity $a^q-b^q=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}a^{q-1-j}b^j$ bounds the difference of each monomial at two points by a finite constant times their Euclidean distance; telescoping over the $N$ factors and summing the finitely many monomials proves that $F$ is locally Lipschitz there. It is also continuous, so [F1] applies at every state.

Put $R_+=\max(1,R)$ and $M_R=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N(\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}|c_{i\alpha}|R_+^{|\alpha|})^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since $|x_j(t)|\le R$ for each coordinate, the finite polynomial sums give $\|F(x(t))\|_2\le M_R$ for all $t<T_*$.

For $0\le s<t<T_*$, apply [F3] to $x|_{[s,t]}$ to obtain $\|x(t)-x(s)\|_2\le M_R(t-s)$. Thus, for $t_n=T_*(1-1/n)$, $n\ge2$, each coordinate sequence $(x_i(t_n))_{n\ge2}$ is Cauchy because $|x_i(t_n)-x_i(t_m)|\le\|x(t_n)-x(t_m)\|_2\le M_R|t_n-t_m|$. By [F2], each coordinate has a real limit $\xi_i$; set $x_*=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose for each of the finitely many coordinates an index after which $|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|<\varepsilon/\sqrt N$, and take the maximum of those indices. Then $\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^N|x_i(t_n)-\xi_i|^2<\varepsilon^2$, so $x(t_n)\to x_*$. For any $t<T_*$ and all sufficiently large $n$ with $t_n\ge t$, the same Lipschitz bound gives $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(t_n-t)+\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2$; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(T_*-t)$, so $x(t)\to x_*$. The closed-ball bound passes to the limit, hence $\|x_*\|_2\le R$.
By step 1.1 the polynomial field is locally Lipschitz near $x_*$. Apply [F1] to the IVP at $(T_*,x_*)$ to obtain a local solution $y$ on an open interval about $T_*$.

By [F4], $x(t)=x_0+\int_0^tF(x(s))\,ds$ for $t<T_*$ and $y(t)=x_*+\int_{T_*}^tF(y(s))\,ds$ near $T_*$. The limit in step 3.1 and continuity of $F$ extend the first identity to $t=T_*$. Define $\widetilde x=x$ before $T_*$ and $\widetilde x=y$ from $T_*$ onward, assigning the common value $x_*$ at $T_*$. The joined curve is continuous and the two integral identities add to its Volterra equation on $[0,T_*+\epsilon)$ for some $\epsilon>0$; [F4] therefore makes it a $C^1$ solution of the same ODE extending $x$.
The extension in step 5.1 agrees with the original curve at every $t<T_*$ and is defined beyond $T_*$. This proves the statement.

For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Under Countable Choice, if $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and fix $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. For a vector Fourier coefficient $a(k)\in\mathbb C^d$, define $(Pa)(k)=P_ka(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, where $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k
e0$. For a tensor field $F=(F_{ij})_{i,j=1}^d$ with coefficients in any $H^s(Q_d)$, define the scalar pressure map $Q$ by $\widehat{QF}(0)=0$ and $\widehat{QF}(k)=-\sum_{i,j=1}^d k_i k_j|k|^{-2}\widehat F_{ij}(k)$ for $k
e0$. For $q\in H^s(Q_d)$, define $\partial_jq\in H^{s-1}(Q_d)$ coefficientwise by $\widehat{\partial_jq}(k)=ik_j\widehat q(k)$; for vector fields set $\widehat{
abla q}(k)=ik\widehat q(k)$, and for tensor fields set $\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}_i(k)=i\sum_jk_j\widehat F_{ij}(k)$. These derivative maps are bounded from $H^s$ to $H^{s-1}$. The multipliers $P$ and $Q$ are real-preserving and bounded on every $H^s$, $s\in\mathbb R$; $P$ is an orthogonal projection and commutes with these derivatives. For every $F$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, their exact identity is the coefficientwise equality
$$\widehat{
abla QF}(k)=-(I-P_k)\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k).$$
In particular, both sides have zero coefficient at $k=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and use $H^\sigma(Q_d)$ with the normalized measure and weights in the Definition. For every integer $j\ge0$ and $\sigma>j+d/2$, each scalar $q\in H^\sigma(Q_d)$ has a $C^j$ representative and $\|q\|_{C^j}\le C_{d,\sigma,j}\|q\|_{H^\sigma}$. For every $\sigma>d/2$, pointwise multiplication extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a continuous bilinear map $H^\sigma\times H^\sigma\to H^\sigma$ satisfying $\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C_{d,\sigma}\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$. The assertions extend componentwise to finite-dimensional vector and tensor fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $m\ge s\ge4$ be integers, let $f,g\in C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$, and define $\Lambda^m$ by $\widehat{\Lambda^m q}(k)=w_k^m\widehat q(k)$. For each coordinate $j$,
$$\|[\Lambda^m,f]\partial_jg\|_{L^2}\le C_{d,m,s}\bigl(\|f\|_{H^m}\|g\|_{H^s}+\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^m}\bigr),$$
where $[\Lambda^m,f]h=\Lambda^m(fh)-f\Lambda^mh$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. If $x\in C^1([0,T_*),\mathbb R^N)$ solves $x'(t)=F(x(t))$ and there is $R\ge0$ such that $\|x(t)\|_2\le R$ for every $0\le t<T_*$, then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a solution $\widetilde x\in C^1([0,T_*+\epsilon),\mathbb R^N)$ of the same ODE with $\widetilde x(t)=x(t)$ for $0\le t<T_*$. Thus a finite right endpoint of a bounded finite-dimensional polynomial ODE trajectory is extendible.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ have normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$ and $\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}$. Give $C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$ the Fr'echet topology generated by $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\phi\|_\infty$, for $m\in\mathbb N_0$, where the derivatives are those of the smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^d$. A periodic distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on this test space, extended complex-linearly to complex-valued tests. For such a distribution $S$, define $\widehat S(k)=\langle S,e^{-ik\cdot x}angle$ for $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$ and define its mean to be $\widehat S(0)=\langle S,1angle$. For an integrable function $g$, the pairing is $\langle g,\phiangle=\int_{Q_d}g\phi\,d\mu$. Define distributional derivatives by $\langle\partial_jS,\phiangle=-\langle S,\partial_j\phiangle$. For a smooth scalar test, $
abla\phi=(\partial_1\phi,\ldots,\partial_d\phi)$ and $\Delta\phi=\sum_j\partial_j^2\phi$; for a smooth vector field $v$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_jv_j$, $(v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_iv_j$, and $(v\cdot
abla)v_i=\sum_jv_j\partial_jv_i$. In particular, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means $-\int_{Q_d}u\cdot
abla\phi\,d\mu=0$ for every real test function $\phi$. Equality of periodic distributions means equality on every such test function. Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $s>d/2+1$, and let $u\in H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in this sense. Then $u\otimes u\in H^s$, the mean-zero scalar $\pi=Q(u\otimes u)$ belongs to $H^s$, and in $H^{s-1}$,
$$P(u\cdot
abla u)=u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi.$$
Among mean-zero periodic distributions $\widetilde\pi$ for which this identity holds as an equality of periodic distributions, this pressure is unique. The formula is a torus pressure recovery result and asserts no wall pressure regularity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. In particular, $H^0=L^2$. For a map $z:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha$, $\partial_t^m\partial_x^\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. For a spatial vector field define $\operatorname{div}z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jz_j$ and $\Delta z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2z$. Write $\nabla z$ for the spatial Jacobian and $\|\nabla z(t)\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in Q_d}|\nabla z(t,x)|_F$, where $|\cdot|_F$ is the Euclidean Frobenius matrix norm. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. The equations below hold pointwise on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and at the time endpoints by continuous extension.

(i) If $\nu\ge0$ and $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{u,v\}$,
$$z_t+P((z\cdot\nabla)z)=\nu\Delta z,\qquad \operatorname{div}z=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$, with $w=u-v$,
$$\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_\infty\,d\tau\right).$$

(ii) Let $N\ge1$ and, for $1\le j\le d$, let $A_j:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be a fixed real-linear map whose image consists of symmetric matrices. If $q,r\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{q,r\}$,
$$z_t+\sum_{j=1}^dA_j(z)\partial_jz=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|q(t)-r(t)\|_2^2\le\|q(0)-r(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(C_{d,N,A}\int_0^t(\|\nabla q(\tau)\|_\infty+\|\nabla r(\tau)\|_\infty)\,d\tau\right),$$
where $C_{d,N,A}$ depends only on $d,N$ and the operator norms of the finitely many maps $A_j$. For either pair $(z_1,z_2)=(u,v)$ or $(q,r)$, put $w=z_1-z_2$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be any uniform rate for which the corresponding squared $L^2$ estimate above gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2e^{\Gamma t}$. If $s\ge1$ and $\max_{t\in[0,T]}\max(\|z_1(t)\|_{H^s},\|z_2(t)\|_{H^s})\le M$ for some $M\ge0$, define
$$B_s(M)=\begin{cases}1,&s=1,\\(2M)^{(s-1)/s},&s>1.\end{cases}$$
Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|w(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le B_s(M)\|w(0)\|_2^{1/s}e^{\Gamma t/(2s)}.$$
These are conditional estimates for already given smooth maps on the stated cylinder and assert no existence theorem. All quantities are mathematical and no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Define a canonical extraction $E$ for a bounded real sequence $(b_n)_{n\ge1}$. Let $B\ge1$ be the least integer with $|b_n|\le B$ for every $n$, and put $I_0=[-B,B]$. Having defined $I_\ell$, bisect it into its two closed halves and define $I_{\ell+1}$ to be the left half if that half contains $b_n$ for infinitely many indices $n$, and the right half otherwise. Then $E(b)(\ell)=e_\ell$ is strictly increasing and $(b_{e_\ell})$ is Cauchy: for $p,q\ge\ell$, both values lie in $I_\ell$, whose length is $2B2^{-\ell}$. At $m=s$, set $Y_N=\|u_N\|_{H^s}$. When $Y_N>0$, the inequality in step 1.2 gives $Y_N'\le C_sY_N^2$; if $Y_N(0)=0$, uniqueness of the finite-dimensional ODE makes $u_N\equiv0$. The equicontinuity from step 4.1 upgrades convergence at rational times to uniform-in-time convergence of each fixed Fourier coefficient. The triangle inequality makes each coordinate uniformly Cauchy, and scalar completeness supplies its uniform limit.

Completeness of the coefficient space [F1] yields a limit $u\in\bigcap_{m\ge s}C([0,T],H^m)$; finite sums show $\sup_t\|u(t)\|_{H^m}\le\sup_N\sup_t\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}$, and coefficientwise limits preserve reality, divergence-free constraints, and $u(0)=u_0$.
