**Choice context.** The finite coefficient arrays and weighted coefficient completion below are defined without Countable Choice. In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Under Countable Choice, if $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and use $H^\sigma(Q_d)$ with the normalized measure and weights in the Definition. For every integer $j\ge0$ and $\sigma>j+d/2$, each scalar $q\in H^\sigma(Q_d)$ has a $C^j$ representative and $\|q\|_{C^j}\le C_{d,\sigma,j}\|q\|_{H^\sigma}$. For every $\sigma>d/2$, pointwise multiplication extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a continuous bilinear map $H^\sigma\times H^\sigma\to H^\sigma$ satisfying $\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C_{d,\sigma}\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$. The assertions extend componentwise to finite-dimensional vector and tensor fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $m\ge s\ge4$ be integers, let $f,g\in C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$, and define $\Lambda^m$ by $\widehat{\Lambda^m q}(k)=w_k^m\widehat q(k)$. For each coordinate $j$,
$$\|[\Lambda^m,f]\partial_jg\|_{L^2}\le C_{d,m,s}\bigl(\|f\|_{H^m}\|g\|_{H^s}+\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^m}\bigr),$$
where $[\Lambda^m,f]h=\Lambda^m(fh)-f\Lambda^mh$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\kappa>0$, $\gamma>1$, and put $a=(\gamma-1)/2$. For positive density $\rho>0$, define the polytropic pressure $p(\rho)=\kappa\rho^\gamma$, sound speed $c(\rho)=\sqrt{p'(\rho)}=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\,\rho^a$, and sound-speed variable $r=c/a$. The map $\rho\mapsto r$ is a smooth bijection $(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ with inverse $\rho=(ar/\sqrt{\kappa\gamma})^{1/a}$. For a velocity $u\in\mathbb R^d$, set $q=(r,u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$. Let $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, with $e_0$ the scalar coordinate and $e_j$ the velocity coordinate $u_j$. Define the real matrix
$$A_j(q)=u_j I_{d+1}+ar(e_0e_j^{\mathsf T}+e_je_0^{\mathsf T}),\qquad 1\le j\le d.$$
Each $A_j(q)$ is symmetric and linear in $q$; the same formula defines the linear map $A_j:\mathbb R^{d+1}\to\mathbb R^{(d+1)\times(d+1)}$ even when the scalar coordinate is nonpositive, as needed for polynomial approximations. To interpret derivatives, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, or let $\Omega=Q_d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$. Take fields $\rho\in C^1(I\times\Omega;(0,\infty))$ and $u\in C^1(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, and define $r(t,x)=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\rho(t,x)^a/a$ and $q(t,x)=(r(t,x),u(t,x))$ pointwise. Spatial derivatives on $Q_d$ are derivatives of the periodic lifts. On a closed time interval the same convention means the fields and first derivatives extend continuously to its endpoints, with one-sided time derivatives there. The first-order system $q_t+\sum_{j=1}^d A_j(q)\partial_jq=0$ is a pointwise equality on the time-space domain and means the pair
$$r_t+u\cdot\nabla r+ar\,\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad u_t+u\cdot\nabla u+ar\nabla r=0.$$
For periodic coefficients, let $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ be componentwise integrable (in particular, any continuous periodic spatial field or time slice above), and take normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, Fourier coefficients $\widehat q(k)=\int q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and $\|q\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat q(k)|^2$, componentwise; real fields satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. The coefficient integrals are defined on these integrable fields. For general $H^m$ elements, coefficient coordinates mean those of the weighted completion in the Fourier-space definition; no integral formula is imposed on an element without an integrable representative. These are the periodic Fourier-space conventions used for $H^m$ in this development.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. If $x\in C^1([0,T_*),\mathbb R^N)$ solves $x'(t)=F(x(t))$ and there is $R\ge0$ such that $\|x(t)\|_2\le R$ for every $0\le t<T_*$, then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a solution $\widetilde x\in C^1([0,T_*+\epsilon),\mathbb R^N)$ of the same ODE with $\widetilde x(t)=x(t)$ for $0\le t<T_*$. Thus a finite right endpoint of a bounded finite-dimensional polynomial ODE trajectory is extendible.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Put $q_0=(r(\rho_0),u_0)$. For $N\ge1$, let $S_N$ be the componentwise orthogonal Fourier projection to $|k|_\infty\le N$ and solve $\partial_tq_N+S_N\sum_{j=1}^d A_j(q_N)\partial_jq_N=0$, $q_N(0)=S_Nq_0$. Each coefficient of its finite-dimensional vector field is polynomial. On any bounded coefficient box, the identity $x^n-y^n=(x-y)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x^{n-1-i}y^i$, telescoped over the finitely many factors of each monomial, bounds every monomial difference by a constant times the Euclidean distance; summing the finitely many monomials proves local Lipschitz continuity. Thus [F7] gives a unique local real solution, and the real Fourier cutoff preserves conjugate symmetry.

The analytic suppliers [F2]–[F4] apply under the standing Countable Choice assumption [F6, A1]. For integer $m\ge s$, put $Q=\Lambda^m q_N$ with $\Lambda$ the multiplier $(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. Pair the projected equation with $Q$. Since $S_N$ is self-adjoint and commutes with $\Lambda$, the projection disappears in the inner product. For each $j$, expand $\Lambda^m(A_j(q_N)\partial_jq_N)=A_j(q_N)\partial_jQ+[\Lambda^m,A_j(q_N)]\partial_jq_N$. Symmetry and periodic integration by parts give $\int Q^{\mathsf T}A_j(q_N)\partial_jQ=-\frac12\int Q^{\mathsf T}(\partial_jA_j(q_N))Q$, whose absolute value is at most $C\|\nabla q_N\|_\infty\|q_N\|_{H^m}^2$. The embedding in [F3] bounds this by $C_m\|q_N\|_{H^s}\|q_N\|_{H^m}^2$. Because each $A_j$ is linear in $q_N$, [F4] bounds all commutator terms by the same expression. Thus $\frac12\frac d{dt}\|q_N\|_{H^m}^2\le C_m\|q_N\|_{H^s}\|q_N\|_{H^m}^2$.

Define a canonical extraction $E$ for a bounded real sequence $(b_n)_{n\ge1}$. Let $B\ge1$ be the least integer with $|b_n|\le B$ for every $n$, and put $I_0=[-B,B]$. Having defined $I_\ell$, bisect it into its two closed halves and define $I_{\ell+1}$ to be the left half if that half contains $b_n$ for infinitely many indices $n$, and the right half otherwise. At least one half contains infinitely many such indices, so this rule is defined and unique. Set $e_0=0$ and let $e_\ell$ be the least $n>e_{\ell-1}$ with $b_n\in I_\ell$. These minima exist because the corresponding index sets are infinite. Then $E(b)(\ell)=e_\ell$ is strictly increasing and $(b_{e_\ell})$ is Cauchy: for $p,q\ge\ell$, both values lie in $I_\ell$, whose length is $2B2^{-\ell}$. It converges, since [F10] gives a convergent subsequence of this bounded Cauchy sequence and the Cauchy inequality forces the entire sequence to have the same limit. All intervals and indices are uniquely specified; this defines a function $E$ without any choice principle.

At $m=s$, let $Y_N=\|q_N\|_{H^s}$. If $Y_N(0)>0$, step 1.3 gives $Y_N'\le C_sY_N^2$ while $Y_N>0$; integrating $(1/Y_N)'\ge-C_s$ yields $Y_N(t)\le2\|q_0\|_{H^s}$ for $0\le t\le T_0=(2C_s\|q_0\|_{H^s})^{-1}$. If $q_0=0$, the unique finite-dimensional solution is zero and take $T_0=1$. For each $m>s$, substituting this $H^s$ bound into step 1.3 and multiplying the squared-norm inequality by the corresponding decreasing exponential gives $\|q_N(t)\|_{H^m}\le\|q_0\|_{H^m}e^{2C_m\|q_0\|_{H^s}T_0}$. Parseval [F2] bounds the Euclidean coefficient norm by $\|q_N\|_{H^s}$; since the finite-dimensional state space is $\mathbb R^M$ with $M\ge1$, completeness [F9] supplies the endpoint limit used by the continuation argument [F8]. Thus every finite-dimensional polynomial trajectory continues throughout $[0,T_0]$.

Let $q,v$ be two smooth solutions of the symmetric system with the same initial data and positive first component. Their difference $w=q-v$ satisfies $w_t+\sum_jA_j(q)\partial_jw=-\sum_j(A_j(q)-A_j(v))\partial_jv$. Pair with $w$, integrate over the torus, and use symmetry of $A_j(q)$ to integrate the principal term into $-\frac12\int w^{\mathsf T}(\partial_jA_j(q))w$. Linearity of $A_j$ bounds the right side by $C(\|\nabla q\|_\infty+\|\nabla v\|_\infty)\|w\|_2^2$, so $z(t)=\|w(t)\|_2^2$ satisfies $z'\le C(t)z$, with continuous nonnegative $C$. Multiplying by $e^{-\int_0^tC(s)ds}$ gives a nonincreasing nonnegative function initially zero, hence $w=0$. The inverse change of variables then makes the positive-density Euler solution unique.

For every integer $m\ge s+1$, the product estimate [F3] and the bounds in step 2.1 bound $\partial_tq_N=-S_N\sum_jA_j(q_N)\partial_jq_N$ uniformly in $C([0,T_0],H^{m-1})$. Hence each fixed Fourier coefficient is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous in time.

Enumerate tuples $(k,A,B,j,\epsilon)$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, integers $A\ge0$, $B\ge1$, $\gcd(A,B)=1$, $A/B\le T_0$, $0\le j\le d$, and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$ by increasing $|k|_1+A+B+j+\epsilon$, then lexicographically within each finite level. At tuple $i$, let $b^i_N$ be the real ($\epsilon=0$) or imaginary ($\epsilon=1$) part of the $j$th component of $\widehat q_N(k,A/B)$. Starting with $h_0(n)=n$, define recursively $h_i=h_{i-1}\circ E(b^i\circ h_{i-1})$ and put $N_\ell=h_\ell(\ell)$. The successor in this recursion is a specified function of $h_{i-1}$, so this is ordinary recursion, not a succession of unspecified dependent selections. Each $h_i$ is strictly increasing and its range is contained in every preceding range. Moreover $N_{\ell+1}=h_\ell(E(b^{\ell+1}\circ h_\ell)(\ell+1))\ge h_\ell(\ell+1)>N_\ell$. For each fixed $i$, the tail $(N_\ell)_{\ell\ge i}$ is an increasing subsequence of the range of $h_i$, on which $b^i$ converges. Thus this one subsequence converges at every enumerated coefficient-time coordinate. Countable Choice remains the standing analytic Fourier assumption; the diagonal construction itself does not require dependent choice.

The equicontinuity from step 3.1 upgrades convergence at rational times to uniform-in-time convergence of each fixed Fourier coefficient. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite rational time grid so that every time is close enough to a grid point to make each of the two equicontinuity errors below $\varepsilon/3$; choose the subsequence indices large enough that the finitely many grid values differ by less than $\varepsilon/3$. The triangle inequality makes each coordinate uniformly Cauchy, and scalar completeness supplies its uniform limit.

For every integer $m\ge s$, the $H^{m+1}$ bound from step 2.1 and the coefficient weight give $\|(I-S_K)q_N(t)\|_{H^m}\le K^{-1}\|q_N(t)\|_{H^{m+1}}$ for $K\ge1$. This tail tends to zero uniformly in $N,t$. Combining it with finite-mode convergence from step 5.1 makes the diagonal subsequence Cauchy in $C([0,T_0],H^m)$ for every integer $m\ge s$. Completeness of the weighted coefficient space [F1] yields a limit $q\in\bigcap_{m\ge s}C([0,T_0],H^m)$ with all these uniform bounds; coefficientwise limits preserve reality and the initial data.

Since $q_N\to q$ in $C_tH^m$ for every $m\ge s$, the algebra estimate [F3] gives $A_j(q_N)\partial_jq_N\to A_j(q)\partial_jq$ in $C_tH^{m-1}$. The Fourier cutoffs $S_N$ converge strongly to the identity in that space. They converge uniformly on the compact time image of the continuous curve $t\mapsto\sum_jA_j(q)\partial_jq$: choose a finite $\varepsilon$-net, use strong convergence at its finitely many points, and use $\|S_N\|\le1$ for the net errors. Thus the Galerkin right-hand sides converge uniformly in $C_tH^{m-1}$.

Integrate each Galerkin equation from $0$ to $t$. A continuous curve into the complete weighted coefficient space is Riemann integrable: uniform continuity makes its Riemann sums Cauchy, and completeness supplies the limit; the triangle inequality gives $\|\int G_N-\int G\|_{H^{m-1}}\le T_0\sup_t\|G_N(t)-G(t)\|_{H^{m-1}}$. The right-hand-side convergence in step 7.1 and $S_Nq_0\to q_0$ therefore let the integrals pass to the limit, giving $q(t)=q_0-\int_0^t\sum_jA_j(q(s))\partial_jq(s)\,ds$. The integrand is continuous in every $H^{m-1}$; its integral has derivative equal to the integrand because the difference quotient error is bounded by the maximum oscillation of that continuous integrand on the shrinking time interval. Therefore $q_t+\sum_jA_j(q)\partial_jq=0$ at every Sobolev order, and the embeddings in [F3] imply spatial smoothness. Differentiating this polynomial first-order identity inductively gives all time derivatives: each new derivative is a finite sum of products of already continuous spatial derivatives.

The first component satisfies $r_t=-u\cdot\nabla r-ar\operatorname{div}u$. By [F3], the uniform $H^s$ bound in step 2.1 bounds the right side in $L^\infty$ by $C\|q_0\|_{H^s}^2$. Hence $\|r(t)-r(0)\|_\infty\le Ct\|q_0\|_{H^s}^2$. Choose $0<T\le T_0$ so that this is less than $\frac12\min r(0)$; then $r(t,x)\ge\frac12\min r(0)>0$. The smooth inverse $\rho=(ar/\sqrt{\kappa\gamma})^{1/a}$ and step 1.1 give a smooth positive-density solution of the stated Euler equations. On the compact spacetime cylinder, $r$ stays in a compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$; all derivatives of this inverse power are therefore bounded on the range of $r$, and the repeated chain rule gives $\rho\in C_tH^m$ for every $m$. The choice of $T$ uses only the stated parameters, $\|q_0\|_{H^s}$, and $\min r(0)$.

The compactness, passage, positivity, and uniqueness arguments above give existence, smoothness, positivity, uniqueness, and all-order Sobolev bounds on the same interval. No argument extends the solution through vacuum, a shock, or a finite-time loss of the stated bounds.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all twelve proof steps and every direct supplier, including the exact symmetric-variable map and both directions of its positive-density chain-rule equivalence. Symmetric linear A_j give the integration-by-parts coefficient term; the tame commutator and s>=4>d/2+1 control it uniformly. Finite Galerkin systems are polynomial without requiring positive Galerkin density; positivity is imposed only on the limiting field. Low-norm bounds give T0 independent of higher norms; higher-order integrating factors and ODE continuation hold on that same interval. Real coefficient compactness, canonical least-index subsequence extraction and countable diagonalization plus uniform high-norm tails give all-order strong convergence. Product convergence, uniform cutoff convergence on the compact time image and complete coefficient-space Riemann integration establish the symmetric PDE and all mixed derivatives. The L-infinity bound on r_t, depending only on the low norm and fixed parameters, gives a smaller common T with r>=min(r0)/2. The inverse power and every derivative are bounded on the compact positive range, so rho is smooth and has every claimed finite Sobolev bound. Difference energy proves uniqueness by integrating factor. Vacuum, shocks, nonisentropic and viscous systems are explicitly excluded. The zero-q branch is a harmless general ODE case; positive initial density itself excludes it.

step5_repair_review.notes: Reviewed current symmetric-field/Fourier, embedding/product, tame-commutator and ODE continuation interfaces against every proof step. The linear symmetric Galerkin matrices are defined even before positivity; energy estimates give a common low-norm lifespan and all-order bounds. The explicit dyadic scalar extraction and specified nested index maps give a strictly increasing diagonal without dependent choice. Finite rational grids and uniform high-norm Fourier tails give all-order strong convergence. Polynomial product convergence and the integral equation yield the smooth PDE, the low-norm r_t bound preserves positivity, and the inverse map and difference energy give exactly the existing uniqueness and Sobolev conclusions. The Statement is unchanged. This is the repairing adjudicator’s check, not independent acceptance of its repair.

derivations.claim: The mass residual at $(\rho_*+\epsilon z,\epsilon v)$ is $\epsilon(z_t+\rho_*\operatorname{div}v)+\epsilon^2\operatorname{div}(zv)$. The velocity residual is $\epsilon v_t+\epsilon^2v\cdot\nabla v+\epsilon[P^{\prime}(\rho_*+\epsilon z)/(\rho_*+\epsilon z)]\nabla z$. Differentiating at zero gives exactly the two displayed linear equations because $P^{\prime}(\rho_*)=c_*^2$. Thus the tangent interpretation follows from the defined residual derivative, without assuming that perturbations solve the nonlinear system for nonzero $\epsilon$.

Write Fourier coefficients with kernel $e^{-ik\cdot x}$. For each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, the PDE is the finite-dimensional ODE $\dot{\widehat z}=-i\rho_* k\cdot\widehat v$, $\dot{\widehat v}=-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\widehat z$. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. At $k=0$ both coefficients are constant.

Differentiation of these formulas recovers both mode equations and their initial coefficients. For each $k$, differentiating $E_k=|\widehat v|^2+(c_*^2/\rho_*^2)|\widehat z|^2$ gives zero: the two cross terms are $-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)[(k\widehat z)\cdot\overline{\widehat v}+(k\cdot\widehat v)\overline{\widehat z}]$, whose bracket is real, so its real part vanishes. Thus $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ for every mode. The mode formulas also preserve conjugate symmetry because their coefficients at $-k$ are conjugates of those at $k$.

For each scalar component $f$ of the smooth initial data and every integer $N\ge0$, periodic integration by parts gives $(1+|k|^2)^N\widehat f(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^Nf}(k)$, where $\Delta=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2$; opposite periodic-face terms cancel. Since $(1-\Delta)^Nf$ is continuous on the compact torus, its $L^1$ norm $C_{f,N}$ is finite, and $|\widehat f(k)|\le C_{f,N}(1+|k|^2)^{-N}$.
For any integer $m\ge0$, choose $N$ with $4N-2m>d$. The shell $j\le|k|<j+1$ contains at most $C_d(j+1)^{d-1}$ lattice points, by placing disjoint unit cubes at its lattice points inside a shell of fixed enlarged width, so $\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{m-2N}<\infty$ by comparison with $\sum_{j\ge1}j^{d-1+2m-4N}$. Thus every initial component belongs to every $H^m$ under [F1].
Multiplying the mode identity $E_k(t)=E_k(0)$ from step 2.1 by $(1+|k|^2)^m$ and summing these nonnegative finite-energy series proves, by [F2], the stated conserved weighted energy. In particular both coefficient families remain in every $H^m$, uniformly for all real time.

Fourier synthesis [F2], under the stated Countable Choice assumption [A1], now defines real fields $z(t),v(t)$. The uniform $H^m$ bounds and embeddings [F3] imply convergence of the Fourier series with every spatial derivative, locally uniformly in time. The mode equations pass through these convergent series and give the PDE. Write $q=(z,v)$ and let $\mathcal L$ be the constant-coefficient first-order spatial operator in that system; recursively $\partial_t^nq=\mathcal L^nq$, which is a finite sum of spatial derivatives of order at most $n$. Thus all mixed derivatives are continuous, so $q\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb T^d)$.

For any two smooth solutions with the same data, each Fourier-mode difference solves the same linear ODE with zero initial value. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional linear ODE gives zero difference at each $k$, and Fourier synthesis then gives equality of the fields. Fix lengths $L_1,L_2>0$ and width $h>0$. Define the periodic channel
$$\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}=(\mathbb R/L_1\mathbb Z)\times(0,h)\times(\mathbb R/L_2\mathbb Z)$$
and the infinite channel
$$\Omega_{\infty}=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R.$$
Both have the product Euclidean metric. On $\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}$, the first and third coordinates are periodic quotient coordinates with periods $L_1$ and $L_2$; differential operators are the ordinary coordinate operators applied to periodic lifts. On $\Omega_{\infty}$, all three coordinates are ordinary real coordinates. The closures add the two wall faces at $y=0$ and $y=h$, and no other spatial boundary is imposed. For either channel $\Omega$, let $\Gamma:=\partial\Omega$ denote these two wall faces. A steady velocity field with a classical wall trace is a continuous map $u:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, with trace $u_\Gamma:=u|_\Gamma$; prescribed steady wall data are a continuous map $g:\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$. A vector field is $C^\infty$ up to these walls when it is smooth in the interior and every spatial derivative of every order extends continuously to both faces on each compact coordinate patch. Its homogeneous no-slip boundary condition is $u_\Gamma=0$; prescribed wall velocity means $u_\Gamma=g$. For an evolution on a specified time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the corresponding trace convention uses continuous maps $u:I\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ and $g:I\times\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$, with $u_\Gamma(t,x):=u(t,x)$ and the same trace equalities on $I\times\Gamma$; any additional time or spatial regularity and compatibility required by an evolution result are stated separately. These conventions assert no solution existence for prescribed data. The definition imposes no decay or other condition at infinity on $\Omega_{\infty}$; such conditions must be stated separately.

derivations.claim: For $U(y)=Vy/h$, the traces are $U(0)=0$, $U(h)=V$, and $U''=0$. The field $u=Ue_x$ has zero divergence and zero convective term because $u\cdot\nabla u=U\partial_xu=0$. With constant pressure, $-\nabla p+\eta\Delta u=0$, so the equation [A1] holds.

By the coordinate formula for curl, $\nabla\times(U(y),0,0)=(0,0,-U'(y))=(0,0,-V/h)$. The flux is $\int_0^hVy/h\,dy=Vh/2$. For any competing field in the class stated in the Example, constant pressure and zero convection reduce the streamwise equation to $\eta\widetilde U^{\prime\prime}=0$. Thus $\widetilde U-U$ has zero second derivative and zero endpoint values, hence is the zero affine function. Since $h>0$, the computed vorticity vanishes exactly when $V=0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

**Choice context.** The finite coefficient arrays and weighted coefficient completion below are defined without Countable Choice. In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Under Countable Choice, if $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\kappa>0$, $\gamma>1$, and put $a=(\gamma-1)/2$. For positive density $\rho>0$, define the polytropic pressure $p(\rho)=\kappa\rho^\gamma$, sound speed $c(\rho)=\sqrt{p'(\rho)}=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\,\rho^a$, and sound-speed variable $r=c/a$. The map $\rho\mapsto r$ is a smooth bijection $(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ with inverse $\rho=(ar/\sqrt{\kappa\gamma})^{1/a}$. For a velocity $u\in\mathbb R^d$, set $q=(r,u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$. Let $e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_d$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, with $e_0$ the scalar coordinate and $e_j$ the velocity coordinate $u_j$. Define the real matrix
$$A_j(q)=u_j I_{d+1}+ar(e_0e_j^{\mathsf T}+e_je_0^{\mathsf T}),\qquad 1\le j\le d.$$
Each $A_j(q)$ is symmetric and linear in $q$; the same formula defines the linear map $A_j:\mathbb R^{d+1}\to\mathbb R^{(d+1)\times(d+1)}$ even when the scalar coordinate is nonpositive, as needed for polynomial approximations. To interpret derivatives, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open, or let $\Omega=Q_d=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$. Take fields $\rho\in C^1(I\times\Omega;(0,\infty))$ and $u\in C^1(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, and define $r(t,x)=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\rho(t,x)^a/a$ and $q(t,x)=(r(t,x),u(t,x))$ pointwise. Spatial derivatives on $Q_d$ are derivatives of the periodic lifts. On a closed time interval the same convention means the fields and first derivatives extend continuously to its endpoints, with one-sided time derivatives there. The first-order system $q_t+\sum_{j=1}^d A_j(q)\partial_jq=0$ is a pointwise equality on the time-space domain and means the pair
$$r_t+u\cdot\nabla r+ar\,\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad u_t+u\cdot\nabla u+ar\nabla r=0.$$
For periodic coefficients, let $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^{d+1}$ be componentwise integrable (in particular, any continuous periodic spatial field or time slice above), and take normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, Fourier coefficients $\widehat q(k)=\int q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and $\|q\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat q(k)|^2$, componentwise; real fields satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. The coefficient integrals are defined on these integrable fields. For general $H^m$ elements, coefficient coordinates mean those of the weighted completion in the Fourier-space definition; no integral formula is imposed on an element without an integrable representative. These are the periodic Fourier-space conventions used for $H^m$ in this development.

Assume Countable Choice. Use normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, coefficients $\widehat f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and componentwise norms $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2m}|\widehat f(k)|^2$. For $\rho>0$, set $p(\rho)=\kappa\rho^\gamma$ and $r(\rho)=\sqrt{\kappa\gamma}\,\rho^a/a$. Then there is $T>0$, depending only on $d,s,\kappa,\gamma$, $\|(r(\rho_0),u_0)\|_{H^s}$, and $\min r(\rho_0)$, and a unique smooth real solution $(\rho,u)$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ of
$$\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad u_t+u\cdot\nabla u+\rho^{-1}\nabla(\kappa\rho^\gamma)=0,$$
with initial data $(\rho_0,u_0)$ and $\rho(t,x)>0$. For every integer $m\ge s$, $\sup_{0\le t\le T}(\|\rho(t)\|_{H^m}+\|u(t)\|_{H^m})<\infty$. This conditional smooth periodic theorem concerns the isentropic barotropic model with strictly positive density; it asserts no continuation through vacuum or shocks and no viscous or temperature-coupled result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A bounded wall domain is a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $C^2$ boundary. For $T>0$, its classical velocity fields are maps $u:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ in $C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, and its classical pressures are maps $p:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R$ in $C([0,T];C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R))$. Here spatial derivatives through the indicated order extend continuously to the boundary, and time continuity and differentiability are taken in the corresponding spatial supremum norms. The boundary normal $n$ is the outward unit normal. Write $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ and let $g:[0,T]\times\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$ be prescribed continuous wall-velocity data. The classical trace is the restriction $u_\Gamma(t,x):=u(t,x)$ for $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\Gamma$. A no-slip trace is $u_\Gamma=0$, a prescribed moving-wall trace is $u_\Gamma=g$, and an impermeable trace is $u_\Gamma\cdot n=0$; these are distinct boundary data. Whenever $u_\Gamma=g$ is imposed, the data must be compatible with the stated classical field class; no extension or solution existence for arbitrary continuous $g$ is asserted.

An exterior domain is $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$, where $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ is compact with $C^2$ boundary and $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is connected. The exterior classical fields are maps $u:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}\to\mathbb R$, with $u\in C^1([0,T];C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}};\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C([0,T];C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}};\mathbb R))$. The local spaces require the indicated spatial derivatives to extend continuously up to $\partial K$; their topology is uniform convergence of those derivatives on each compact subset of the closure. The domain definition alone imposes no condition at infinity. An exterior energy argument must state additional decay or weighted-space hypotheses. We call the explicit bounds $|u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, $|\nabla u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-3})$, and $|p(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, uniform for $t\in[0,T]$, a cutoff-decay condition; this is additional solution data, not part of the bare exterior domain, and no energy identity follows from this definition alone.

Throughout this surface-integration page assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the earlier Lebesgue and polar measure machinery. Let $n\ge2$. A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

The convention $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means F is continuously differentiable in $\Omega$, and F and its first derivatives extend continuously to its closure. For $C^2$ require the same for derivatives through order two. No ambient extension across the boundary is required. Derivatives use [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]; products are the real Euclidean inner products of [[def-inner-product-space]]. Write $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_i\partial_iF_i$, $Du=(\partial_iu)_i$ and $\Delta u=\sum_i\partial_i^2u$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\ell>0$, and $\nu\ge0$, and write $Q_\ell=\mathbb R^d/(\ell\mathbb Z)^d$. For a period cell, define $\|f\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_\ell)}=(\int_{[0,\ell]^d}|f(x)|^2dx)^{1/2}$.

First, for $T>0$ and either $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$ or $\Omega=Q_\ell$, let $u\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ and $\pi\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a velocity-pressure pair solving the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes system
$$u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla\pi+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$
then for any $\lambda>0$,
$$u_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda u(\lambda^2t,\lambda x),\qquad \pi_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^2\pi(\lambda^2t,\lambda x)$$
solves the same system with the same viscosity on $\mathbb R^d$ or on the torus of period $\ell/\lambda$, respectively, for $0\le t\le T/\lambda^2$. On the torus, use the Fourier Leray multiplier $P_0=I$, $P_\xi=I-\xi\xi^{\mathsf T}/|\xi|^2$ for $\xi\ne0$; the projected equation is preserved as well because $P_{\lambda\xi}=P_\xi$. For a cell-volume $L^2$ norm, $\|u_\lambda(0)\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_{\ell/\lambda})}=\lambda^{1-d/2}\|u(0)\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_\ell)}$.

Second, for any $\alpha,\beta>0$, if $T>0$, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ is open, $u\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, and $\pi\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R)$ solve the unforced incompressible Euler system $u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla\pi$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, then on the scaled domain $\beta^{-1}\Omega$,
$$u_{\alpha,\beta}(t,x)=\alpha u(\alpha\beta t,\beta x),\qquad \pi_{\alpha,\beta}(t,x)=\alpha^2\pi(\alpha\beta t,\beta x)$$
solves the same equation on the correspondingly scaled domain and time interval $0\le t\le T/(\alpha\beta)$. These transformations are equation symmetries; on a torus they transform its period.

Finally, let $U,L,\rho_*,\eta>0$ be physical scales in SI units, where $U$ is in m/s, $L$ in m, $\rho_*$ is a constant positive reference density in kg/m$^3$, and dynamic viscosity $\eta$ is in Pa$\cdot$s. Set kinematic viscosity $\nu=\eta/\rho_*$, in m$^2$/s. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be an open dimensionless spatial region and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an open time interval; set $\Omega_{\rm phys}=L\Omega$ and $I_{\rm phys}=(L/U)I$. Take $u,v\in C^\infty(\Omega\times I;\mathbb R^d)$ and $\pi,\delta\rho'\in C^\infty(\Omega\times I;\mathbb R)$; the scaled fields $u,v,\pi,\delta\rho'$ are dimensionless. Define physical velocity maps $u_{\rm phys},v_{\rm phys}\in C^\infty(\Omega_{\rm phys}\times I_{\rm phys};\mathbb R^d)$, physical-pressure maps $p_{\rm phys},\pi_{\rm phys}\in C^\infty(\Omega_{\rm phys}\times I_{\rm phys};\mathbb R)$, and density-perturbation map $\delta\rho\in C^\infty(\Omega_{\rm phys}\times I_{\rm phys};\mathbb R)$ by
$$u_{\rm phys}(X,t_{\rm phys})=Uu(X/L,Ut_{\rm phys}/L),\quad p_{\rm phys}(X,t_{\rm phys})=\rho_*U^2\pi(X/L,Ut_{\rm phys}/L),$$
$$v_{\rm phys}(X,t_{\rm phys})=Uv(X/L,Ut_{\rm phys}/L),\quad \delta\rho(X,t_{\rm phys})=\rho_*\delta\rho'(X/L,Ut_{\rm phys}/L).$$
Adopt the constant-reference-density kinematic-pressure convention $\pi_{\rm phys}:=p_{\rm phys}/\rho_*$; thus $\pi_{\rm phys}=U^2\pi$ has units m$^2$/s$^2$, while $p_{\rm phys}$ has units Pa. If $u_{\rm phys},\pi_{\rm phys}$ satisfy the constant-density incompressible system
$$\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}u_{\rm phys}+(u_{\rm phys}\cdot\nabla_X)u_{\rm phys}=-\nabla_X\pi_{\rm phys}+\nu\Delta_Xu_{\rm phys},\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu_{\rm phys}=0,$$
then the stated substitution gives the dimensionless system
$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u=-\nabla_x\pi+Re^{-1}\Delta_xu,\qquad \operatorname{div}_xu=0,$$
where $Re=UL/\nu=\rho_*UL/\eta$. Let $p_{\rm eos}:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable equation-of-state pressure map, measured in Pa, at $\rho_*$, with $p_{\rm eos}'(\rho_*)>0$ in m$^2$/s$^2$, and set the sound speed $c_*=\sqrt{p_{\rm eos}'(\rho_*)}$ in m/s. For the linear acoustic tangent system, let the physical fields $\delta\rho:\Omega_{\rm phys}\times I_{\rm phys}\to\mathbb R$ and $v_{\rm phys}:\Omega_{\rm phys}\times I_{\rm phys}\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfy
$$\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}\delta\rho+\rho_*\operatorname{div}_Xv_{\rm phys}=0,\qquad \partial_{t_{\rm phys}}v_{\rm phys}+(c_*^2/\rho_*)\nabla_X\delta\rho=0.$$
Here $\delta\rho$ has units kg/m$^3$. The scales $X=Lx$, $t_{\rm phys}=(L/U)t$, $\delta\rho=\rho_*\delta\rho'$, and $v_{\rm phys}=Uv$ give the momentum coefficient $Ma^{-2}$, where $Ma=U/c_*$. Both $Re$ and $Ma$ are dimensionless. These are chain-rule identities and assert no continuum limit or empirical similarity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

**Choice context.** The finite coefficient arrays and weighted coefficient completion below are defined without Countable Choice. In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In this coefficient-only reading, a finite real trigonometric polynomial is specified by a finite coefficient array $(a_k)$, extended by zero and satisfying $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$, and $\widehat q(k):=a_k$ denotes its specified coefficient coordinate. For the normalized Haar-measure conventions, integral Fourier coefficients and $L^2$ realization below, additionally assume Countable Choice, as in the declared measure and Fourier suppliers. In that analytic context the coefficient coordinates agree with the integral coefficients.

Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\ell>0$, and $\nu\ge0$, and write $Q_\ell=\mathbb R^d/(\ell\mathbb Z)^d$. For a period cell, define $\|f\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_\ell)}=(\int_{[0,\ell]^d}|f(x)|^2dx)^{1/2}$.

First, for $T>0$ and either $\Omega=\mathbb R^d$ or $\Omega=Q_\ell$, let $u\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ and $\pi\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a velocity-pressure pair solving the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes system
$$u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla\pi+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$
then for any $\lambda>0$,
$$u_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda u(\lambda^2t,\lambda x),\qquad \pi_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^2\pi(\lambda^2t,\lambda x)$$
solves the same system with the same viscosity on $\mathbb R^d$ or on the torus of period $\ell/\lambda$, respectively, for $0\le t\le T/\lambda^2$. On the torus, use the Fourier Leray multiplier $P_0=I$, $P_\xi=I-\xi\xi^{\mathsf T}/|\xi|^2$ for $\xi\ne0$; the projected equation is preserved as well because $P_{\lambda\xi}=P_\xi$. For a cell-volume $L^2$ norm, $\|u_\lambda(0)\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_{\ell/\lambda})}=\lambda^{1-d/2}\|u(0)\|_{L^2_{\rm vol}(Q_\ell)}$.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval. Use the Cartesian inertial-chart convention of the adopted continuum balances on Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$: $E$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space, and the event-coordinate map is $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$ with $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant. Time is absolute and measured in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, and $w$ in metres per second. All derivatives below use this fixed chart. Let $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ be open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $L>0$, reference density $\rho_*>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, reference speed $U_*>0$ in metres per second, physical polytropic coefficient $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}>0$ in pascals times $(\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{kg})^\gamma$, and dimensionless exponent $\gamma>1$. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval containing $0$ and $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/(2\pi L\mathbb Z))^d$, with position $X$ in metres and time $t$ in seconds; this is the physical cell for $d=3$ and the reduced coordinate torus for $d=1,2$, whose physical cell is $\mathbb T_L^3$. The smooth model fields are $\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}\in C^\infty(I\times\mathbb T_L^d;(0,\infty))$ and $u_{\mathrm{phys}}\in C^\infty(I\times\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$. Torus fields are understood as smooth periodic lifts to Euclidean coordinates when applying the local continuum equations. The physical density $\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}$ is measured in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in metres per second, and pressure $p_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in pascals. Adopt the unforced, positive-density barotropic Euler model
$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_X\cdot(\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}u_{\mathrm{phys}})=0,\qquad \partial_tu_{\mathrm{phys}}+(u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_X)u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_X\!\left(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma\right)=0,$$
where the same fixed $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}$ and $\gamma$ apply throughout the flow. Also adopt the specific internal-energy closure $e_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^{\gamma-1}/(\gamma-1)$ in joules per kilogram, so the model internal-energy density is $\rho e_{\mathrm{phys}}=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^\gamma/(\gamma-1)$ in pascals and $\rho^2 e_{\mathrm{phys}}\prime(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^\gamma=p_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho)$ for $\rho>0$. This is an additional constitutive assumption for the model energy; neither it nor the pressure law is derived from molecular mechanics or from an empirical measurement here.

For $d=3$, these are the direct three-dimensional equations. For $d=1,2$, define $J_d:\mathbb T_L^3\to\mathbb T_L^d$ by $J_d(X_1,X_2,X_3)=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$, with coordinates modulo $2\pi L$, and lift reduced fields by
$$\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,X)=\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,J_dX),\qquad \widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,X)=\bigl((u_{\mathrm{phys}})_1(t,J_dX),\ldots,(u_{\mathrm{phys}})_d(t,J_dX),0,\ldots,0\bigr).$$
The three-dimensional pressure and Cauchy stress are $\widetilde p_{\mathrm{phys}}=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma$ and $\widetilde\sigma=-\widetilde p_{\mathrm{phys}}I_3$. Direct differentiation gives
$$\partial_t\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_3\cdot(\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}})=\bigl(\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_d\cdot(\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}u_{\mathrm{phys}})\bigr)\circ J_d,$$
$$\partial_t\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}+(\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_3)\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_3(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma)=\bigl(\partial_tu_{\mathrm{phys}}+(u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_d)u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_d(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma),0,\ldots,0\bigr)\circ J_d.$$
Thus the lower-dimensional equations are exactly the mass and momentum reduction of the adopted three-dimensional barotropic Euler model for fields independent of the omitted coordinates and with zero omitted velocity components. Conversely, every smooth three-dimensional solution in this invariant class reduces to the stated equations. For a scalar field $f$ on $\mathbb T_L^d$ and its lift $\widetilde f=f\circ J_d$, the physical-cell means satisfy
$$\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\widetilde f(X)\,dX=\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^d}\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f(X_1,\ldots,X_d)\,dX_1\cdots dX_d;$$
this follows by integrating the constant-in-transverse-coordinate lift over the remaining $3-d$ periodic coordinates.

Set $x=X/L\in\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z))^d$, $\tau=tU_*/L$, $R=\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}/\rho_*$, $V=u_{\mathrm{phys}}/U_*$, $P=p_{\mathrm{phys}}/(\rho_*U_*^2)$, and $\bar\kappa=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_*^{\gamma-1}/U_*^2>0$. Put $a=(\gamma-1)/2$ and $r(R)=\sqrt{\bar\kappa\gamma}\,R^a/a$. For smooth periodic $f$, use normalized measure $d\mu_x=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, Fourier coefficients $\widehat f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu_x$, and $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+|k|^2)^m|\widehat f(k)|^2$. Let $\rho_0:\mathbb T_L^d\to(0,\infty)$ and $u_0:\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be smooth real periodic initial data, and define $R_0(x)=\rho_0(Lx)/\rho_*$ and $V_0(x)=u_0(Lx)/U_*$. Then for every integer $s\ge4$ there is $T>0$, depending only on $d,s,\bar\kappa,\gamma,\|(r(R_0),V_0)\|_{H^s}$, and $\min r(R_0)$, such that the normalized system
$$\partial_\tau R+\nabla_x\cdot(RV)=0,\qquad \partial_\tau V+(V\cdot\nabla_x)V+R^{-1}\nabla_x(\bar\kappa R^\gamma)=0,\qquad R(0,\cdot)=R_0,\quad V(0,\cdot)=V_0$$
has a unique smooth real solution on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $R(\tau,x)>0$ and every integer Sobolev order $m\ge s$ bounded on that same interval. The dimensionless mean total-energy density
$$\overline E(\tau)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\left(\tfrac12 R|V|^2+\frac{\bar\kappa}{\gamma-1}R^\gamma\right)d\mu_x$$
is constant. Equivalently, $\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\left(\tfrac12\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}|\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}|^2+\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma/(\gamma-1)\right)\,dX$ is constant and has units of pascals; for $d=3$ the tildes are omitted, and for $d=1,2$ this mean equals the reduced $d$-dimensional cell mean by the formula above. The polytropic pressure law is an adopted constitutive closure, not a molecular derivation. No temperature-coupled equation, vacuum or shock continuation, spatially varying constitutive parameters, or empirical validity claim is included.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $L>0$, reference density $\rho_*>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, reference speed $U_*>0$ in metres per second, physical polytropic coefficient $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}>0$ in pascals times $(\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{kg})^\gamma$, and dimensionless exponent $\gamma>1$. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval containing $0$ and $\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/(2\pi L\mathbb Z))^d$, with position $X$ in metres and time $t$ in seconds; this is the physical cell for $d=3$ and the reduced coordinate torus for $d=1,2$, whose physical cell is $\mathbb T_L^3$. The smooth model fields are $\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}\in C^\infty(I\times\mathbb T_L^d;(0,\infty))$ and $u_{\mathrm{phys}}\in C^\infty(I\times\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$. Torus fields are understood as smooth periodic lifts to Euclidean coordinates when applying the local continuum equations. The physical density $\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}$ is measured in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in metres per second, and pressure $p_{\mathrm{phys}}$ in pascals. Adopt the unforced, positive-density barotropic Euler model
$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_X\cdot(\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}u_{\mathrm{phys}})=0,\qquad \partial_tu_{\mathrm{phys}}+(u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_X)u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_X\!\left(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma\right)=0,$$
where the same fixed $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}$ and $\gamma$ apply throughout the flow. Also adopt the specific internal-energy closure $e_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^{\gamma-1}/(\gamma-1)$ in joules per kilogram, so the model internal-energy density is $\rho e_{\mathrm{phys}}=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^\gamma/(\gamma-1)$ in pascals and $\rho^2 e_{\mathrm{phys}}\prime(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho^\gamma=p_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho)$ for $\rho>0$. This is an additional constitutive assumption for the model energy; neither it nor the pressure law is derived from molecular mechanics or from an empirical measurement here.

For $d=3$, these are the direct three-dimensional equations. For $d=1,2$, define $J_d:\mathbb T_L^3\to\mathbb T_L^d$ by $J_d(X_1,X_2,X_3)=(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$, with coordinates modulo $2\pi L$, and lift reduced fields by
$$\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,X)=\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,J_dX),\qquad \widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,X)=\bigl((u_{\mathrm{phys}})_1(t,J_dX),\ldots,(u_{\mathrm{phys}})_d(t,J_dX),0,\ldots,0\bigr).$$
The three-dimensional pressure and Cauchy stress are $\widetilde p_{\mathrm{phys}}=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma$ and $\widetilde\sigma=-\widetilde p_{\mathrm{phys}}I_3$. Direct differentiation gives
$$\partial_t\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_3\cdot(\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}})=\bigl(\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}+\nabla_d\cdot(\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}u_{\mathrm{phys}})\bigr)\circ J_d,$$
$$\partial_t\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}+(\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_3)\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_3(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma)=\bigl(\partial_tu_{\mathrm{phys}}+(u_{\mathrm{phys}}\cdot\nabla_d)u_{\mathrm{phys}}+\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^{-1}\nabla_d(\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma),0,\ldots,0\bigr)\circ J_d.$$
Thus the lower-dimensional equations are exactly the mass and momentum reduction of the adopted three-dimensional barotropic Euler model for fields independent of the omitted coordinates and with zero omitted velocity components. Conversely, every smooth three-dimensional solution in this invariant class reduces to the stated equations. For a scalar field $f$ on $\mathbb T_L^d$ and its lift $\widetilde f=f\circ J_d$, the physical-cell means satisfy
$$\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\widetilde f(X)\,dX=\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^d}\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f(X_1,\ldots,X_d)\,dX_1\cdots dX_d;$$
this follows by integrating the constant-in-transverse-coordinate lift over the remaining $3-d$ periodic coordinates.

Set $x=X/L\in\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z))^d$, $\tau=tU_*/L$, $R=\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}/\rho_*$, $V=u_{\mathrm{phys}}/U_*$, $P=p_{\mathrm{phys}}/(\rho_*U_*^2)$, and $\bar\kappa=\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_*^{\gamma-1}/U_*^2>0$. Put $a=(\gamma-1)/2$ and $r(R)=\sqrt{\bar\kappa\gamma}\,R^a/a$. For smooth periodic $f$, use normalized measure $d\mu_x=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, Fourier coefficients $\widehat f(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu_x$, and $\|f\|_{H^m}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+|k|^2)^m|\widehat f(k)|^2$. Let $\rho_0:\mathbb T_L^d\to(0,\infty)$ and $u_0:\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be smooth real periodic initial data, and define $R_0(x)=\rho_0(Lx)/\rho_*$ and $V_0(x)=u_0(Lx)/U_*$. Then for every integer $s\ge4$ there is $T>0$, depending only on $d,s,\bar\kappa,\gamma,\|(r(R_0),V_0)\|_{H^s}$, and $\min r(R_0)$, such that the normalized system
$$\partial_\tau R+\nabla_x\cdot(RV)=0,\qquad \partial_\tau V+(V\cdot\nabla_x)V+R^{-1}\nabla_x(\bar\kappa R^\gamma)=0,\qquad R(0,\cdot)=R_0,\quad V(0,\cdot)=V_0$$
has a unique smooth real solution on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $R(\tau,x)>0$ and every integer Sobolev order $m\ge s$ bounded on that same interval. The dimensionless mean total-energy density
$$\overline E(\tau)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\left(\tfrac12 R|V|^2+\frac{\bar\kappa}{\gamma-1}R^\gamma\right)d\mu_x$$
is constant. Equivalently, $\frac{1}{(2\pi L)^3}\int_{\mathbb T_L^3}\left(\tfrac12\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}|\widetilde u_{\mathrm{phys}}|^2+\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\widetilde\rho_{\mathrm{phys}}^\gamma/(\gamma-1)\right)\,dX$ is constant and has units of pascals; for $d=3$ the tildes are omitted, and for $d=1,2$ this mean equals the reduced $d$-dimensional cell mean by the formula above. The polytropic pressure law is an adopted constitutive closure, not a molecular derivation. No temperature-coupled equation, vacuum or shock continuation, spatially varying constitutive parameters, or empirical validity claim is included.

Thus the mass equation holds.

The pressure $\kappa_{\mathrm{phys}}\rho_*^\gamma$ is constant, so its gradient vanishes; the momentum equation also holds. The density stays strictly positive, and all fields are smooth and periodic.

derivations.claim: Let $\widetilde\Omega=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R$ and $\Lambda=\{(mL_x,0,nL_z):m,n\in\mathbb Z\}$. For $U=U_P$ in the Poiseuille case and $U=U_C$ in the Couette case, define the lifted material map for each $t$ by $\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z)=(x+tU(y),y,z)$. Both profiles are smooth, so this map is $C^\infty$; its inverse is $(x-tU(y),y,z)$. It maps $\widetilde\Omega$ onto itself, fixes the $y$ coordinate, and obeys $\widetilde\chi^U_t(a+\lambda)=\widetilde\chi^U_t(a)+\lambda$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$. Its Jacobian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&tU'(y)&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $1>0$. Since $y$ is unchanged, $\partial_t\widetilde\chi^U_t=(U(y),0,0)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z))$, so each map descends to the periodic channel and has the example's velocity as its Eulerian velocity. Thus both profiles meet the material-motion hypothesis of [F1].

In the Poiseuille case, $U_P(0)=U_P(h)=0$ and $U_P''=-G/\eta$. Thus $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x+\rho b_x=\eta U_P''+G=0$, and the other momentum components vanish, proving the steady equations and no-slip compatibility. Direct integration gives $Q_P=\int_0^hU_P(y)\,dy=Gh^3/(12\eta)$ and $\omega_{P,z}=-U_P'=-G(h-2y)/(2\eta)$.

In the Couette case, $U_C(0)=0$, $U_C(h)=V$, and $U_C''=0$, so the momentum equation holds with constant pressure and no body force; the velocity traces equal the stated wall velocities. Direct integration gives $Q_C=\int_0^hU_C(y)\,dy=Vh/2$ and $\omega_{C,z}=-U_C'=-V/h$.

By the defined squared norm $|D|^2=D:D$, for either profile $|D|^2=(U')^2/2$, hence viscous dissipation per unit streamwise/spanwise wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(U')^2\,dy$. In the Poiseuille case this is $\frac{G^2}{4\eta}\int_0^h(h-2y)^2\,dy=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$, while body-force power is $\int_0^h\rho(G/\rho)U_P\,dy=GQ_P=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$; stationary-wall power is zero. This agrees with the stationary no-slip case of [F1].

In the Couette case viscous dissipation per unit wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(V/h)^2\,dy=\eta V^2/h$. At the top wall $n=(0,1,0)$ and $\sigma n$ has tangential component $\eta(V/h)(1,0,0)$, so wall power per unit area is $g\cdot\sigma n=\eta V^2/h$; the lower wall has $g=0$. This agrees with the tangential no-slip case of [F1]. Finally, a purported periodic pressure $p_0-Gx$ changes by $-GL_x$ under $x\mapsto x+L_x$, so it is not single-valued on $\Omega$ when $G>0$; the body-force formulation in the Example avoids that incompatibility.

For either profile $u=(U(y),0,0)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $\partial_tu=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=U(y)\partial_xu=0$. The only nonzero entries of $D$ are $D_{xy}=D_{yx}=U'/2$, so the only nonzero viscous shear entries are $\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}=\eta U'$, and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x=-\partial_xp+\eta U''$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.
