Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. derivations.claim: For every $k\ne0$, the multiplier $P_k$ is the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto $\kappa_k^\perp$, since it is symmetric, $P_k^2=P_k$, and $P_k\kappa_k=0$; $P_0=I$ leaves constant vector fields unrestricted.

By [F1], coefficient sequences in the displayed weighted square-sum define unique $L^2$ classes, and Fourier truncations converge in the stated $H^s$ norm whenever that sum is finite. The conjugation condition is exactly the real-valued condition. Under the periodic distribution definition in the Definition, testing $\operatorname{div}u$ against $e_{-k}$ gives $i\kappa_k\cdot\widehat u(k)$, so zero distributional divergence implies $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$ for each $k\ne0$. Conversely, if these coefficients vanish, every trigonometric-polynomial test pairs to zero. A smooth periodic test has rapidly decaying Fourier coefficients by repeated integration by parts, so its Fourier partial sums converge with every derivative uniformly; continuity of the divergence functional then gives zero pairing with every smooth test. This proves the equivalence and defines the stated real Hilbert coefficient spaces and projections.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Under Countable Choice, each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

derivations.claim: The weak-continuity clause is the continuity of all scalar coordinate maps $t\mapsto(u(t),h)_H$ and therefore defines a property of an actual map; it makes no assertion of norm continuity. The Bochner conditions, by contrast, are properties of almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

If $u,v\in C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere, then for each fixed $h\in H$ the continuous scalar function $t\mapsto(u(t)-v(t),h)_H$ vanishes almost everywhere. A continuous scalar function that is nonzero at any point is nonzero on a relative interval of positive measure, including at an endpoint, so this function vanishes everywhere. Taking $h=u(t)-v(t)$ gives $u(t)=v(t)$ for every $t$. Thus a weakly continuous representative, if it exists for a Bochner class, is unique.

Under the Countable Choice convention in [F1], the periodic targets are separable. Consider finite vector Fourier arrays with coefficients in $\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, support in $\{|k|_\infty\le N\}$ for an integer $N$, and conjugate symmetry; their associated real polynomials form a countable family. For $H$ and $V$, apply $P_k$ to each coefficient. This preserves conjugate symmetry and gives finite solenoidal arrays; $P_0=I$ retains the mean mode. Given a target field, first truncate its coefficient series in its target norm, then approximate the finitely many coefficients by rational real and imaginary coordinates with the opposite modes paired by conjugation. Since $P_k$ is a contraction and fixes the target solenoidal coefficients, the projected rational approximants converge in the $H$ or $V$ norm. For the real $H^{-r}$ space, omit the projections: its definition as the weighted completion of finite conjugate-symmetric arrays gives the same density argument. Complex targets use the corresponding unpaired rational complex arrays. Thus every periodic target named here is separable; [F2] supplies the bounded-domain targets under its own Axiom of Choice hypothesis. Finally, $L^p_{\rm loc}$ is exactly the conjunction of the Bochner-class conditions over finite intervals. No stronger assumption on the abstract spaces in the Definition is needed.

$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any

$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$

([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert

2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;

   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The zero-extension map embeds $H$ isometrically into $L^2$ of a periodic cube containing $\overline\Omega$ in its interior. By [F2], it embeds $V$ into the finite product consisting of the zero extension and its three first derivatives in $L^2$ of that cube. Each ambient space is separable by [F4]. Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable: take its countable base of intersections with ambient rational balls and, using [F5], choose one point from each nonempty intersection. Thus $H$ and $V$ are separable.

The $L^2$ and $H^1$ graph inner products make the ambient spaces Hilbert: completeness of $L^2$ and the Sobolev completeness in [F3] give convergence of Cauchy sequences in the function and all derivative coordinates, and the weak-derivative identity passes to the limit against each test. The spaces $H,V$ are closed by their definitions as closures, so they inherit Hilbert structure. The $V$ norm dominates the $H$ norm; since $D_\sigma$ is dense in both closures, the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous with dense image.

Separability of $V$ and density of $D_\sigma$ in $V$ allow Countable Choice to select $d_j\in D_\sigma$ approximating a countable dense subset of $V$ to every rational precision; the selected countable collection is dense in $V$ and, because $D_\sigma$ is also dense in $H$, its linear span is dense in $H$. The space $D_\sigma$ is infinite dimensional: choose countably many disjoint balls in one ball contained in $\Omega$ and in each choose a nonzero smooth compactly supported curl field; their disjoint supports give linear independence. Apply Gram–Schmidt in $H$ to the selected collection, discarding zero remainders. Each resulting $e_j$ is a finite linear combination of elements of $D_\sigma$, so is still in $D_\sigma$; its span contains every selected $d_j$ after the corresponding finite stage and is therefore dense in $V$ and $H$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

$$|w(x-h)-w(x)|^2\le |h|^2\int_0^1|\nabla w(x-sh)|^2ds.$$
Integrating in $x$, using translation invariance and [F4], yields
$\|w(\cdot-h)-w\|_2\le|h|\|\nabla w\|_2$. Density and the isometric zero extension [F3] extend this estimate to every $a\in V$.

Fix a nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with integral one and set $\eta_\epsilon(x)=\epsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\epsilon)$. For each $x$, Cauchy–Schwarz with respect to the probability density $\eta_\epsilon(h)$ gives $|\int\eta_\epsilon(h)(E_0a(x)-E_0a(x-h))dh|^2\le\int\eta_\epsilon(h)|E_0a(x)-E_0a(x-h)|^2dh$. Integrating in $x$, applying [F4] to interchange the integrals, and using step 1.1 give
$$\|E_0a-\eta_\epsilon*E_0a\|_2^2\le\int\eta_\epsilon(h)\|E_0a(\cdot-h)-E_0a\|_2^2dh\le C_\eta^2\epsilon^2\|\nabla a\|_2^2.$$

[F6] bounds their sup norms by $\|\eta_\epsilon\|_2\|a\|_2$ and their first derivatives by $\|\nabla\eta_\epsilon\|_2\|a\|_2$, uniformly on the $V$ unit ball. Cover the box by a finite grid fine enough that the derivative bound changes every value by less than a prescribed tolerance; quantize the bounded vector values at grid points in a finite lattice. The resulting finitely many piecewise-constant fields approximate every mollified field in sup norm, hence in $L^2$ on the finite box. Step 2.1 transfers these finite nets to finite $L^2$ nets for the original $V$ unit ball, with arbitrarily small error. Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

derivations.claim: For each fixed $k$, the coefficients are bounded by $A$ and have common Lipschitz constant $C_k$. The following deterministic rule extracts a convergent subsequence from any sequence in the closed cube $[-A,A]^{2d}$ underlying $\mathbb C^d$. Order the finitely many closed half-sized subcubes lexicographically, retain the first containing infinitely many terms of the current index set, and repeat inside that cube. Select from the $j$th retained infinite index set the least index greater than the previously selected index. The selected terms converge because the cubes are nested, closed, and have diameters tending to zero. Enumerate the countable pairs $(k,q)$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and $q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,T]$. Apply this fixed rule recursively to the preceding subsequence for each successive pair, and take diagonal indices, each the least available index greater than the preceding one. For any fixed pair the diagonal is eventually a subsequence of its convergent extraction. Thus it converges at every such pair without any dependent sequence of arbitrary choices. For each fixed $k$, the common Lipschitz bound and a finite rational mesh make the coefficients uniformly Cauchy on $[0,T]$, including its endpoints. Thus one subsequence converges uniformly in every Fourier coefficient.

At each time, every finite Fourier sum of squared limiting coefficients is at most $A^2$; Parseval therefore defines $z(t)\in H$ with norm at most $A$. Pairings with finite Fourier sums are continuous in time. For arbitrary $h\in H$, approximate $h$ by its finite Fourier truncations; the pairing error is at most $2A\|h-\Pi_Kh\|_2$, uniformly in time, so $t\mapsto(z(t),h)$ is continuous. Finite gradient sums integrated in time pass to the limit and are bounded by $B$; monotone convergence gives a finite gradient square sum for almost every $t$. On that full-measure set, the finite Fourier truncations $\Pi_Mz(t)$ converge to $z(t)$ in $V$. Each $\Pi_Mz$ is continuous with values in a finite-dimensional subspace of $V$, hence is a uniform limit of measurable simple maps by uniform continuity on $[0,T]$. Keep the actual map $z:[0,T]\to H$ defined by its limiting coefficients at every time. Define a separate $V$-valued representative $\widetilde z(t)=z(t)$ where the gradient square sum is finite and $\widetilde z(t)=0$ on the exceptional null set. The continuous finite-dimensional maps $\Pi_Mz$ converge to $\widetilde z$ in $V$ almost everywhere, so $\widetilde z$ is strongly measurable. Its $V$ norm is integrable in square because the integrated $H$ norm is at most $TA^2$ and the integrated gradient square sum is at most $B$. Thus $\widetilde z$ defines a class in $L^2(0,T;V)$ whose $H$-valued class is represented by the unchanged weakly continuous map $z$. The asserted pointwise $H$ bound and every limiting Fourier coefficient continue to refer to that unchanged map; only the Bochner representative has been assigned zero on the exceptional set.

If $|k|_\infty>K$, then $|\kappa_k|\ge2\pi K/L$, so Parseval and the gradient bound give
$\int_0^T\sum_{|k|_\infty>K}|\widehat z_n(k,t)|^2dt\le BL^2/(4\pi^2K^2)$; the same estimate holds for $z$. On the finitely many modes $|k|_\infty\le K$, uniform coefficient convergence gives strong $L^2$ convergence. Letting $K\to\infty$ proves strong convergence in $L^2(0,T;H)$.

The product estimate
$\|z_n\otimes z_n-z\otimes z\|_{L^1_{t,x}}\le(\|z_n\|_{L^2_{t,x}}+\|z\|_{L^2_{t,x}})\|z_n-z\|_{L^2_{t,x}}$
proves strong $L^1$ convergence of the quadratic tensors. Recursively choose the least index larger than its predecessor for which the squared $L^2_tH$ error is at most $2^{-j}$ at stage $j$; strong convergence ensures such an index exists. The resulting squared errors have finite sum. By [F3], their pointwise sum is finite for almost every time, so the subsequence converges strongly in $H$ at each such time.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Under Countable Choice, each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

Assume Countable Choice and let $V$ be any separable real Hilbert space. Its continuous real-linear dual $V^*$,
with norm $\|\ell\|_{V^*}=\sup_{\|v\|_V\le1}|\ell(v)|$, is a separable real
Hilbert space. The Riesz map
$$J:V\to V^*,\qquad Jw(v)=(w,v)_V$$
is a surjective linear isometry.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, [F9] and the local closure formulas in the Statement give $H_0^1=H=V=\{0\}$. The only linear functional on $V$ is zero, so $V^*=\{0\}$ as well; each zero space is a separable real Hilbert space (the singleton $\{0\}$ is dense). Every spatial $L^p$ class and every time-dependent map with one of these zero targets is zero, with the constant zero simple map proving strong measurability. Thus both spatial inequalities, time integrability, representative independence, the defining formula for $b_u$, and the $V^*$ norm bound all hold with zero on both sides, for the same positive universal constant as in the nonempty case. No basis, approximation sequence or zero-extension theorem for a nonempty domain is applied here. Henceforth assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$; all uses of [F1], [F6] and [F8] below are in that case.

For real $g\in C^1([a,b])$, put $G(t)=\int_a^t g'(s)ds$. The difference between its difference quotient at an interior $t$ and $g'(t)$ is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}|g'(s)-g'(t)|$, which tends to zero. Hence $(G-g)'=0$ everywhere inside the interval; the mean value theorem and endpoint continuity give $g(b)-g(a)=\int_a^b g'$. For $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ define $A_1(x_2,x_3)=\int_{\mathbb R}|\partial_1h(x_1,x_2,x_3)|dx_1$, and define $A_2(x_1,x_3)$ and $A_3(x_1,x_2)$ analogously. Applying the endpoint identity along each coordinate line from a point outside the support gives $|h(x)|\le A_i(x_{\widehat i})$ for each $i$, hence $|h|^{3/2}\le(A_1A_2A_3)^{1/2}$. Put $B_2(x_3)=\int A_2(x_1,x_3)dx_1$ and $B_3(x_2)=\int A_3(x_1,x_2)dx_1$. Cauchy–Schwarz in $x_1$ gives $\int(A_2A_3)^{1/2}dx_1\le(B_2B_3)^{1/2}$; applying Cauchy–Schwarz in $(x_2,x_3)$ to the remaining $A_1^{1/2}(B_2B_3)^{1/2}$ gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|h|^{3/2}\le(\int_{\mathbb R^2}A_1)^{1/2}(\int_{\mathbb R}B_2)^{1/2}(\int_{\mathbb R}B_3)^{1/2}=\prod_{i=1}^3(\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\partial_i h|)^{1/2}.$$
The changes of integration order are justified by [F3]. Raising to the power $2/3$ yields $\|h\|_{3/2}\le\prod_i\|\partial_i h\|_1^{1/3}$.

For a smooth compactly supported vector field $w$, set $h=|w|^4$, which is smooth, and note $|\partial_i h|\le4|w|^3|\partial_iw|$. Hölder gives $\|\partial_i h\|_1\le4\|w\|_6^3\|\partial_iw\|_2$. Substitution into step 1.2 yields $\|w\|_6^4\le4\|w\|_6^3\prod_i\|\partial_iw\|_2^{1/3}\le4\|w\|_6^3\|\nabla w\|_2$. Divide when $\|w\|_6>0$; if it is zero the inequality is immediate.

By [F1] and [F5], choose $w_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ converging to $a$ in $H^1$. The inequality of step 2.1 applied to differences makes $(w_n)$ Cauchy in $L^6$; on bounded $\Omega$, convergence in $L^6$ also implies convergence in $L^2$, so its $L^6$ limit is the given $L^2$ class $a$. Passing to the limit proves the first inequality. Finally, $\int|a|^4\le(\int|a|^2)^{1/2}(\int|a|^6)^{1/2}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, which proves the interpolation inequality. For almost every $t$, raising it to power $8/3$ gives $\|u(t)\|_4^{8/3}\le\|u(t)\|_2^{2/3}\|u(t)\|_6^2\le C\|u(t)\|_H^{2/3}\|u(t)\|_V^2$. Integrating and using $u\in L^\infty_tH\cap L^2_tV$ proves the stated $L^{8/3}_tL^4_x$ bound.

Fix the strongly measurable representative $\widetilde u$ chosen in the Statement. For almost every time, Hölder gives $|b_u(t)(\phi)|\le\|\widetilde u(t)\|_4^2\|\nabla\phi\|_2$, so $b_u(t)\in V^*$ and its norm is at most $\|\widetilde u(t)\|_4^2$. The map $a\mapsto b_a$ is continuous from $L^4$ to $V^*$ because $\|b_a-b_c\|_{V^*}\le(\|a\|_4+\|c\|_4)\|a-c\|_4$. Composing simple-map approximations to $\widetilde u$ with the continuous embedding $V\to L^4$ and this map therefore gives strongly measurable $V^*$-valued $b_u$, up to the permitted null-set assignment; [F6,F8] provide the separable Hilbert target. Two representatives of the same $L^2_tV$ class agree in $V$ almost everywhere, hence agree in $L^4$ there and define the same $b_u$ almost everywhere. Thus its Bochner class is independent of the representative. Finally $\int_0^T\|b_u(t)\|_{V^*}^{4/3}dt\le\int_0^T\|\widetilde u(t)\|_4^{8/3}dt<\infty$ by step 3.1; [F7] gives $b_u\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$.

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, $u_0\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time
conventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and
Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
$u:[0,\infty)\to H$ such that its restriction to each finite interval is in
$C_w([0,T];H)$ and its Bochner equivalence classes satisfy
$u\in L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$. All clauses
involving $u(t)$ at a specified time, including the initial trace and energy
inequalities, refer to this weakly continuous map. By the uniqueness result in
Weak time continuity and energy spaces, it is the unique weakly continuous
representative of those Bochner classes. It must satisfy $u(0)=u_0$ in $H$,
$\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for
every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field
$\phi:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d\to\mathbb R^d$ compactly supported in
time,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It must also satisfy, for every $t\ge0$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u(s)\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2,$$
and there must be a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for
every $s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and every $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u(\tau)\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
For a matrix field $A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The tensor pairing means $(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$;
the gradient pairing means $\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$.
All derivatives in the weak identity are distributional; the definition
asserts neither uniqueness nor smoothness.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, and $T>0$. Let $z_n:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous
finite-Fourier-sum curves such that, for constants $A,B<\infty$,
$$\sup_{n,t}\|z_n(t)\|_H\le A,\qquad \sup_n\int_0^T\|\nabla z_n(t)\|_2^2dt\le B,$$
and for each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ there is $C_k<\infty$ with
$|\widehat z_n(k,t)-\widehat z_n(k,s)|\le C_k|t-s|$ for all $n,s,t$.
Then some subsequence converges uniformly in each Fourier coefficient to
$z\in C_w([0,T];H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, with
$\sup_t\|z(t)\|_H\le A$ and $\int_0^T\|\nabla z\|_2^2dt\le B$; it also
converges strongly to $z$ in $L^2(0,T;H)$ and, after a further subsequence,
strongly in $H$ for almost every $t$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $r>d/2+1$, and $a\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$.
Use the Fourier multipliers $P_k$, negative-space norm and divergence convention of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces. Identify an $H^{-r}$ coefficient sequence $c=(c_k)$ with the periodic distribution
$$\langle T_c,\varphi\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}c_k\cdot\widehat\varphi(-k)\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C^d)),$$
using the bilinear pairing and normalized measure. On $H^{-r}$ define $P$ by $(Pc)_k=P_kc_k$; this is the extension of the $L^2$ projection under this distribution identification. Then $\operatorname{div}(a\otimes a)$ and $P\operatorname{div}(a\otimes a)$ belong to $H^{-r}$, and the projected distribution satisfies
$$\|P\operatorname{div}(a\otimes a)\|_{H^{-r}}\le C(d,L,r)\|a\|_2^2.$$
Here $(a\otimes a)_{ij}=a_i a_j$ and
$(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. The estimate uses no
three-dimensional singular-integral bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

derivations.claim:
For $N\ge1$, let $X_N=\operatorname{ran}\Pi_N\cap H$ and solve in this finite-dimensional real space
$$\partial_tu_N+\Pi_NP\operatorname{div}(u_N\otimes u_N)=\nu\Delta u_N,\qquad u_N(0)=\Pi_Nu_0.$$
Choose real orthonormal coordinates on $X_N$, whose finite Fourier coefficients satisfy the real conjugation and solenoidal conditions. The right side preserves this real space and is a polynomial vector field $F_N:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$. It is continuous on the open time-state domain $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m$; its derivative is bounded on each closed coefficient ball, so integration along line segments gives a Lipschitz bound there. Thus [F6] gives a unique local solution through the projected initial value. Pairing with $u_N$ removes $P,\Pi_N$ by orthogonality, and periodic integration by parts gives $\int (u_N\cdot\nabla)u_N\cdot u_N=\int\operatorname{div}(u_N|u_N|^2/2)=0$. Thus
$$\|u_N(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u_N\|_2^2d\tau=\|u_N(s)\|_2^2$$
on every local existence interval. [given, F1, F6, algebra]

By the overlap uniqueness in [F6], all local solutions through the initial data glue on their interval union to one maximal solution. The energy identity bounds its coordinates in the fixed finite-dimensional real space $X_N$ for all nonnegative times of existence. The polynomial vector field is bounded on that closed coefficient ball, so the coordinate curve is uniformly Lipschitz in time. If its positive endpoint $\beta$ were finite, completeness of $\mathbb R^m$ would give a limit $a_*$ as $t\uparrow\beta$. Apply [F6] at $(\beta,a_*)$ and join the resulting local solution to the old curve. The derivatives match because both approach $F_N(a_*)$, so this is a $C^1$ solution extending the maximal interval, a contradiction. Therefore every $u_N$ is forward global and the energy identity holds for all $0\le s\le t$. [given, F6, step 1.1]

For fixed $k$, the nonlinear coefficient is bounded by $C|\kappa_k|\|u_N\|_2^2$ and the viscous coefficient by $\nu|\kappa_k|^2\|u_N\|_2$. The energy identity supplies uniform $L^\infty H$ and $L^2V$ bounds. The fixed-mode derivative bound is therefore uniform in $N$; [F3] gives subsequential compactness on each finite horizon. Applying [F5] diagonally over integer horizons yields one global limit $u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}V$ with the stated energy bounds. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

For a finite Fourier divergence-free test, uniform coefficient convergence passes the time-linear terms, strong $L^2_tH$ convergence passes the quadratic term by [F3], and the viscous term passes after integration by parts as $+\nu(u_N,\Delta\phi)$, using strong $L^2_tH$ convergence. A smooth periodic test and its time derivative have uniformly convergent Fourier truncations on their compact time support, by repeated integration by parts in space; the uniform energy bound controls the truncation errors. Thus the weak identity in [F2] holds for every admissible test, including its initial term because $\Pi_Nu_0\to u_0$ in $H$.

For each fixed $t$, finite coefficient convergence gives $\|u(t)\|_2^2\le\liminf_N\|u_N(t)\|_2^2$. For the gradient integral on $[s,t]$, each finite Fourier sum is the limit of the corresponding Galerkin sum and is bounded above by the full Galerkin integral; increasing the finite sets gives the lower-semicontinuous bound for $\int_s^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2$. At $s=0$, use $\Pi_Nu_0\to u_0$ in the Galerkin equality to obtain the initial energy inequality for every $t$. By step 2.2, the selected sequence converges strongly in $L^2(0,m;H)$ to $u$ for every positive integer $m$. Countable Choice therefore selects one increasing subsubsequence $(N_j)$ such that $\|u_{N_j}-u\|_{L^2(0,j;H)}^2\le2^{-j}$ for each $j$. For each integer $m$, Tonelli [F3] gives $\sum_{j\ge m}\|u_{N_j}(s)-u(s)\|_H^2<\infty$ for almost every $s\in(0,m)$; intersecting these full-measure sets over $m$ gives one full-measure $S\subset(0,\infty)$ with strong $H$ convergence at every $s\in S$. For each such $s$, passing the Galerkin equality at $s$ and any fixed $t\ge s$ gives the restart inequality; since the lower-semicontinuity bounds hold for every fixed $t$, this establishes the inequality for all $t\ge s$.

The coefficient convergence implies $u(t)\rightharpoonup u_0$ in $H$ as $t\downarrow0$. The initial energy inequality gives $\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\|u(t)\|_2\le\|u_0\|_2$; weak convergence and the Hilbert identity for $\|u(t)-u_0\|_2^2$ then imply strong convergence to $u_0$. Together the compactness, weak-limit, and energy arguments verify every clause of the Leray–Hopf definition; the finite-dimensional local existence and continuation used above are supplied by [F6]. [given, F2, F5, F6, step 2.2, step 3.2] ∎

Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

derivations.claim: Write $T=u\otimes u$. The global $L^\infty_tL^2_x$ bound makes $u,T$ locally integrable on the time-periodic cylinder, and their regular pairings on each fixed compact time support are bounded by local $L^1$ norms times $p_{K,0}$. Their absolute-value seminorms therefore belong to the test topology defined in the Statement, so $u,T$ are spacetime distributions and their derivatives use the stated transpose convention. The quadratic map $a\mapsto a\otimes a$ is continuous from $L^2_x$ to $L^1_x$, making each Fourier coefficient measurable and bounded on finite time intervals. The multiplier formula defines $\widehat\pi(k,t)$; its coefficients are bounded in $k$ by $C_d\|u(t)\|_2^2$. Repeated spatial integration by parts gives rapid uniform decay of smooth-test Fourier coefficients. The pairing series for $\pi$ is absolutely convergent and bounded by a finite-order test seminorm, hence continuous in the stated test topology and zero at the spatial mean mode.

At each nonzero frequency, the Fourier multiplier identity gives $i\kappa_k\widehat\pi(k)=- (I-P_k)\,i\sum_b\kappa_{k,b}\widehat T_{\cdot b}(k)$; the zero-frequency identity is also valid because both sides vanish. The weak identity in [F1] is exactly $\partial_tu+P\operatorname{div}T-
u\Delta u=0$ after testing against solenoidal fields. Adding the displayed gradient identity yields $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}T+
abla\pi-
u\Delta u=0$ for every smooth periodic vector test, which is the claimed equation.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ are two such mean-zero distributions, their difference $Q$ has zero spatial gradient. Its $k$th spatial Fourier coefficient, a distribution in time, therefore vanishes for every $k\ne0$ since $i\kappa_k\ne0$; its zero coefficient vanishes by the mean-zero normalization. For any compactly time-supported smooth periodic test $\phi(t,x)$, repeated integration by parts in $x$ makes its spatial Fourier coefficients and all their time derivatives decay faster than every power of $|k|$, uniformly on the compact time support. Thus its rectangular Fourier partial sums converge to $\phi$ in the smooth test-function topology. Continuity of $Q$ and vanishing of all its spatial Fourier coefficients give $\langle Q,\phi\rangle=0$. Hence $Q=0$ as a spacetime distribution, proving uniqueness.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, and $u_0\in H$ for the
periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces on $\mathbb T_L^d$. Let $u$ be any global
unforced periodic Leray–Hopf solution with data $(\nu,u_0)$ supplied by Global
periodic weak viscous existence under these hypotheses. Put
$U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d$, and let $\mathcal D_{\rm per}(U)$ be the
space of smooth complex-valued functions on $U$, represented by smooth
$L$-periodic lifts in space, that are compactly supported in time. For tests
supported in a fixed compact interval $K\subset(0,\infty)$, use the seminorms
$$p_{K,m}(\phi)=\max_{j+|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{(t,x)\in K\times\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial_t^j\partial_x^\alpha\phi(t,x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0);$$
equip $\mathcal D_{\rm per}(U)$ with the locally convex inductive-limit
topology over these fixed-time-support spaces, generated by all seminorms whose
restriction to every fixed-time-support space is continuous. A spacetime distribution means a
continuous complex-linear functional on this test space; all pairings are
bilinear, and derivatives act by transposing the corresponding test derivative
with a minus sign. Then there is a unique mean-zero-in-space
distribution $\pi$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb T_L^d$ such that
$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nabla\pi=\nu\Delta u$
as a spacetime distribution, normalized by requiring its zero spatial Fourier
coefficient to vanish. Specifically, for $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, its $k$th spatial
Fourier coefficient is the time distribution defined by
$\langle\widehat\pi(k),\psi\rangle=\langle\pi,\psi(t)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\rangle$
for $\psi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$, with the spacetime
distribution pairing taken using $dt\,L^{-d}dx$ and extended complex-linearly;
normalization means $\widehat\pi(0)=0$. No
function-space or pointwise regularity for $\pi$ is
asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set. Let
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ denote smooth compactly supported vector
fields and set
$$D_\sigma(\Omega)=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}.$$
Let $H$ be the closure of $D_\sigma(\Omega)$ in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and let $V$ be its closure in
$H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, where $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of
$C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and weak derivatives define the $H^1$
norm. Use $\|a\|_H=\|a\|_2$ and
$\|a\|_V^2=\|a\|_2^2+\|\nabla a\|_2^2$. Under Countable Choice, each $V$ element has zero
extension in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ and distributional divergence zero. This
closure definition does not identify $V$ with every divergence-free member
of $H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ on an arbitrary open set, and it makes no
pointwise boundary trace assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every nonempty bounded open
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, the closure spaces $H,V$ of
Bounded no-slip solenoidal closure spaces are separable Hilbert spaces, with
$V\hookrightarrow H$ continuous and dense. There is a countable sequence
$e_j\in D_\sigma(\Omega)$ that is orthonormal in $H$ and whose finite linear
span is dense in both $H$ and $V$. No Stokes eigenfunction regularity or
identification of $V$ with a larger solenoidal space is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and open, and let $H,V$ and
$(e_j)_{j\ge1}$ be as in the bounded closure-space and basis results on this
page. The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact. If $\Pi_K$ is the
$H$-orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_K)$, then
there are numbers $\delta_K\downarrow0$ such that
$$\|(I-\Pi_K)a\|_H\le\delta_K\|a\|_V\qquad(a\in V).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and
open, and let $H,V$ be the closure spaces defined above when $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, use the same closure formulas: take the finite product of scalar $W^{1,2}$ spaces as $H^1$, let $H_0^1$ be the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, let $D_\sigma=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}$, and let $H$ and $V$ be the $L^2$ and $H_0^1$ closures of $D_\sigma$. All these spaces are then $\{0\}$. There is a constant $C$ independent of $\Omega$
and $a$ such that every $a\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies
$$\|a\|_{L^6(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla a\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|a\|_{L^4(\Omega)}\le\|a\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^{1/4}\|a\|_{L^6(\Omega)}^{3/4}.$$
For $T>0$, if $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, then
$u\in L^{8/3}(0,T;L^4(\Omega))$. Here the time-dependent $L^p$ notation
means strong measurability and integrability of the displayed norm; the
continuous embedding $V\to L^4(\Omega)$ carries strongly measurable
$V$-valued maps to strongly measurable $L^4$-valued maps. Let $V^*$ be the
continuous real-linear dual of $V$ with its operator norm. Choose any strongly measurable representative $\widetilde u:(0,T)\to V$ of the $L^2(0,T;V)$ class of $u$; through the embedding $V\to H$, it represents the same $H$-valued class almost everywhere. For almost every $t\in(0,T)$ define
$$b_u(t)(\phi)=-\int_\Omega \widetilde u_i(t,x)\widetilde u_j(t,x)\partial_j\phi_i(x)dx,\qquad\phi\in V,$$
and assign $b_u(t)=0$ on any exceptional null set. Then $b_u(t)\in V^*$ for almost every $t$, $t\mapsto b_u(t)$ is strongly measurable, and its equivalence class is independent of the chosen representative $\widetilde u$. This class belongs to $L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$ and satisfies
$$\|b_u(t)\|_{V^*}\le\|\widetilde u(t)\|_{L^4(\Omega)}^2\quad\text{for almost every }t\in(0,T).$$

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $H$ be a Hilbert space over
$\mathbb K$, let $X$ be a separable Hilbert space over $\mathbb K$, and let
$T>0$. Define $C_w([0,T];H)$ to be the set of actual maps $u:[0,T]\to H$
such that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$;
membership here is pointwise and is not an almost-everywhere equivalence
class. A map $u:(0,T)\to X$ is strongly measurable if it is an almost-everywhere
pointwise limit of measurable simple $X$-valued maps. For $1\le p<\infty$,
$L^p(0,T;X)$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of strongly
measurable maps with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_X^pdt<\infty$; $L^\infty(0,T;X)$
consists of such classes with finite essential supremum norm. In this page,
$L^p_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;X)$ means membership on every finite interval
$(0,T)$. These conventions apply to any of the periodic spaces $H,V,H^{-r}$
and to the bounded-domain Hilbert spaces $H,V$ whenever the target space $X$
is separable.

If two maps in $C_w([0,T];H)$ agree almost everywhere on $(0,T)$, they agree
at every $t\in[0,T]$. Consequently, a Bochner equivalence class has at most
one weakly continuous representative; whenever it has one, all pointwise
values associated with that class mean the values of this unique representative.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under

Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each

$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization

to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge2$, $L>0$, $\nu>0$, $u_0\in H$, and use the spaces and weak-time
conventions of Periodic solenoidal Fourier spaces and
Weak time continuity and energy spaces. A **global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf
solution** with data $(\nu,u_0)$ is a map
