Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and open, assume the Axiom of
Choice, let $\nu>0$, and let $u_0\in H$ for the bounded closure spaces
defined above when $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. For $\Omega=\varnothing$, use the same closure formulas: $H^1$ is the finite product of scalar $W^{1,2}$ spaces, $H_0^1$ is the $H^1$ closure of compactly supported smooth vector fields, $D_\sigma=\{a\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{div}a=0\}$, and $H,V$ are its $L^2$ and $H_0^1$ closures. Thus $H_0^1=H=V=\{0\}$ in this case. There exists
$$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$$
with $u(0)=u_0$ and $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, satisfying for
every compactly time-supported $C^1$ map $\phi:[0,\infty)\to V$,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It also satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2\quad(t\ge0),$$
and there is a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for every
$s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
The conclusion is a velocity result for the specified unforced closure-space
formulation; it asserts no uniqueness, smoothness, pressure regularity, or
boundary trace beyond membership in $H_0^1$. Here
$(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$ and
$\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$. For a matrix field
$A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. Write $D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $D_0(\Omega)=\{h\in D(\Omega):\int_\Omega h=0\}$. For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

derivations.claim:
Extend the real-linear supplier $R$ to complex mean-zero tests by $R_{\mathbb C}(h_1+ih_2)=Rh_1+iRh_2$, where $h_1,h_2$ are real. Their integrals both vanish. Real linearity makes this extension complex-linear; applying the supplier bounds to the two parts preserves fixed-support continuity, the same output-support set, and $\operatorname{div}R_{\mathbb C}h=h$. In the rest of the proof $R$ denotes this extension. On $U=(0,\infty)\times\Omega$, $u\in L^2_{\rm loc}$ and $u\otimes u\in L^1_{\rm loc}$. For a compact $K\subset U$, let $p_{m,K}$ be the maximum of the suprema on $K$ of all component derivatives of order at most $m$. The same local estimate $|\int_K f\psi|\le\|f\|_{L^1(K)}p_{0,K}(\psi)$ shows that the regular pairings of $u$ and $u\otimes u$ are continuous on every fixed-support test space, hence are distributions. The residual functional
$$\langle T,\psi\rangle=\int_U\bigl(u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(u\otimes u):\nabla_x\psi+\nu u\cdot\Delta_x\psi\bigr)\,dt\,dx$$
is well-defined and satisfies
$$|\langle T,\psi\rangle|\le C_d\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(K)}+\|u\otimes u\|_{L^1(K)}\bigr)p_{1,K}(\psi)+C_d\nu\|u\|_{L^1(K)}p_{2,K}(\psi)$$
for every test supported in $K$. Thus its absolute value is a seminorm whose restriction to each fixed-support test space is continuous; by the test-function topology in [F4], $T$ is a spacetime distribution. By [F3], this formula is exactly the residual $-\partial_tu-\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nu\Delta u$ of those regular distributions. For a scalar test $\phi(t,x)$ put $\phi_0=\phi-\theta(x)\int_\Omega\phi(t,y)dy$ and define
$$\langle\pi,\phi\rangle=-\langle T,R_x\phi_0\rangle.$$
The map $R$ is applied at each time. The spatial supports of $\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ lie in one compact subset of $\Omega$, since they are contained in the union of the spatial support of $\phi$ and $\operatorname{supp}\theta$. For each time derivative order, $t\mapsto\partial_t^j\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ is continuous in every fixed-support test seminorm. Linearity and continuity of $R$ on that fixed-support space imply that $t\mapsto R\phi_0(t,\cdot)$ is smooth with derivatives $R\partial_t^j\phi_0$; the support condition in [F2] puts all outputs in one compact spatial set. Thus $R_x\phi_0$ is a smooth spacetime test with compact temporal support, and the displayed functional is continuous by the same fixed-support estimate for $T$. It is a distribution.

For a compact smooth vector test $\psi$, $h=\operatorname{div}_x\psi$ has spatial integral zero by coordinate integration, so $h\in D_0(\Omega)$ and $\psi-Rh$ is compactly supported, smooth, and divergence free. By [F1], $\langle T,\psi-Rh\rangle=0$. Moreover,
$$\langle\nabla_x\pi,\psi\rangle=-\langle\pi,h\rangle=\langle T,Rh\rangle=\langle T,\psi\rangle.$$
Substituting the definition of $T$ proves the full distributional momentum equation. The normalization holds because $(a\theta)_0=0$.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ have the same spatial gradient, their difference $q$ has $\nabla_xq=0$. For an arbitrary scalar spacetime test $\phi$, put $a(t)=\int_\Omega\phi(t,x)dx$ and $\phi_0=\phi-a\theta$. Step 1.1 gives a spacetime vector test $R_x\phi_0$ with spatial divergence $\phi_0$. Hence $\langle q,\phi_0\rangle=-\langle\nabla_xq,R_x\phi_0\rangle=0$, and $\langle q,\phi\rangle=\langle q,a\theta\rangle=0$ by the shared normalization. Thus $q=0$, proving uniqueness conditional on [F2].

Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$
A periodic distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test space, with bilinear pairing. Its derivative is defined by
$$\langle\partial_j T,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
For $f\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, its associated regular distribution is $T_f(\varphi)=\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}f\varphi\,d\mu$; vector fields are treated componentwise. This is continuous since $|\int f\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|f\|_2p_0(\varphi)$. For a vector distribution $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_d)$, define
$$\langle\operatorname{div}U,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_{j=1}^d\langle U_j,\partial_j\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus, for $u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means
$$\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}u(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,L^{-d}dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)).$$

For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

$$u_n(x)=\sin(2\pi n x_1/L)e_2,\qquad u(x)=0.$$
Each $u_n$ has only the Fourier modes $k=\pm ne_1$ and its vector coefficient is perpendicular to $k$, so $u_n\in H$. For a finite trigonometric polynomial $g$, $(u_n,g)_H=0$ for all sufficiently large $n$ because its Fourier support is finite. Approximate an arbitrary $g\in H$ by such polynomials using [F2]; the error is at most $\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$ times the approximation error. Hence $u_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $H$.

The only nonzero entry of $u_n\otimes u_n$ is its $(2,2)$ entry, equal to
$$\sin^2(2\pi n x_1/L)=\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos(4\pi n x_1/L).$$
The oscillatory cosine has zero pairing eventually with every finite trigonometric polynomial and its $L^2$ norm is uniformly bounded; density and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore show it converges weakly to zero in $L^2$. Thus $u_n\otimes u_n\rightharpoonup\tfrac12 e_2\otimes e_2$ in $L^2$, while $u\otimes u=0$. This refutes the false statement. For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

The test-function topology exists as a Hausdorff locally convex vector topology, induces the prescribed topology on each $\mathcal D_K$, and is the finest locally convex topology making all inclusions $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous. A linear map $L:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to E$ to a locally convex space is continuous if and only if each restriction $L|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous. An increasing compact exhaustion whose interiors cover $\Omega$ gives the same topology, independently of the exhaustion. Thus this is an LF topology of the complete metrizable fixed-support spaces. All these claims hold in ZF.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be the state domain of a conservation system, $n\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $|n|=1$, and $s\in\mathbb R$. The planar interface and its two open sides are
$$\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st=0\},\qquad Q^-=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st<0\},\qquad Q^+=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x-st>0\}.$$
A state field is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$ if on each side it is $C^1$ and, near every point of $\Sigma$, each side field is the restriction of a $C^1$ map from a neighborhood in $I\times\Omega$ into $\mathcal O$. The left and right traces $U_L,U_R:\Sigma\to\mathcal O$ are the restrictions of those extensions to $\Sigma$; they are independent of the chosen extensions because they agree with the same field on their respective open sides. For any state or flux quantity $G$ with these traces, define its jump by $[G]=G_R-G_L$. A planar shock profile is such a piecewise $C^1$ state field with its specified constant interface normal $n$ and speed $s$; the definition does not assert that it solves a conservation system.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. Require integrability of the state and fluxes up to the initial boundary:
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|U|+\sum_{j=1}^d|F_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact}).$$
This condition uses only positive-time values and does not assert a strong trace at $t=0$. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The stated integrability up to the initial boundary makes every term finite, including for tests nonzero at $t=0$; a weak solution with initial data $U_0$ must satisfy these integrability conditions and this identity for all such tests.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, require also
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|\eta(U)|+\sum_{j=1}^d|q_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact})$$
and $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Use every nonnegative scalar test up to the initial boundary defined above and add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ to the entropy integral. These conditions make all terms finite even when the test is nonzero at $t=0$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
The integral of a nonnegative simple function.

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple (Nonnegative simple measurable functions).

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^m)$. Choose an orthonormal basis of $n^\perp$ and write $x=y+(st+r)n$, with $y\in n^\perp$ and $r=n\cdot x-st$. In these coordinates $\Phi(t,y,r)=(t,y+(st+r)n)$ is a linear bijection with absolute determinant $1$, and $y\mapsto y+stn$ is an isometry from $n^\perp$ onto the full spatial plane $\{x\in\mathbb R^d:n\cdot x=st\}$, whose restriction gives the slice in $\Omega$. [F4] states scaling for measurable sets. For a nonnegative simple function, [F6] and the set-scaling identity for $\Phi^{-1}$ give equality of the integrals of the function and its pullback by summing over the measurable level sets; since $\Phi$ is bijective, pullback gives a bijection between the simple minorants of a nonnegative measurable function and those of its pullback, so [F7] gives the same integral identity for nonnegative measurable functions. Apply that identity to the positive and negative parts of each signed integrable real integrand; [F8] then gives equality for the integrable integrands used here. Every test-supported integrand is integrable after extension by zero, since the coefficients are locally integrable and the test derivatives are bounded on compact support. Thus this chart preserves the required volume integrals, and [F5] permits their iterated evaluation. The coordinate measure $dy$ is the pushforward of $\lambda_{d-1}$ by the chosen linear isometry $E$. Replacing $E$ by another such isometry changes $z$ by an orthogonal linear map, whose determinant has absolute value $1$, so [F4] and the same simple-function argument prove independence of the basis; when $d=1$ this is the one-point measure specified in the Statement. Let $H(r)=1$ for $r>0$ and $H(r)=0$ for $r<0$. By [F3], one-dimensional integration by parts in $r$ gives, for every $C^1$ coefficient field $a$, $\partial_t(aH)=H\partial_ta-s\,a|_\Sigma\delta_\Sigma$ and $\partial_{x_j}(aH)=H\partial_{x_j}a+n_j\,a|_\Sigma\delta_\Sigma$, where $\delta_\Sigma$ pairs with $dt\,dy$ on the spatial plane, with the coordinate Lebesgue measure just defined. The time derivative is at fixed $x$, so in this chart $\partial_t|_x=\partial_t|_{y,r}-s\partial_r$; this produces the factor $-s$ and the stated normalization. Tangential spatial derivatives have no boundary term, while the normal derivative contributes $n_j$.

On a neighborhood of $\Sigma$, write $U=U_L+[U]H$ and $F_j(U)=F_j(U_L)+[F_j(U)]H$, using the $C^1$ side extensions from [F1]. Apply the derivative formulas of step 1.1. The regular terms are the classical residuals on the two open sides, hence vanish by the given equations; the remaining interface term is $\left(\sum_jn_j[F_j(U)]-s[U]\right)\delta_\Sigma$. A partition of unity over the compact support of $\varphi$ gives the same formula throughout $I\times\Omega$.

If the coefficient vanishes on $\Sigma$, the residual distribution is zero. Conversely, if it is nonzero at a point of $\Sigma$, continuity of the traces gives a neighborhood on which one component has a fixed strict sign. A nonnegative compactly supported test in that interface patch, placed in the corresponding vector component, has a nonzero pairing with the residual, contradicting that it is the zero distribution. If $\Sigma$ is empty in the cylinder, the equivalence is vacuous. Thus the residual vanishes exactly when the vector Rankine–Hugoniot equality holds pointwise on $\Sigma$.

finite_checks: In d=m=1 with n=1, the coefficient reduces to [F(U)]−s[U]; it is a vector coefficient componentwise and no division by [U] occurs.
Normalization regression: d=3, n=e1, s=1, F=0, U=1_{x1>t} has residual -dt dx2 dx3. The explicit plane Lebesgue pushforward now gives this exact residual; d=1 uses lambda_0({0})=1.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, and $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and let $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $\partial_tU+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(F_j(U))=0$ pointwise on both open sides, and $U,F_j(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional residual is
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]-s[U]\right)\delta_\Sigma,$$
Here spatial plane measure means the pushforward of Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{d-1}$ by $z\mapsto Ez+stn$, where $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to n^\perp$ is any linear isometry onto $n^\perp$. Explicitly, $\langle A\delta_\Sigma,\varphi\rangle=\int_I\int_{\{z:Ez+stn\in\Omega\}}A(t,Ez+stn)\cdot\varphi(t,Ez+stn)\,d\lambda_{d-1}(z)\,dt$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\lambda_0(\{0\})=1$. This definition is independent of $E$ and specifies the normalization without Hausdorff-measure notation. Consequently, $U$ solves the conservation system in distributions if and only if
$$s[U]=\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]\quad\text{at every point of }\Sigma.$$
This is a vector equality; no division by the vector jump is made.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On either open side, [F4] and entropy compatibility give $\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)=D\eta(U)\left(\partial_tU+\sum_jDF_j(U)\partial_{x_j}U\right)=0$.

The fields $\eta(U)$ and $q_j(U)$ have $C^1$ extensions to each side of $\Sigma$. Apply the normal-coordinate distribution calculation from [F3] under the stated Countable Choice assumption [F5] to this scalar density and its scalar fluxes; the bulk residuals vanish by step 1.1, leaving the interface coefficient $\sum_jn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]$. The interface measure is the time integral of the isometric pushforward of Lebesgue measure specified in [F3].

If this coefficient is nonpositive everywhere, pairing the residual with any nonnegative test gives a nonpositive value, which is the distributional inequality. If the coefficient is positive at a point, continuity makes it positive on a smaller interface patch; a nonnegative test supported there has positive pairing, contradicting the inequality. Thus the distributional inequality holds exactly under the stated pointwise condition.

finite_checks: For a scalar convex flux and a quadratic entropy, the residual sign is checked by evaluating the oriented jump [q]−s[η] at the two traces.

boundaries.evidence: If the interface is empty, step 2.1 has no singular residual and the side identities hold.
A zero entropy jump coefficient gives the zero interface distribution in step 2.1.
The Statement's coefficient and sign criterion reduce to the scalar formula when d=m=1.
Affine entropies have η''=0 and the entropy production can vanish; steps 2.1–3.1 still cover zero coefficients.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is on an open cylinder and states no initial or terminal trace.

boundaries.evidence: Countable Choice is explicit in the Statement for the RH coordinate calculation used by step 2.1.
Step 3.1 proves a nonpositive coefficient pairs nonpositively with every nonnegative test.
Step 3.1 localizes a nonnegative test where a continuous positive coefficient would violate the inequality.

risk_review.notes: Read steps 1.1–3.1 against chain rule, entropy compatibility and repaired normal-coordinate jump calculation. Chain-rule bulk residual vanishes; scalar density and flux have C1 side extensions, so use of the supplier calculation is justified even though entropy need not be an invertible state map. Repaired public measure convention to explicitly match the supplier isometric Lebesgue pushforward; no bare unnormalized Hausdorff measure is used. Nonpositive coefficient suffices by positive plane measure; positivity at any point yields a smooth nonnegative test on a patch by continuity, proving necessity. Empty interface is vacuous and d=1 uses mass one. AC_omega carried. Direct consumers are scalar Riemann theorem and expansion shock, both owned; their one-dimensional coefficients/signs are unchanged.

This condition uses only positive-time values and does not assert a strong trace at $t=0$. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The stated integrability up to the initial boundary makes every term finite, including for tests nonzero at $t=0$; a weak solution with initial data $U_0$ must satisfy these integrability conditions and this identity for all such tests.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, require also
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|\eta(U)|+\sum_{j=1}^d|q_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact})$$
and $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Use every nonnegative scalar test up to the initial boundary defined above and add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ to the entropy integral. These conditions make all terms finite even when the test is nonzero at $t=0$. A weak solution satisfying this inequality is entropy-admissible relative to that pair.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, and $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and let $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $\partial_tU+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(F_j(U))=0$ pointwise on both open sides, and $U,F_j(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional residual is
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]-s[U]\right)\delta_\Sigma,$$
Here spatial plane measure means the pushforward of Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{d-1}$ by $z\mapsto Ez+stn$, where $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to n^\perp$ is any linear isometry onto $n^\perp$. Explicitly, $\langle A\delta_\Sigma,\varphi\rangle=\int_I\int_{\{z:Ez+stn\in\Omega\}}A(t,Ez+stn)\cdot\varphi(t,Ez+stn)\,d\lambda_{d-1}(z)\,dt$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\lambda_0(\{0\})=1$. This definition is independent of $E$ and specifies the normalization without Hausdorff-measure notation. Consequently, $U$ solves the conservation system in distributions if and only if
$$s[U]=\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]\quad\text{at every point of }\Sigma.$$
This is a vector equality; no division by the vector jump is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, and let $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and set $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $U_t+\sum_jDF_j(U)\partial_{x_j}U=0$ classically on each open side, and the state, flux, and entropy compositions are locally integrable. Let $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ be convex and let $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)DF_j(V)$ for every $V\in\mathcal O$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional entropy residual is
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\right)\delta_\Sigma.$$
Here $\delta_\Sigma$ uses the plane measure defined in the vector jump-residual theorem: integrate in $t$ and in $z\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with $x=Ez+stn\in\Omega$, where $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to n^\perp$ is a linear isometry onto $n^\perp$, using Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{d-1}$ and singleton mass one when $d=1$. The entropy inequality $\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0$ holds near the interface if and only if $\sum_jn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\leq0$ at every interface point. Entropy admissibility is an additional condition; the conservation jump equality alone does not imply it.

For a one-dimensional system $U_t+\partial_xF(U)=0$ with $F\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$ on an open state domain $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, the system is strictly hyperbolic at $V\in\mathcal O$ if the Jacobian $DF(V)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues. Write them in increasing order as $\lambda_1(V)<\cdots<\lambda_m(V)$. For states $U_L,U_R\in\mathcal O$ and speed $s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the Rankine–Hugoniot equality
$$F(U_R)-F(U_L)=s(U_R-U_L),$$
assume strict hyperbolicity at both states. The jump is a $k$-Lax shock, $1\leq k\leq m$, if
$$\lambda_k(U_R)<s<\lambda_k(U_L),$$
and also $\lambda_{k-1}(U_L)<s$ when $k>1$, and $s<\lambda_{k+1}(U_R)$ when $k<m$. The outer inequality is omitted at each endpoint $k=1$ or $k=m$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $a=b$, the profile and initial data are constant. For every compactly supported test, integration of $\varphi_t$ over $[0,T)$ gives $-\varphi(0,x)$ and integration of $\varphi_x$ over $\mathbb R$ gives zero. The weak identity follows; the same calculation with the constants $\eta(a)$ and $q(a)$ gives equality in every entropy identity.

Suppose $a>b$. Apply [F5] to $F$ on $[b,a]$ to obtain $s=F'(\xi)$ for some $\xi\in(b,a)$. Apply [F5] to $F'$ on any subinterval of $[b,a]$; since its derivative $F''$ is positive, $F'$ is strictly increasing there. Hence $F'(b)<s<F'(a)$, which is the scalar Lax pattern in [F4].

Suppose $a<b$. Applying [F5] to $F'$ on any subinterval of $[a,b]$ shows it is strictly increasing, so it has an inverse $g$ on $[F'(a),F'(b)]$. This inverse is continuous: for each interior $z$, strict inequalities $F'(z-\delta)<F'(z)<F'(z+\delta)$ trap $g(y)$ near $z$ whenever $y$ is sufficiently near $F'(z)$, and the endpoint argument is one-sided. For $y=F'(z)$, the difference quotient $(g(y+h)-z)/h$ equals $(x-z)/(F'(x)-F'(z))$ with $x=g(y+h)$; as $h\to0$, continuity gives $x\to z$, and differentiability of $F'$ gives limit $1/F''(z)$. Thus $g'(y)=1/F''(g(y))$ on the interior. Applying [F7] to $u(t,x)=g(x/t)$ gives $u_t=-x/(t^2F''(u))$ and $u_x=1/(tF''(u))$, whence $u_t+F'(u)u_x=0$. The constant branches solve the equation too, and the profile is continuous at both fan edges.

The shock is constant on each open side, so the classical equation holds there. Its traces are $u_L=a$ and $u_R=b$, and the Rankine–Hugoniot coefficient is $[F]-s[u]=F(b)-F(a)-s(b-a)=0$. By [F2] under [F8], the distributional equation holds on $(0,T)\times\mathbb R$.
The traces at each fan edge agree, so both the state and flux jumps vanish there. By [F2], the distributional conservation residual is zero; hence the weak equation holds on $(0,T)\times\mathbb R$.

On any compact spatial set, $u(t,\cdot)$ differs from $u_0$ only between $0$ and $st$, an interval of length $|s|t$, and $|u-u_0|\leq|a-b|$. Hence $\|u(t,\cdot)-u_0\|_{L^1(K)}\leq |a-b||s|t$. For an arbitrary initial-boundary test $\varphi$, take smooth cutoffs $\chi_\epsilon$ that vanish on $[0,\epsilon]$, equal $1$ for $t\geq2\epsilon$, and have $\chi_\epsilon'\geq0$ with integral $1$. Apply the interior weak identity from step 2.1 to $\chi_\epsilon\varphi$. The term $\int u\chi_\epsilon'\varphi$ tends to $\int u_0\varphi(0,\cdot)$ by the displayed local $L^1$ estimate and uniform continuity of $\varphi$; the terms over $0<t<2\epsilon$ tend to zero because $u,F(u)$ and the test derivatives are bounded on the compact support. Taking the limit gives the initial weak identity.

Let $\eta\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be convex with compatible flux $q$, and let $C(z)=F(b)+s(z-b)$ be the chord joining $(b,F(b))$ to $(a,F(a))$. For $b<z<a$, [F5] gives points $\xi_1\in(b,z)$ and $\xi_2\in(z,a)$ whose derivatives equal the secant slopes on $[b,z]$ and $[z,a]$. Applying [F5] to $F'$ between $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ shows $F'(\xi_1)<F'(\xi_2)$; rearranging the secant-slope inequality gives $F(z)<C(z)$. At the endpoints $F=C$. Convexity of $\eta$ gives $\eta''\geq0$, since its nonnegative symmetric second differences divided by $h^2$ converge to $\eta''$. The jump coefficient is
$$[q]-s[\eta]=-\int_b^a\eta'(z)(F'(z)-s)\,dz=\int_b^a\eta''(z)(F(z)-C(z))\,dz\leq0.$$
The integral identity follows by applying [F6] to the $C^1$ function $\eta'(F-C)$; its endpoint values are zero. By [F3] under [F8] the entropy residual is nonpositive. Apply the cutoff argument of step 3.1 to this interior entropy inequality. The entropy density is Lipschitz on $[b,a]$, so the local $L^1$ trace estimate in step 3.1 gives the initial entropy term; boundedness makes the omitted time strip vanish.

For each $k$, the compositions $\eta_k(u)$ and $q_k(u)$ are constant on each open side of the shock; splitting an interior test at $x=st$ and integrating by parts on the two sides therefore gives their distributional residual coefficient $[q_k]-s[\eta_k]$. If $k<b$ or $k>a$, the sign of $z-k$ is constant for $z\in[b,a]$, so $(\eta_k(z),q_k(z))$ is, up to additive constants, the same signed multiple of $(z,F(z))$; its coefficient vanishes by the Rankine–Hugoniot equality from step 2.1. If $b\leq k\leq a$, direct substitution gives $[q_k]-s[\eta_k]=2(F(k)-C(k))\leq0$, with equality at $k=b,a$, since the strict convexity calculation in step 4.1 puts $F$ below its chord $C$ on $[b,a]$. Thus the Kružkov residual is nonpositive without applying the smooth entropy-jump result to the nonsmooth pair. Apply the cutoff argument of step 3.1 to this interior inequality; $\eta_k$ and $q_k$ are Lipschitz on $[b,a]$, so the local trace and bounded-strip limits give the required initial term.

Write $\alpha=F'(a)$ and $\beta=F'(b)$, so $\alpha<\beta$ by [A1]. The fan and the initial step can differ only on $[\min(0,\alpha t),\max(0,\beta t)]$, whose length is $t(\max(0,\beta)-\min(0,\alpha))\leq t(|\alpha|+|\beta|)$. On this interval both values lie in $[a,b]$, so $\|u(t,\cdot)-u_0\|_{L^1(K)}\leq(b-a)t(|\alpha|+|\beta|)$ for every compact $K$. Since $F$ is Lipschitz on $[a,b]$, its composition has the same local strong-trace property. Apply the same cutoff argument as in step 3.1 to the interior weak identity of step 2.2; the local $L^1$ bound makes the cutoff boundary term converge to the prescribed initial value, and boundedness makes the omitted time strip vanish. This proves the weak identity with the prescribed initial data.

For each compatible convex $C^2$ pair, [F7] and $q'=\eta'F'$ give $\partial_t\eta(u)+\partial_xq(u)=\eta'(u)(u_t+F'(u)u_x)=0$ in the fan. Outside the fan both compositions are constant. Their traces agree at the edges, so [F3] gives zero interface residual. Apply the cutoff argument of step 4.2 to this interior identity; the Lipschitz continuity of $\eta$ and $q$ on $[a,b]$ gives the required initial entropy term.

Fix $k\in\mathbb R$. If $k\notin[a,b]$, $\eta_k$ is affine on the range of $u$ and the chain-rule computation of step 5.2 applies directly. If $k\in[a,b]$, split the fan at the ray $x=tF'(k)$; on both open pieces the Kružkov compositions are $C^1$ and [F7] gives zero classical entropy residual. At the new interface both $\eta_k(u)$ and $q_k(u)$ have equal traces because $u=k$ there and $q_k(k)=0$; the interface calculation from [F2] then gives zero singular residual. Apply the cutoff argument of step 4.2 to the resulting interior inequality; both compositions are Lipschitz on $[a,b]$, so the local trace estimate supplies the initial term. This proves every stated inequality, with equality for the fan.

Strict positivity of continuous F_second on the closed state interval gives the continuous inverse with finite endpoint derivatives and explicit C1 extension; chain rule solves fan interiors. Both jump suppliers use lambda_0 mass one in d=1 after normalization repair, so every actual use is unchanged. No general uniqueness or empirical conclusion. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
By [F2], the chain rule and compatibility give, pointwise for each $\epsilon>0$,
$$\partial_t\eta(u^\epsilon)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(u^\epsilon)=\epsilon\eta'(u^\epsilon)\Delta u^\epsilon.$$
Applying the chain rule twice in each spatial coordinate and the product rule yields $\eta'(u^\epsilon)\Delta u^\epsilon=\Delta\eta(u^\epsilon)-\eta''(u^\epsilon)|\nabla u^\epsilon|^2$. Since $\eta''\geq0$, the entropy residual is at most $\epsilon\Delta\eta(u^\epsilon)$.

Multiply by $\psi\geq0$ and integrate. By [F4], the integrals can be taken iteratively in time and each spatial coordinate. Applying [F3] to the smooth compactly supported products gives integration by parts twice in each spatial coordinate and once in time, with $\psi$ vanishing near $T$, and yields
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\eta(u^\epsilon)\psi_t+\sum_jq_j(u^\epsilon)\psi_{x_j}\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\eta(u_0^\epsilon)\psi(0,x)\,dx\geq-\epsilon\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\eta(u^\epsilon)\Delta\psi\,dx\,dt.$$

- If $a=b$, let $u(t,x)=a$.
- If $a>b$, let $s=(F(a)-F(b))/(a-b)$ and let $u(t,x)=a$ for $x<st$ and $u(t,x)=b$ for $x>st$; its value on $x=st$ is arbitrary.

For every $T>0$ and every real test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$, the initial-value weak identity
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\left(u\varphi_t+F(u)\varphi_x\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
holds. For every convex $\eta\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and $q\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ with $q'=\eta'F'$, and for every $k\in\mathbb R$ with $\eta_k(z)=|z-k|$ and $q_k(z)=\operatorname{sgn}(z-k)(F(z)-F(k))$, the initial entropy inequality
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\left(\eta(u)\varphi_t+q(u)\varphi_x\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}\eta(u_0(x))\varphi(0,x)\,dx\geq0$$
holds for each nonnegative test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$. In the rarefaction case $a<b$, both inequalities are equalities. In the shock case $a>b$, the speed satisfies $F'(b)<s<F'(a)$, so the shock has the scalar Lax pattern.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. $$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|U|+\sum_{j=1}^d|F_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact}).$$

for every such real vector test function. The stated integrability up to the initial boundary makes every term finite, including for tests nonzero at $t=0$; a weak solution with initial data $U_0$ must satisfy these integrability conditions and this identity for all such tests.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. $$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, require also
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|\eta(U)|+\sum_{j=1}^d|q_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact})$$
and $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Use every nonnegative scalar test up to the initial boundary defined above and add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ to the entropy integral. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, and $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and let $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $\partial_tU+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}(F_j(U))=0$ pointwise on both open sides, and $U,F_j(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional residual is
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]-s[U]\right)\delta_\Sigma,$$
Here spatial plane measure means the pushforward of Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{d-1}$ by $z\mapsto Ez+stn$, where $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to n^\perp$ is any linear isometry onto $n^\perp$. Explicitly, $\langle A\delta_\Sigma,\varphi\rangle=\int_I\int_{\{z:Ez+stn\in\Omega\}}A(t,Ez+stn)\cdot\varphi(t,Ez+stn)\,d\lambda_{d-1}(z)\,dt$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $\lambda_0(\{0\})=1$. This definition is independent of $E$ and specifies the normalization without Hausdorff-measure notation. Consequently, $U$ solves the conservation system in distributions if and only if
$$s[U]=\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[F_j(U)]\quad\text{at every point of }\Sigma.$$
This is a vector equality; no division by the vector jump is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, and let $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$. Let $n\in\mathbb R^d$ have $|n|=1$, let $s\in\mathbb R$, and set $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in I\times\Omega:n\cdot x=st\}$. Suppose $U$ is piecewise $C^1$ across $\Sigma$, satisfies $U_t+\sum_jDF_j(U)\partial_{x_j}U=0$ classically on each open side, and the state, flux, and entropy compositions are locally integrable. Let $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ be convex and let $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)DF_j(V)$ for every $V\in\mathcal O$. With $[G]=G_R-G_L$, the distributional entropy residual is
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)=\left(\sum_{j=1}^dn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\right)\delta_\Sigma.$$
Here $\delta_\Sigma$ uses the plane measure defined in the vector jump-residual theorem: integrate in $t$ and in $z\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with $x=Ez+stn\in\Omega$, where $E:\mathbb R^{d-1}\to n^\perp$ is a linear isometry onto $n^\perp$, using Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{d-1}$ and singleton mass one when $d=1$. The entropy inequality $\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0$ holds near the interface if and only if $\sum_jn_j[q_j(U)]-s[\eta(U)]\leq0$ at every interface point. Entropy admissibility is an additional condition; the conservation jump equality alone does not imply it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$).

Let $F\in C^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$. Let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. If $a\ne b$, assume $F''(z)>0$ for every $z$ in the closed interval with endpoints $a,b$. Set $u_0(x)=a$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=b$ for $x>0$; its value at $x=0$ is arbitrary. For $t>0$ define the following profile:

- If $a=b$, let $u(t,x)=a$.
- If $a>b$, let $s=(F(a)-F(b))/(a-b)$ and let $u(t,x)=a$ for $x<st$ and $u(t,x)=b$ for $x>st$; its value on $x=st$ is arbitrary.
- If $a<b$, let $u(t,x)=a$ for $x/t\leq F'(a)$, let $u(t,x)=(F'|_{[a,b]})^{-1}(x/t)$ for $F'(a)<x/t<F'(b)$, and let $u(t,x)=b$ for $x/t\geq F'(b)$.

For each $T>0$, $C_c^\infty([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$ denotes restrictions of smooth functions defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\mathbb R$ and having compact support in that half-open cylinder; such a test may be nonzero at $t=0$. For every $T>0$ and every real test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$, the initial-value weak identity
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\left(u\varphi_t+F(u)\varphi_x\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
holds. For every convex $\eta\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and $q\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ with $q'=\eta'F'$, and for every $k\in\mathbb R$ with $\eta_k(z)=|z-k|$ and $q_k(z)=\operatorname{sgn}(z-k)(F(z)-F(k))$, the initial entropy inequality
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\mathbb R}\left(\eta(u)\varphi_t+q(u)\varphi_x\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}\eta(u_0(x))\varphi(0,x)\,dx\geq0$$
holds for each nonnegative test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$. In the rarefaction case $a<b$, both inequalities are equalities. In the shock case $a>b$, the speed satisfies $F'(b)<s<F'(a)$, so the shock has the scalar Lax pattern.

The sign function is $1$ on positive numbers, $0$ at zero, and $-1$ on negative numbers. The statement concerns these exact Riemann profiles and makes no general existence or uniqueness claim.

Let $d,m\in\mathbb N$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex. Put $Q=I\times\Omega$. A first-order conservation system on $\mathcal O$ consists of fluxes $F_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R^m)$, $1\leq j\leq d$, and the equation
$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}F_j(U)=0.$$
A state field $U:Q\to\mathcal O$ is locally bounded if it is measurable and essentially bounded on every compact subset of $Q$. For an open set $Q$, $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$ means $g$ is measurable and $\int_K|g|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq Q$. Require also $U,F_1(U),\ldots,F_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q;\mathbb R^m)$. These fields then define regular distributions componentwise. The conservation system holds in distributions on $Q$ when, for every real-valued $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$,
$$\int_Q\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt=0.$$
This is the test-function meaning of the displayed derivative equation, using the distributional derivative convention in the supplied mathematics. The pairing is bilinear, without complex conjugation.

For an initial-value problem on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, $T>0$, let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathcal O$ be measurable and locally integrable. Require integrability of the state and fluxes up to the initial boundary:
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|U|+\sum_{j=1}^d|F_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact}).$$
This condition uses only positive-time values and does not assert a strong trace at $t=0$. A test function up to the initial boundary is the restriction of a smooth function defined on a neighborhood of $[0,T)\times\Omega$, with compact support in $[0,T)\times\Omega$; its value at $t=0$ need not vanish. The initial-value weak identity is
$$\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega\left(U\cdot\partial_t\varphi+\sum_{j=1}^dF_j(U)\cdot\partial_{x_j}\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(0,x)\,dx=0$$
for every such real vector test function. The stated integrability up to the initial boundary makes every term finite, including for tests nonzero at $t=0$; a weak solution with initial data $U_0$ must satisfy these integrability conditions and this identity for all such tests.

A convex entropy-flux pair for the system is a function $\eta\in C^2(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ that is convex on the convex state domain $\mathcal O$ and functions $q_j\in C^1(\mathcal O;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$Dq_j(V)=D\eta(V)\,DF_j(V)\qquad(V\in\mathcal O,\ 1\leq j\leq d),$$
where convexity means $\eta((1-\theta)V+\theta W)\leq(1-\theta)\eta(V)+\theta\eta(W)$ for $V,W\in\mathcal O$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, and $D\eta,Dq_j$ are row derivatives while $DF_j$ is the Jacobian matrix. For a state field $U$, require $\eta(U),q_1(U),\ldots,q_d(U)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ before using their distributions. The entropy inequality on $Q$ means
$$\partial_t\eta(U)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}q_j(U)\leq0,$$
with the sign convention that this holds exactly when
$$\int_Q\left(\eta(U)\,\partial_t\psi+\sum_{j=1}^dq_j(U)\,\partial_{x_j}\psi\right)\,dx\,dt\geq0$$
for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$. With initial data on $(0,T)\times\Omega$, require also
$$\int_0^\tau\!\!\int_K\left(|\eta(U)|+\sum_{j=1}^d|q_j(U)|\right)\,dx\,dt<\infty\qquad(0<\tau<T,\ K\subseteq\Omega\text{ compact})$$
and $\eta(U_0)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Use every nonnegative scalar test up to the initial boundary defined above and add $\int_\Omega\eta(U_0)\psi(0,x)\,dx$ to the entropy integral. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds. Fix $L>0$ as the numerical period in the declared SI metre unit, so the physical side length is $L\,\mathrm m$, and use the flat periodic cell $\mathbb T_L^3=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$ with normalized spatial measure $L^{-3}dx$. Spatial coordinates in physical volume integrals are measured in metres. Assume Countable Choice for the stated Fourier and Sobolev space conventions. The velocity is a vector field $u:I\times\mathbb T_L^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with SI units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the mass density is a constant primitive parameter $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; the dynamic viscosity is a constant primitive parameter $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$; and the mechanical pressure $p$ has units $\mathrm{Pa}$. The body-force density is zero (its SI unit is $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$), and there is no temperature variable in this model.

For classical fields take $u\in C^1(I;C^2(\mathbb T_L^3;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C^1(I;C^1(\mathbb T_L^3))$. Adopt incompressibility $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and the local momentum balance
$$\rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)\bigr)=\operatorname{div}\sigma,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D(u),\qquad D(u)=\tfrac12\bigl(\nabla u+(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}\bigr).$$
Here $\sigma$ is the Cauchy stress, so its traction on an oriented surface with unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; $D(u)$ is the symmetric rate-of-deformation tensor; and $\nabla$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. Every term in the momentum balance has units $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$. Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, this equation is equivalently
$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)+\nabla\pi=\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nu=\mu/\rho_0>0,\qquad \pi=p/\rho_0.$$
where kinematic viscosity $\nu$ and kinematic pressure $\pi$ have units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, respectively. All fields are periodic in each spatial coordinate; this is an ideal cell, not a wall-bounded vessel.

For the weak regime, use the global unforced periodic Leray–Hopf class. The spaces are $H$, the real $L^2$ vector fields whose divergence vanishes distributionally on $\mathbb T_L^3$, with unrestricted constant Fourier mode, and $V=H\cap H^1$, where $H^1$ consists of fields and first weak derivatives in $L^2$; use normalized spatial norms. Here $C_w([0,\infty);H)$ means that $t\mapsto (u(t),h)_H$ is continuous for every fixed $h\in H$; the time-dependent $L^p$ spaces are the corresponding Bochner spaces. A weak velocity has $u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$, strongly attains $u_0\in H$ as $t\downarrow0$, and satisfies, for every smooth real periodic divergence-free test field $\phi$ compactly supported in time,
$$
