> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

**Function spaces.** Write $L^2:=L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ for the real Hilbert space of (equivalence classes of) real Borel vector fields $u:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|u|_2^2\,dx<+\infty$, inner product $\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u\cdot v\,dx$ and norm $|u|_2:=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}$; here $u\cdot v$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. For $u\in L^2\subset L^1$ (finite measure) the coefficient map is the one of the imported theorem, which states: $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$, the finite-subset-net expansion $u=\sum_k\widehat u(k)e_k$ and the Parseval identities hold, and $u\mapsto\widehat u$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]); the last statement applied componentwise gives $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ for real $u,v\in L^2$.

**Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ derived above from the Fourier coefficients is called the Hodge decomposition of the torus; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

and there is a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for every

formulation; it asserts no uniqueness, smoothness, pressure regularity, or
boundary trace beyond membership in $H_0^1$. Here
$(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$ and
$\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$. For a matrix field
$A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be periods measured in metres, and let
$$\Omega:=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z).$$
Write $C:=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\Omega$ be the quotient map. Define $dx$ on Borel subsets $E\subseteq\Omega$ by
$$dx(E):=\lambda_3(C\cap\pi^{-1}(E)),$$
and use its completion as the spatial measure. Thus $dx$ is the pushforward of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open fundamental cell $C$, is not divided by the cell volume, and satisfies $dx(\Omega)=L_1L_2L_3$. Velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second and $dv$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Time integration uses Lebesgue measure $dt$ on $I$; product integrals use the corresponding product measures. In this definition $f\,dx\,dv$ is a number count, so a density $f$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Set $v_*:=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $k=2,3$, define the dimensionless polynomial weight $\omega_k(v):=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$. A kinetic density is a finite-valued measurable function $f:I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ for which, at every $(t,x)$ under discussion,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)f(t,x,v)\,dv<\infty.$$
Define number density $n:=\int f\,dv$ and mass density $\rho:=mn$ for a fixed particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms. Where $n>0$, define
$$u:=\frac1n\int_{\mathbb R^3}vf\,dv,\qquad c:=v-u,\qquad T:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2f\,dv,$$
for a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The velocity is $u$ in metres per second and the temperature is $T$ in kelvins. Where also $T>0$, define the candidate monatomic Maxwellian
$$M_{n,u,T}(v):=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$
Its normalization and moments are established by a separate proposition; this formula is a definition here. At $n=0$, $u$ and $T$ are undefined, and statements using them assume $n>0$. A zero centered second moment gives $T=0$ and does not define the positive-temperature Maxwellian.

Define the pressure tensor, heat-flux vector, and kinetic-energy density by
$$P:=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}c\otimes c\,f\,dv,\qquad q:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2c\,f\,dv,\qquad E:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f\,dv.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2], $D_x\ge0$ for almost every $x$. Since its spatial integral is zero, $D_x=0$ for almost every $x$. Fix any such $x$ and write $g(v)=\log(f(x,v)/f_{\rm ref})$, where $f_{\rm ref}>0$ is a constant with the units of $f$. The integrand defining $D_x$ is continuous and nonnegative in the collision variables. If it were positive at any elastic quadruple, it would be bounded below by a positive constant on a relatively open neighborhood; full support would make that neighborhood have positive measure, contradicting $D_x=0$. Therefore $f(v)f(w)=f(v')f(w')$ for every elastic quadruple, equivalently $g(v)+g(w)=g(v')+g(w')$.

For arbitrary $a,z\in\mathbb R^3$ and any rotation $R\in SO(3)$, the incoming pair $(a+z,a-z)$ and outgoing pair $(a+Rz,a-Rz)$ have equal total momentum $2a$ and equal total squared speed $2|a|^2+2|z|^2$. The collision identity from step 1.1 gives
$$g(a+z)+g(a-z)=g(a+Rz)+g(a-Rz).$$
Thus for fixed $a$ and radius $|z|$, the left side is independent of the direction of $z$.

Fix a unit vector $\xi$ and any other unit vector $\eta$. Choose a rotation taking $\xi$ to $\eta$, put $z=s\xi$ in step 2.1, and expand each side at $s=0$ using [F3]. The constant and linear terms cancel in each symmetric pair. Dividing the resulting equality by $s^2$ and taking $s\to0$ gives $\xi^{\mathsf T}D^2g(a)\xi=\eta^{\mathsf T}D^2g(a)\eta$. Hence the quadratic form of the symmetric Hessian is constant on the unit sphere. Testing $e_i$ gives equal diagonal entries; testing $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ gives zero off-diagonal entries. Therefore $D^2g(a)=\lambda(a)I$.

Since the mixed second derivatives vanish, $\partial_i g(v)$ is constant along every coordinate segment in a direction $e_j$ with $j\ne i$, by [F4]. Connecting points with the same $i$th coordinate by three coordinate segments shows $\partial_i g(v)=G_i(v_i)$ for a differentiable one-variable function $G_i$. The Hessian identity in step 3.1 yields $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for every pair $i\ne j$ and every independent choice of $v_i,v_j$. Fixing $v_j$ while varying $v_i$ shows $G_i'$ is constant; equality then makes the constants the same $\lambda$. Thus $G_i(s)=\lambda s+b_i$, and integrating the gradient along coordinate segments gives
$$g(v)=\alpha+b\cdot v+\frac{\lambda}{2}|v|^2$$
for constants $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $b\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.

Because $f$ is integrable and positive on $\mathbb R^3$, $\lambda$ cannot be positive: the quadratic term then makes $e^{g(v)}$ nonintegrable at infinity. If $\lambda=0$, an affine exponential is either constant or grows on a half-space, and is again nonintegrable. Hence $\lambda<0$. Completing the square gives $g(v)=\alpha' - |v-U|^2/(2\theta)$ with $\theta=-1/\lambda>0$ and $U=-b/\lambda$. Exponentiating gives the asserted profile.

For the profile obtained in step 5.1, $A=B$ on every elastic quadruple because its logarithm is a constant plus a linear and a quadratic collision invariant. The Definition's weak identity for each compactly supported smooth test therefore gives $\int\varphi Q_\nu(f(x,\cdot))\,dv=0$; the collision integrand also vanishes, so $D_x=0$. Conversely, the same calculation applies to every profile of this form, with weak annihilation conditional on its membership in $\mathcal D_\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] coordinatewise with $v=u+\sqrt{\theta}\,z$. Then $dv=\theta^{3/2}dz$, and the prefactor becomes $n(2\pi)^{-3/2}$. By [F1], [F3], and [F6], the one-dimensional Gaussian Lebesgue integrals are finite and equal their improper Riemann values, and Tonelli/Fubini factors the three-dimensional product integral to $n$. Each centered first moment is zero because $z_i e^{-|z|^2/2}$ is odd in $z_i$ and absolutely integrable. Hence $\int M\,dv=n$ and $\int vM\,dv=nu$.

For $i\ne j$, the integral of $z_i z_j e^{-|z|^2/2}$ is zero by oddness in one coordinate. For each $i$, [F4] gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}z_i^2(2\pi)^{-3/2}e^{-|z|^2/2}\,dz=1,$$
using [F1] and [F6] for the other coordinates. Thus $\int (v-u)_i(v-u)_jM\,dv=n\theta\,\delta_{ij}$, and multiplication by $m$ gives $mn\theta I_3=nk_BT I_3$.

Each component of $|z|^2z e^{-|z|^2/2}$ is odd under $z\mapsto-z$, with absolute integrability, so its integral is zero and the centered heat flux vanishes. Finally write $|v|^2=|u|^2+2u\cdot(v-u)+|v-u|^2$. The middle term integrates to zero by step 1.1, and the last term has integral $3n\theta$ by step 1.2. Multiplying by $m/2$ yields the stated energy.

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$

$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be periods measured in metres, and let
$$\Omega:=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z).$$
Write $C:=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\Omega$ be the quotient map. Define $dx$ on Borel subsets $E\subseteq\Omega$ by
$$dx(E):=\lambda_3(C\cap\pi^{-1}(E)),$$
and use its completion as the spatial measure. Thus $dx$ is the pushforward of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open fundamental cell $C$, is not divided by the cell volume, and satisfies $dx(\Omega)=L_1L_2L_3$. Velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second and $dv$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Time integration uses Lebesgue measure $dt$ on $I$; product integrals use the corresponding product measures. In this definition $f\,dx\,dv$ is a number count, so a density $f$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Set $v_*:=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $k=2,3$, define the dimensionless polynomial weight $\omega_k(v):=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$. A kinetic density is a finite-valued measurable function $f:I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ for which, at every $(t,x)$ under discussion,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)f(t,x,v)\,dv<\infty.$$
Define number density $n:=\int f\,dv$ and mass density $\rho:=mn$ for a fixed particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms. Where $n>0$, define
$$u:=\frac1n\int_{\mathbb R^3}vf\,dv,\qquad c:=v-u,\qquad T:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2f\,dv,$$
for a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The velocity is $u$ in metres per second and the temperature is $T$ in kelvins. Where also $T>0$, define the candidate monatomic Maxwellian
$$M_{n,u,T}(v):=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$
Its normalization and moments are established by a separate proposition; this formula is a definition here. At $n=0$, $u$ and $T$ are undefined, and statements using them assume $n>0$. A zero centered second moment gives $T=0$ and does not define the positive-temperature Maxwellian.

Define the pressure tensor, heat-flux vector, and kinetic-energy density by
$$P:=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}c\otimes c\,f\,dv,\qquad q:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2c\,f\,dv,\qquad E:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f\,dv.$$
Here $(a\otimes b)_{ij}=a_i b_j$. The finite absolute third moment makes these integrals finite. Their SI units are respectively pascals, watts per square metre, and joules per cubic metre. This is the monatomic translational model: no internal rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom and no isotropy assumption are included.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: The uniform bounds on $n,u,T$ and the Gaussian formula give $\sup_{(t,x)\in[0,T_*]\times\Omega}\int\omega_3(v)M_{n,u,T}(v)\,dv<\infty$, by the affine change $v=u+\sqrt{\theta}z$ and Gaussian decay. Since the first convergence limit is as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, its error integral is finite for every sufficiently small $\epsilon$; then $\omega_3 f^\epsilon\le\omega_3|f^\epsilon-M_{n,u,T}|+\omega_3M_{n,u,T}$ gives the local weighted $L^1$ hypothesis required by [F1]. Multiply the scaled kinetic equation in [A1] by $m$, $mv_i$, and $m|v|^2/2$ and integrate over velocity. Each collision bracket is zero, so division by $\epsilon>0$ gives the same mass, momentum, and energy balances as [F1] for these $\epsilon$. The derivative envelopes permit passing each time derivative of a moment density and each corresponding coordinate derivative of a flux component through the velocity integral. Pointwise continuity of the integrands and the common envelopes make those derivatives continuous by dominated convergence; the local weighted $L^1$ bound makes the moment densities and fluxes locally integrable. Thus [F5] applies coordinatewise to the balances and the $C^1$ periodic tests: opposite spatial faces cancel and the tests vanish near $T_*$. The initial $\omega_2$ convergence makes the initial moment terms finite, and the time-derivative envelopes give their traces at $t=0$ as the velocity integrals of $f^\epsilon(0)$. This yields the three weak identities on $[0,T_*]$ for every sufficiently small $\epsilon$.

Let $\phi,\eta,$ and $\zeta$ be any scalar and vector test functions allowed in the Statement. The coefficients in the weak moment identities are velocity polynomials of degree at most three; the initial terms have degree at most two. By [F3] and [A2], the absolute difference between an $f^\epsilon$ moment or flux and the corresponding Gaussian moment is bounded by a constant (depending on the test and fixed physical coefficients) times the displayed $\omega_3$ spacetime error. The initial-moment difference is bounded by the analogous $\omega_2$ error. Both bounds tend to zero.

By [F2], the limiting Gaussian moment fluxes are $\rho u$, $\rho u\otimes u+pI_3$, and $(E+p)u$. Pass to the limit in each weak identity from step 1.1 using step 2.1. This gives the three Euler equations in distributions and the stated initial traces.

Each residual component is continuous because $n,u,T$ are $C^1$. If one residual were nonzero at a point, continuity would give a coordinate ball whose closure lies in $(0,T_*)$ times a flat torus chart and on which that component has a constant strict sign. Choose concentric coordinate balls with radii $0<r<R$ inside this neighborhood. By [F4] there is a smooth nonnegative bump equal to one on the inner ball and supported in the outer ball; extend it by zero from the chart to the periodic domain. Its pairing with the residual has strict sign, contradicting the distributional equation from step 3.1. Therefore every residual component vanishes pointwise.

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the kinetic-density definition. Fix the particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms, Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin, and velocity Lebesgue measure $dv$ from the kinetic-density definition. Put $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\omega_3(v)=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$. Here $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second, and $f$ is a number density in velocity space with units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$. For a finite-valued nonnegative measurable velocity density $f:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ with finite absolute third moment $\int\omega_3(v)f(v)\,dv<\infty$, set $n:=\int f\,dv$. Where $n>0$, set $u:=n^{-1}\int vf\,dv$ and $T:=m(3k_Bn)^{-1}\int|v-u|^2f\,dv$; then $n$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $u$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $T$ has units kelvins. Define the admissible BGK input domain
$$\mathcal D_{\rm BGK}:=\left\{f:\int\omega_3f\,dv<\infty,\ f\ge0\text{ finite-valued measurable},\ n>0,\ \int|v-u|^2f\,dv>0\right\}.$$
Fix a relaxation time $\tau>0$ measured in seconds. For $f\in\mathcal D_{\rm BGK}$, the temperature $T$ is strictly positive, $\theta:=k_BT/m$ has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and the moment-matched Maxwellian $M[f]$ and relaxation operator are defined by the following formulas; $M[f]$ has the same units as $f$:
$$M[f](v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta)),\qquad Q_{\rm BGK}(f):=\frac{M[f]-f}{\tau}.$$
The displayed formula defines the single-species Bhatnagar–Gross–Krook (BGK) relaxation operator pointwise on $\mathcal D_{\rm BGK}$, with $Q_{\rm BGK}(f)$ in units of $f$ per second. The corresponding accelerated homogeneous model with dimensionless parameter $\epsilon>0$ is $\partial_t f=Q_{\rm BGK}(f)/\epsilon$. Outside $\mathcal D_{\rm BGK}$ this item assigns no BGK operator. This is a prescribed relaxation model. It is distinct from the binary collision operator and does not by itself assert a derivation from microscopic mechanics or an inhomogeneous hydrodynamic limit.

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$
and
$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$
Thus its pressure tensor is isotropic and its centered heat flux vanishes; these conclusions concern this Gaussian profile and do not impose isotropy on a general kinetic density.

Put $a(t)=e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}$. Then $0<a(t)\le1$ and $f^\epsilon=(1-a(t))M+ a(t)f_0$, so $f^\epsilon\ge0$. Since $M,f_0\in L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$, this formula is continuously differentiable in that Banach space and
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=-\frac{a(t)}{\epsilon\tau}(f_0-M)=\frac{M-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau}.$$

By [F2], the invariant moments of $M$ and $f_0$ agree. The affine formula for $f^\epsilon$ therefore preserves them. In particular its positive number density and positive centered second moment stay fixed, so $M[f^\epsilon(t)]=M$ for every $t$. Step 1.1 is consequently the stated nonlinear BGK equation with the correct moment-matched target.

Let $\tilde f$ be any other solution in the stated class. For each invariant polynomial $\psi$ of degree at most two, the functional $\Lambda_\psi(g)=\int\psi g\,dv$ is bounded on $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$ because $|\psi(v)|\le C_\psi\omega_3(v)$. Continuity of this linear functional and the defining Banach-space derivative give $(\Lambda_\psi\circ\tilde f)\prime(t)=\Lambda_\psi(\partial_t\tilde f)$. Integrating the equation against these invariants shows each derivative is zero, because $M[\tilde f]$ and $\tilde f$ have the same defining moments by [F2]. Its moments are therefore those of $f_0$, so $M[\tilde f(t)]=M$. The equation reduces to $\partial_t(\tilde f-M)=-(\tilde f-M)/(\epsilon\tau)$ in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$. Multiplication by $e^{t/(\epsilon\tau)}$ has zero derivative, hence $\tilde f(t)=M+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0-M)=f^\epsilon(t)$.

Homogeneity of the weight and the exact formula give
$$\int\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv=a(t)\int\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the kinetic-density definition. Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\omega_3(v):=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$, let $\tau>0$ be a relaxation time in seconds, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. Let $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable velocity density with units fixed by the kinetic-density definition, with $\int\omega_3f_0\,dv<\infty$, number density $n>0$, and strictly positive centered second moment. Let $M=M[f_0]$ be its positive-temperature Gaussian from the single-species BGK definition. Fix a constant reference density $f_{\rm ref}>0$ with the same units as $f_0$ and assume $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,dv<\infty$, with $0\log0:=0$ and the integrand $f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|$ assigned value zero where $f_0=0$. Define
$$f^\epsilon(t,v):=M(v)+e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)),\qquad t\ge0\text{ in seconds}.$$
Then $f^\epsilon\ge0$, has the same mass, momentum, and kinetic energy as $f_0$ for every $t$, belongs to $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$, and solves, as an equality in $L^1(\omega_3\,dv)$,
$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=\frac{M[f^\epsilon]-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau},\qquad f^\epsilon(0)=f_0.$$
A solution means a nonnegative $C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,dv))$ function satisfying this equality at each time. The solution is unique among nonnegative solutions in this function class whose density and temperature remain strictly positive. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon(t)-M|\,dv =e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv,$$
and for every $T_*>0$,
$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f^\epsilon-M|\,dv\,dt \le\epsilon\tau\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3|f_0-M|\,dv.$$
Thus the equilibrium limit is exact for each fixed $t>0$ and in spacetime weighted $L^1$, but need not be uniform at $t=0$. This branch has stationary homogeneous Euler moments; it gives no evolving inhomogeneous Euler limit.

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be periods measured in metres, and let
$$\Omega:=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z).$$
Write $C:=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\Omega$ be the quotient map. Define $dx$ on Borel subsets $E\subseteq\Omega$ by
$$dx(E):=\lambda_3(C\cap\pi^{-1}(E)),$$
and use its completion as the spatial measure. Thus $dx$ is the pushforward of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open fundamental cell $C$, is not divided by the cell volume, and satisfies $dx(\Omega)=L_1L_2L_3$. Velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second and $dv$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Time integration uses Lebesgue measure $dt$ on $I$; product integrals use the corresponding product measures. In this definition $f\,dx\,dv$ is a number count, so a density $f$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Set $v_*:=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $k=2,3$, define the dimensionless polynomial weight $\omega_k(v):=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$. A kinetic density is a finite-valued measurable function $f:I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ for which, at every $(t,x)$ under discussion,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)f(t,x,v)\,dv<\infty.$$
Define number density $n:=\int f\,dv$ and mass density $\rho:=mn$ for a fixed particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms. Where $n>0$, define
$$u:=\frac1n\int_{\mathbb R^3}vf\,dv,\qquad c:=v-u,\qquad T:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2f\,dv,$$
for a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The velocity is $u$ in metres per second and the temperature is $T$ in kelvins. Where also $T>0$, define the candidate monatomic Maxwellian
$$M_{n,u,T}(v):=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$
Its normalization and moments are established by a separate proposition; this formula is a definition here. At $n=0$, $u$ and $T$ are undefined, and statements using them assume $n>0$. A zero centered second moment gives $T=0$ and does not define the positive-temperature Maxwellian.

Define the pressure tensor, heat-flux vector, and kinetic-energy density by
$$P:=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}c\otimes c\,f\,dv,\qquad q:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2c\,f\,dv,\qquad E:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f\,dv.$$
Here $(a\otimes b)_{ij}=a_i b_j$. The finite absolute third moment makes these integrals finite. Their SI units are respectively pascals, watts per square metre, and joules per cubic metre. This is the monatomic translational model: no internal rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom and no isotropy assumption are included.

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the kinetic-density definition. Let $n>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, $T>0$, particle mass $m>0$, and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$. Set $\theta=k_BT/m$ and define $M_{n,u,T}(v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta))$. Its Lebesgue moments are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$
and
$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$
Thus its pressure tensor is isotropic and its centered heat flux vanishes; these conclusions concern this Gaussian profile and do not impose isotropy on a general kinetic density.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Put $z_0=f_0/M$ and $\Phi(z)=z\log z-z+1$, with $\Phi(0)=1$. Since $M$ is a positive Gaussian, $\log(M/f_{\rm ref})$ is a quadratic polynomial plus a constant. The assumed finite absolute entropy and second moments make $\int f_0\log(f_0/M)$ finite; the negative part is bounded by $M/e$. Equal mass, momentum, and energy moments then give
$$H(f_0)-H(M)=\int M\Phi(z_0)\,dv<\infty.$$
At zeros of $f_0$, the formula uses $0\log0=0$; continuity of $z\log z$ at zero follows from [F5].

Let $a=e^{-t/(\epsilon\tau)}$. By [F1], $f^\epsilon/M=az_0+(1-a)$. Convexity [F4] and $\Phi(1)=0$ imply pointwise
$$0\le\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\le a\Phi(z_0).$$
Integrating against $M$ and using step 1.1 shows the relative-entropy integral is finite and
$$\int M\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\,dv\le a\bigl(H(f_0)-H(M)\bigr).$$

The same moment cancellation as in step 1.1 gives
$$H(f^\epsilon)-H(M)=\int\bigl[f^\epsilon\log(f^\epsilon/M)-f^\epsilon+M\bigr]\,dv=\int M\Phi(f^\epsilon/M)\,dv.$$
The identity also proves $H(f^\epsilon)$ is finite: the relative-entropy integrand is integrable by step 2.1, $\log(M/f_{\rm ref})$ grows at most quadratically, and $f^\epsilon$ has finite second moment. Nonnegativity follows from [F3]. Combining this equality with step 2.1 yields both asserted bounds.

Each velocity is in $\mathbb R^3$ measured in metres per second, $dv=\lambda_3$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure, and $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is the fixed reference speed. The elastic collision set is
$$Q_{m el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{12}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $
u$ on this set, invariant under particle exchange in either pair and under interchange of incoming and outgoing pairs. Symmetry is a model hypothesis; it does not follow merely from the conservation equations.

The collision model declares an input domain $\mathcal D_
u$ contained in the finite-valued, positive, Lebesgue-measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^3	o(0,\infty)$ for which each of the four coordinate evaluations $f(v),f(w),f(v'),f(w')$ on $Q_{m el}$ is $
u$-measurable. For each $f\in\mathcal D_
u$, it supplies a chosen measurable locally integrable representative $Q_
u(f)\in L^1_{m loc}(\mathbb R^3,dv)$. For finite-valued complex Lebesgue-measurable $\varphi$, set
$$A:=f(v)f(w),\qquad B:=f(v')f(w'),\qquad \delta\varphi:=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w').$$
Let $\mathcal T_f$ be the class of those $\varphi$ for which $\delta\varphi$ is $
u$-measurable and both integrals
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\varphi(v)Q_
u(f)(v)|\,dv,\qquad \int_{Q_{m el}}|(B-A)\delta\varphi|\,d
u$$
are finite. For each $f\in\mathcal D_
u$, the model declares a complex linear subspace $\mathcal S_f\subseteq\mathcal T_f$ containing every compactly supported smooth complex-valued velocity test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Require the weak collision identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\varphi(v)Q_
u(f)(v)\,dv = rac14\int_{Q_{m el}}(B-A)\delta\varphi\,d

for every $\varphi\in\mathcal S_f$. derivations.claim: The origin quadruple is elastic and is fixed by particle exchange and incoming/outgoing interchange, so its Dirac measure is symmetric and locally finite. Every positive finite-valued Borel-measurable density has Borel-measurable collision evaluations on $Q_{\rm el}$. At the only point in the support, $v=w=v'=w'=0$, hence $A=B$ and $\delta\varphi=0$ for every compact smooth test and every polynomial/logarithmic test in $\mathcal S_f$. The collision integral is absolutely zero; the left side is zero because $Q_\nu(f)=0$. Thus the declared collision model satisfies the weak identity on the test subspace required by the elastic-collision definition, and its entropy production is exactly zero.

The density in [A2] is positive, smooth, and integrable with every polynomial velocity weight because its oscillatory factor is bounded above and below by positive constants and the Gaussian factor decays at infinity. Its logarithm has second derivative in $v_1$ equal to the constant $-2/v_*^2$ plus the second derivative of $\log(2+\tfrac12\sin s)$ divided by $v_*^2$, where $s=v_1/v_*$. The latter second derivative is $-1/16$ at $s=0$ and $-1/5$ at $s=\pi/2$. Therefore the Hessian of $\log f$ is not constant. The logarithm of any Maxwellian has constant Hessian, so this $f$ is not Maxwellian despite zero production.

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the kinetic-density definition. Let $n>0$, $u\in\mathbb R^3$, $T>0$, particle mass $m>0$, and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$. Set $\theta=k_BT/m$ and define $M_{n,u,T}(v):=n(2\pi\theta)^{-3/2}\exp(-|v-u|^2/(2\theta))$. Its Lebesgue moments are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}M_{n,u,T}\,dv=n,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^3}vM_{n,u,T}\,dv=nu,$$
$$m\int_{\mathbb R^3}(v-u)\otimes(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=nk_BT\,I_3,\qquad \frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u|^2(v-u)M_{n,u,T}\,dv=0,$$
and
$$\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2M_{n,u,T}\,dv =\frac{mn|u|^2}{2}+\frac{3nk_BT}{2}.$$

Adopt Countable Choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval measured in seconds, let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be periods measured in metres, and let
$$\Omega:=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z).$$
Write $C:=\prod_{j=1}^3[0,L_j)$ and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\Omega$ be the quotient map. Define $dx$ on Borel subsets $E\subseteq\Omega$ by
$$dx(E):=\lambda_3(C\cap\pi^{-1}(E)),$$
and use its completion as the spatial measure. Thus $dx$ is the pushforward of three-dimensional Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open fundamental cell $C$, is not divided by the cell volume, and satisfies $dx(\Omega)=L_1L_2L_3$. Velocity $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is measured in metres per second and $dv$ is three-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Time integration uses Lebesgue measure $dt$ on $I$; product integrals use the corresponding product measures. In this definition $f\,dx\,dv$ is a number count, so a density $f$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^{-3}$.

Set $v_*:=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For $k=2,3$, define the dimensionless polynomial weight $\omega_k(v):=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$. A kinetic density is a finite-valued measurable function $f:I\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ for which, at every $(t,x)$ under discussion,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)f(t,x,v)\,dv<\infty.$$
Define number density $n:=\int f\,dv$ and mass density $\rho:=mn$ for a fixed particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms. Where $n>0$, define
$$u:=\frac1n\int_{\mathbb R^3}vf\,dv,\qquad c:=v-u,\qquad T:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2f\,dv,$$
for a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. The velocity is $u$ in metres per second and the temperature is $T$ in kelvins. Where also $T>0$, define the candidate monatomic Maxwellian
$$M_{n,u,T}(v):=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$
Its normalization and moments are established by a separate proposition; this formula is a definition here. At $n=0$, $u$ and $T$ are undefined, and statements using them assume $n>0$. A zero centered second moment gives $T=0$ and does not define the positive-temperature Maxwellian.

Define the pressure tensor, heat-flux vector, and kinetic-energy density by
$$P:=m\int_{\mathbb R^3}c\otimes c\,f\,dv,\qquad q:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|c|^2c\,f\,dv,\qquad E:=\frac m2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f\,dv.$$
Here $(a\otimes b)_{ij}=a_i b_j$. The finite absolute third moment makes these integrals finite. Their SI units are respectively pascals, watts per square metre, and joules per cubic metre. For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

$$\partial_t f^\epsilon=\frac{M[f^\epsilon]-f^\epsilon}{\epsilon\tau},\qquad f^\epsilon(0)=f_0.$$

Write $\sigma_1^2=\theta-a^2$ and $\sigma_2^2=\sigma_3^2=\theta$. Each factor $g_{\mu_i,\sigma_i}(v_i)=(2\pi\sigma_i^2)^{-1/2}e^{-(v_i-\mu_i)^2/(2\sigma_i^2)}$ has mass one, mean $\mu_i$, and centered second moment $\sigma_i^2$ by [F1]–[F2]. Since $\Sigma$ is positive definite, eigenvalue bounds give constants $C,c>0$ such that $f_0(v)\le C e^{-c|v|^2}$ and $f_0(v)\ge C^{-1}e^{-C(1+|v|^2)}$. $$e^{-s^2/(2(\theta-a^2))}\cosh\!\left(\frac{as}{\theta-a^2}\right).$$
The second derivative of its logarithm contains
$$\left(\frac{a}{\theta-a^2}\right)^2 \operatorname{sech}^2\!\left(\frac{as}{\theta-a^2}\right),$$
which is nonconstant because $a>0$. The logarithm of any Maxwellian is quadratic with constant Hessian, so $f_0\ne M$. It tends to zero for each fixed $t>0$, equals $C$ at $t=0$, and its time integral is at most $\epsilon\tau C$. Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every $\mathbb N$-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^3(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$ be a fixed rectangular periodic cell with periods $L_j>0$ in metres, $T_*>0$ in seconds, and $\varepsilon>0$ a dimensionless fast-collision parameter. Spatial position $x$ is measured in metres, velocity $v$ in metres per second, and $f^\varepsilon d^3x\,d^3v$ counts particles, so $f^\varepsilon$ has units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$. Put $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\omega_k(v)=\sum_{j=0}^k(|v|/v_*)^j$ for $k=2,3$. For each $\varepsilon$, let $f^\varepsilon>0$ be periodic on $\Omega$, continuously differentiable in $t,x$, and twice continuously differentiable in $v$ on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^3\times[0,T_*]$. Let $f_{\rm ref}>0$ be constant in the same units as $f^\varepsilon$ and put $\ell^\varepsilon=\log(f^\varepsilon/f_{\rm ref})$. On each compact time interval, require integrable velocity majorants uniform in $x,t$ for each of $\omega_3 f^\varepsilon$, $\omega_3|\partial_t f^\varepsilon|$, $\omega_3|v\cdot\nabla_xf^\varepsilon|$, $f^\varepsilon|\ell^\varepsilon|$, $|v|f^\varepsilon|\ell^\varepsilon|$, $(1+|\ell^\varepsilon|)|\partial_t f^\varepsilon|$, and $(1+|\ell^\varepsilon|)|v||\nabla_x f^\varepsilon|$. Require the collision logarithmic test to be absolutely integrable. Define

$$Q_{\rm el}=\{(v,w,v',w')\in(\mathbb R^3)^4:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\}$$

with its relative Borel sigma-algebra and let $\nu$ be the nonnegative symmetric collision-rate measure on this set. For each admissible velocity test $\psi$ with absolute convergence, the collision operator is assumed to satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi(v)Q_\nu(f^\varepsilon)(x,v,t)\,d^3v=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(B-A)\bigl(\psi(v)+\psi(w)-\psi(v')-\psi(w')\bigr)\,d\nu,$$

where $A=f^\varepsilon(x,v,t)f^\varepsilon(x,w,t)$ and $B=f^\varepsilon(x,v',t)f^\varepsilon(x,w',t)$. In particular require this identity for $\psi=1,mv_i,m|v|^2/2$; the elastic collision constraints make each corresponding collision bracket zero. Require $f^\varepsilon$ to solve

$$\varepsilon\bigl(\partial_t f^\varepsilon+v\cdot\nabla_x f^\varepsilon\bigr)=Q_\nu(f^\varepsilon),$$

Let $m>0$ in kilograms and $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. Let $n,u,T$ be $C^1$ periodic fields, with $n,T$ bounded above and bounded away from zero and $u$ bounded, and define their local Maxwellian by

$$M_{n,u,T}(v)=n\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{m|v-u|^2}{2k_BT}\right),$$

where $n$ is number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $u$ is velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $T$ is translational temperature in kelvins, $p$ is pressure in pascals ($\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$), and $I_3$ below is the identity tensor on $\mathbb R^3$.

For the fixed velocity unit $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, assume

$$\int_0^{T_*}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)|f^\varepsilon-M_{n,u,T}|\,d^3v\,d^3x\,dt\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to0,$$

and assume the initial convergence

$$\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_2(v)|f^\varepsilon(x,v,0)-M_{n(x,0),u(x,0),T(x,0)}(v)|\,d^3v\,d^3x\longrightarrow0.$$

Then, with $\rho=mn$, $E=\frac12\rho|u|^2+\frac32nk_BT$, and local-equilibrium scalar pressure $p=nk_BT$, the limiting fields satisfy the compressible ideal-monatomic-gas Euler equations

$$\partial_t\rho+\nabla_x\cdot(\rho u)=0,$$

$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\nabla_x\cdot(\rho u\otimes u+pI_3)=0,$$

$$\partial_tE+\nabla_x\cdot((E+p)u)=0.$$

The equations hold distributionally and pointwise because the limiting fields are $C^1$; the initial trace is the one supplied by the initial convergence. The weighted strong convergence is a hypothesis, not a consequence of small $\varepsilon$, the entropy estimate, or the adopted model alone. This is a conditional model deduction, not an empirical claim.

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$

arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $\alpha \in
\mathbb{R}$. Suppose the limits of $f$ and of $g$ at $c$ exist, and write
$L := \lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ and $M := \lim_{x \to c} g(x)$
([[def-function-limit]]). Then:

1. the limit of $f + g$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f + g)(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} f(x) + \lim_{x \to c} g(x) \;=\; L + M ;$$
2. the limit of $\alpha f$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (\alpha f)(x) \;=\; \alpha \lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; \alpha L ;$$
3. the limit of $fg$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (fg)(x) \;=\; \Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\Bigr)\Bigl(\lim_{x \to c} g(x)\Bigr) \;=\; LM ;$$
4. if $M \ne 0$, then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point
   $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $f/g$ is defined on $A_0$ by
   $(f/g)(x) = f(x) / g(x)$, the limit of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ at $c$ exists, and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} (f/g)|_{A_0}(x) \;=\; \frac{\lim_{x \to c} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to c} g(x)} \;=\; \frac{L}{M} .$$

Each equation asserts two things at once: that the limit on the left exists, and
that it has the stated value. Both are proved. The symbols denote by
[[lem-function-limit-unique]].

**Everything below is proved directly from $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$.** No
sequence is constructed and no choice principle is used, so all four claims are
theorems of ZF. Passing through
[[thm-sequential-criterion-for-function-limits]] instead would import the
countable choice spent in that theorem's converse direction, for no gain; see
[[rem-heine-criterion-choice-cost]].

**Why the quotient is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is simply not defined
where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ arbitrarily far from
$c$; restricting to $A_0$ is therefore forced. That this restriction still has
$c$ as a limit point, so that the limit there means anything at all, is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]]. The sequential analogue
[[thm-algebra-of-limits]] needs the corresponding hypothesis in the form "the
denominator sequence is nonzero at every index".

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\omega_3(v)=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$. A velocity density $g:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ is admissible when it is finite-valued and Lebesgue measurable, $g\,d^3v$ is a number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (so $g$ has units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$), and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\omega_3(v)g(v)\,d^3v<\infty.$$
The primitive parameters are species mass $m>0$ in kilograms and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per kelvin. For an admissible $g$ with $n[g]:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g\,d^3v>0$ and positive centered second moment, define
$$u[g]:=\frac{1}{n[g]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}v g(v)\,d^3v,\qquad T[g]:=\frac{m}{3k_Bn[g]}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v-u[g]|^2g(v)\,d^3v.$$
The domain condition ensures $T[g]>0$.
Define its moment-matched Maxwellian by
$$M[g](v)=n[g]\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT[g]}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{m|v-u[g]|^2}{2k_BT[g]}\right).$$
It has the same number, momentum, and kinetic-energy moments as $g$. For a constant relaxation time $\tau>0$ in seconds, adopt the homogeneous collision model
$$Q_{\rm BGK}(g)=\frac{M[g]-g}{\tau}.$$

Let $f_0$ be an admissible initial density with positive number density and positive centered second moment. For each dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$, a trajectory considered in the accelerated model is a continuously differentiable map
$$f^\varepsilon\in C^1\!\left([0,\infty);L^1\!\left(\mathbb R^3,\omega_3(v)\,d^3v\right)\right),$$
whose states have nonnegative admissible representatives with positive number density and positive centered second moment at every $t\ge0$, and whose initial trace satisfies $f^\varepsilon(0)=f_0$ in this weighted $L^1$ space. The derivative is the Banach-space derivative, with the right derivative at $t=0$. Adopt
$$\frac{d}{dt}f^\varepsilon(t)=\frac{M[f^\varepsilon(t)]-f^\varepsilon(t)}{\varepsilon\tau},\qquad t\ge0,$$
as an equality in $L^1(\mathbb R^3,\omega_3(v)\,d^3v)$ at every $t\ge0$.

The model also permits pointwise solution representatives $\widetilde f:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ that are jointly measurable, have finite $\omega_3$-weighted velocity integral at every time, and satisfy $\widetilde f(v,0)=f_0(v)$ for almost every $v$. Require their velocity sections to be continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ for almost every $v$, with positive number density and centered second moment at every time. In this solution sense, require one full-measure set of velocities on which
$$\partial_t\widetilde f(v,t)=\frac{M[\widetilde f(\cdot,t)](v)-\widetilde f(v,t)}{\varepsilon\tau}$$
holds for every $t>0$, and require on each compact time interval a velocity-integrable majorant for $\omega_3(v)|\partial_t\widetilde f(v,t)|$ independent of $t$. The Banach-space and pointwise equalities specify two solution senses for the same adopted model; neither asserts solution existence. This is a separate phenomenological relaxation model. It does not replace or follow from the binary Boltzmann postulate, and the relaxation-time form is not asserted to be an exact microscopic collision operator. No empirical premise or measured relaxation time is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every $\mathbb N$-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $v_*=1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and
$\omega_3(v)=\sum_{j=0}^3(|v|/v_*)^j$. Let
$f_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be a measurable velocity number density,
with $f_0$ in $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$ and $f_0\,d^3v$ measured in
$\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, satisfying
$\int\omega_3 f_0\,d^3v<\infty$, number density
$n_0=\int f_0\,d^3v>0$, positive centered second moment, and finite
reference-relative entropy $\int f_0|\log(f_0/f_{\rm ref})|\,d^3v$, where
$f_{\rm ref}>0$ is constant in the same units as $f_0$. Take the primitive
particle mass $m>0$ in kilograms and Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in joules per
kelvin. Define $u_0=n_0^{-1}\int v f_0\,d^3v$ and
$T_0=m(3k_Bn_0)^{-1}\int |v-u_0|^2f_0\,d^3v>0$. For any nonnegative velocity
density $g$ with finite $\omega_3$ moment, number density
$n[g]=\int g\,d^3v>0$, and positive centered second moment, define
$u[g]=n[g]^{-1}\int vg\,d^3v$,
$T[g]=m(3k_Bn[g])^{-1}\int|v-u[g]|^2g\,d^3v$, and its normalized
moment-matched Maxwellian

$$M[g](v)=n[g]\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT[g]}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{m|v-u[g]|^2}{2k_BT[g]}\right).$$

Write $M=M[f_0]$; it has the same number, momentum, and kinetic-energy
moments as $f_0$.
For $\tau>0$ in seconds and dimensionless $\varepsilon>0$, consider the
homogeneous equation

$$\partial_t f^\varepsilon(v,t)=\frac{M[f^\varepsilon](v,t)-f^\varepsilon(v,t)}{\varepsilon\tau},\qquad f^\varepsilon(v,0)=f_0(v),\quad t\ge0.$$

There is a nonnegative solution
$f^\varepsilon\in C^1([0,\infty);L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v))$ given by

$$f^\varepsilon(v,t)=M(v)+e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}(f_0(v)-M(v)).$$

It solves the equation in $L^1(\omega_3\,d^3v)$ and preserves the number,
momentum, and kinetic-energy moments of $f_0$. It is also the unique solution
in the following pointwise class: a jointly measurable
$\tilde f:\mathbb R^3\times[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with finite
$\omega_3$-weighted velocity integral at every time and initial trace
$\tilde f(v,0)=f_0(v)$ for almost every $v$, whose velocity sections are
continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ for almost
every $v$. Require a common full-measure set of velocities on which the
equation holds for every $t>0$, and, on each compact time interval, an
integrable $\omega_3$-weighted majorant for $\partial_t\tilde f$ independent
of $t$. Also require the density and temperature of $\tilde f$ to remain
positive. These envelopes permit differentiation of the three moment
integrals and justify the conservation argument in the proof.

For each $T_*>0$, with the dimensionless fixed velocity weight
$\|g\|_{1,3}=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|v/v_*|^3)|g(v)|\,d^3v$, which has
units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for velocity densities $g$, it satisfies

$$\|f^\varepsilon(t)-M\|_{1,3}=e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\|f_0-M\|_{1,3},\qquad \int_0^{T_*}\|f^\varepsilon(t)-M\|_{1,3}\,dt\le\varepsilon\tau\|f_0-M\|_{1,3}.$$

Writing $H(g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g\log(g/f_{\rm ref})\,d^3v$ with $0\log0:=0$,
which has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ for velocity densities $g$, the entropy
gap obeys

$$0\le H(f^\varepsilon(t))-H(M)\le e^{-t/(\varepsilon\tau)}\bigl(H(f_0)-H(M)\bigr).$$

Thus for each fixed $t>0$, $f^\varepsilon(t)\to M$ in this weighted $L^1$
norm as $\varepsilon\to0$, while $f^\varepsilon(0)=f_0$; if $f_0$ differs
from $M$ on a set of positive measure, the initial mismatch is nonzero. If
$f_0=M$ almost everywhere, the formula gives the stationary equilibrium with
zero norm and entropy gaps. This is an exact homogeneous BGK model prediction
and does not assert an inhomogeneous Boltzmann-to-Euler limit or an observed
relaxation.
