Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a bounded open time interval measured in seconds and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed bounded open spatial domain measured in metres whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph after rigid coordinate changes. Take $\rho_0>0$ kilograms per cubic metre and $\mu_0>0$ pascal seconds as primitive branch-local physical parameters: this forced branch adopts them as constant density and dynamic shear viscosity inputs and derives neither from another framework nor from observations. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be a twice continuously differentiable velocity in metres per second, $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ a once continuously differentiable pressure multiplier in pascals, and $b:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ a continuous body-acceleration field in metres per second squared. Define $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$ and the stress tensor $\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu_0D$ in pascals, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$.

The forced incompressible Newtonian branch adopts

$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)=\rho_0b+\operatorname{div}\sigma.$$

Equivalently, since $\mu_0$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, its momentum equation is

$$\rho_0\bigl(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nabla p=\mu_0\Delta u+\rho_0b.$$

The derived kinematic viscosity is $\nu_{\mathrm{phys}}=\mu_0/\rho_0$ in square metres per second. Pressure is a constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure. When the stationary no-slip branch is selected, additionally require that $u$ admit a continuous extension $\overline u:I\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of its interior values, and define its classical wall trace by $u_\Gamma(t,x):=\overline u(t,x)$ for $(t,x)\in I\times\partial\Omega$. This extension, when it exists, is unique because $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$. The separately selected no-slip boundary datum is $u_\Gamma=0$; the extension requirement is additional boundary regularity, and neither it, this equality, nor the body force follows from the interior balance. This is a forced branch of the Newtonian model: it adds the prescribed acceleration field to the unforced branch and makes no claim of solution existence or empirical validity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected Lipschitz polygonal or polyhedral open set, let $T>0$ and $\nu>0$, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be a conforming shape-regular affine simplicial mesh of $D$. Let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$ be a finite time partition with $\tau_n=t_n-t_{n-1}>0$, and put $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and $\tau_{\max}=\max_n\tau_n$.

Write $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, $Q=L^2_0(D)=\{q\in L^2(D):\int_Dq=0\}$, and $V_\sigma=\{v\in V:\operatorname{div}v=0\}$. Let $S^1_h$ be the continuous piecewise-affine scalar space on $\mathcal T_h$. For each simplex $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_{K,0},\ldots,\lambda_{K,d}$, set $b_K=(d+1)^{d+1}\prod_{j=0}^d\lambda_{K,j}$ on $K$ and extend $b_K$ by zero outside $K$. The conforming MINI spaces are
$$V_h=[S^1_h\cap H^1_0(D)]^d\oplus\bigoplus_{K\in\mathcal T_h}b_K\mathbb R^d,\qquad Q_h=S^1_h\cap Q,$$
and their weak divergence kernel is $Z_h=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\}$. Let $P_{Z_h}$ denote the $L^2(D)^d$-orthogonal projection onto this finite-dimensional subspace.

For $v,w\in V$, set $\varepsilon(v)=(\nabla v+\nabla v^{\mathsf T})/2$, $a_\nu(v,w)=2\nu\int_D\varepsilon(v):\varepsilon(w)\,dx$, and $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v\,dx$. For $a,v,w\in V$, use the real skew convective form
$$c(a;v,w)=\frac12\int_D\big((a\cdot\nabla)v\cdot w-(a\cdot\nabla)w\cdot v\big)\,dx.$$
Thus $c(a;v,w)=-c(a;w,v)$ and $c(a;v,v)=0$.

A smooth MINI interface consists of a forcing $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$, an exact no-slip velocity-pressure pair $(u,p)$, and a mixed backward Euler MINI solution $(u_h^n,p_h^n)_{n=0}^N$ with the following conditions. The exact pair has $u\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;H^2(D)^d\cap V_\sigma)$, $p\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;H^1(D)\cap Q)$, and satisfies
$$(\partial_tu(t),v)_{L^2}+a_\nu(u(t),v)+c(u(t);u(t),v)+b(v,p(t))=(f(t),v)_{L^2},\qquad b(u(t),q)=0$$
for every $v\in V$, $q\in Q$, and almost every $t\in(0,T)$. The continuous representatives of $u$ and $p$ are used at the time nodes, and $u_0=u(0)$. The discrete initial value is $u_h^0=P_{Z_h}u_0$. With $f_h^n=\tau_n^{-1}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}f(t)\,dt$, each $u_h^n\in V_h$ and $p_h^n\in Q_h$ satisfies
$$\left(\frac{u_h^n-u_h^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_h\right)_{L^2}+a_\nu(u_h^n,v_h)+c(u_h^n;u_h^n,v_h)+b(v_h,p_h^n)=(f_h^n,v_h)_{L^2},\qquad b(u_h^n,q_h)=0$$
for every $v_h\in V_h$, $q_h\in Q_h$, and $1\le n\le N$.

For a family of bounded real-linear velocity sensors $\ell_n\in V^*$, define the endpoint-sampled exact and discrete observations by
$$\mathcal O(\ell;u)=\sum_{n=1}^N\tau_n\ell_n(u(t_n)),\qquad \mathcal O_h(\ell;u_h)=\sum_{n=1}^N\tau_n\ell_n(u_h^n).$$

Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an event-coordinate map with absolute-time coordinate and spatial maps $X_t(q)=b(q)+tw$, where $b:M\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry and $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant in metres per second. Write $X=(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ for the spatial event coordinates of one selected such chart. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. For this one-dimensional weak branch, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and use the all-dimensional Euclidean Lebesgue convention of the conservative weak-form definition. Space-time fields use the restriction of $\lambda_2$ to $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ and initial data the restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $\Omega$, with the corresponding trace sigma-algebras, measurable-map and almost-everywhere conventions. Integrals use the signed Lebesgue integral and completed-product almost-everywhere section convention from that definition. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the adopted specific-heat-at-constant-volume parameter and $R>0$ the adopted specific gas-constant parameter, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives
$$T(v,s)=\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\qquad p(v,s)=(\gamma-1)\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$
For density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=p(1/\rho,s)$ for $\rho>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\in\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by
$$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$
Consequently $T(t,x)=e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\gamma-1)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\gamma-1)\rho(t,x)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s=\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho}$. Thus $\gamma$ is dimensionless, sound speed has units of metres per second, and pressure has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. The corresponding numerical state is $U(t,x):=(\rho(t,x),m(t,x),E(t,x))\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\gamma>1$, set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\},\qquad p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right).$$
Since $\rho(t,x)>0$ and $e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)>0$, $U(t,x)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. For this state, $E-m^2/(2\rho)=\rho e_{\mathrm{int}}$ and $p(U(t,x))=p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)$, so the numerical and thermodynamic pressure maps agree. With $u=m/\rho$, its one-dimensional Euler flux and isentropic sound speed are
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$
The components of $F$ are mass flux in kilograms per square metre second, momentum flux in pascals, and energy flux in watts per square metre. The speed $c$ is in metres per second.

Adopt the inviscid one-dimensional branch with zero body acceleration, zero specific heat supply, zero conductive heat flux, and isotropic three-dimensional Cauchy stress $\sigma=-p_{\mathrm{th}}I_3$ in the tension-positive convention in which traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$; here $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Its restriction to the selected axis is the scalar normal stress $\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}:=\sigma_{11}=-p_{\mathrm{th}}$ in pascals, so the one-dimensional momentum flux is $\rho u^2-\sigma_{\mathrm{1D}}=\rho u^2+p_{\mathrm{th}}$. In the following weak identities, write $p:=p_{\mathrm{th}}$. Assume the locally integrable conservative variables, fluxes, entropy density, and entropy flux satisfy the identities in the distributional sense. Let $\rho_0,m_0,E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ be the initial mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, momentum density in kilograms per square metre second, total energy density in joules per cubic metre, and entropy density in joules per cubic metre kelvin, respectively. Require all displayed densities, fluxes, and products to be locally integrable up to $t=0$: their absolute values have finite integrals on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using the fields for $t>0$. This requirement assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Test functions $\phi,\psi,\eta,\zeta\in C^1(\Omega\times[0,T_f))$ are compactly supported in space-time and vanish near $T_f$; $\zeta$ is nonnegative, and tests may be nonzero at $t=0$. Then adopt
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\,\partial_x\phi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho u\,\partial_t\psi+(\rho u^2+p)\partial_x\psi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\psi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(E\,\partial_t\eta+u(E+p)\partial_x\eta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
and
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+\rho u s\,\partial_x\zeta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$

The associated one-step update in conservative finite-volume form is $$U_i^+=U_i-\lambda\left(\widehat F_{i+1/2}-\widehat F_{i-1/2}\right).$$

Then $U_i^+\in\mathcal G_\gamma$ for every cell $i$; in particular, each updated density and pressure is strictly positive. This conclusion is for the specified one-step symmetric branch and does not assert positivity for other HLL speed pairs or a fully discrete entropy inequality.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

derivations.claim:
1.1 By [A1] and [F4], scalar $L^2(D,\lambda)$ and $L^1(D,\lambda)$ are complete. The $H$ norm is the finite $\ell^2$ product of the component $L^2$ norms. For a matrix field $A$, $\|A\|_K=\int_D|A|_F\,d\lambda$, and
$$\|A\|_K\le\sum_{i,j}\|A_{ij}\|_1\le d\|A\|_K.$$
Thus a Cauchy sequence in either $H$ or $K$ is Cauchy in each scalar component; the component limits exist by [F4], and the displayed norm formulas show convergence to their assembled vector or matrix field. Hence $H$ and $K$ are Banach spaces under [A1]. [A1, F1, F4, construct, algebra]

1.2 For representatives $v,w$, the Frobenius norm satisfies $|v(x)\otimes w(x)|_F=|v(x)|\,|w(x)|$. Holder's inequality [F3] therefore gives $\|v\otimes w\|_K=\int_D|v|\,|w|\,d\lambda\le\|v\|_H\|w\|_H<\infty$. Changing either representative on a null set changes the product only on a null set [F1], so the tensor is well-defined as a $K$-class. The same estimate applied to differences proves continuity of the bilinear tensor map. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

By [F2], choose simple $H$-valued maps $U_n$ with $U_n(\omega)\to U(\omega)$ in $H$ outside a measurable null set. Each $U_n\otimes U_n$ is a finite-valued measurable $K$-valued simple map. Step 1.2 gives
$$\|U_n\otimes U_n-U\otimes U\|_K\le \|U_n-U\|_H(\|U_n\|_H+\|U\|_H)\longrightarrow0$$
outside that null set, since norm convergence makes $(\|U_n\|_H)$ bounded there. Hence $U\otimes U$ is strongly measurable.

2.1 Holder's inequality on the probability space gives $\mathbb E\|U\|_H\le(\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Together with the given strong measurability, [F5] makes $U$ Bochner integrable. The identity $|v\otimes v|_F=|v|^2$ gives $\|U(\omega)\otimes U(\omega)\|_K=\|U(\omega)\|_H^2$ for almost every $\omega$, so its norm is integrable as well; [F5] and step 2.1 make $U\otimes U$ Bochner integrable and yield the displayed norm identity. [A1, F3, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $H$, and the finite-second-moment probability law $\mu$ be as in the Definition. For every $\psi\in H$, the integral defining $S_\psi(v)$ is finite and independent of the representatives of $v$ and $\psi$. The map $S_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ is linear and continuous, with
$$|S_\psi(v)|\le \|v\|_H\|\psi\|_H.$$
Its centered observable $f_\psi(v)=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi\,d\mu$ is Borel measurable and belongs to $L^2(\mu)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ and $H=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ be as in the Definition, and let $K:=L^1(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ use the Frobenius norm on matrices. For $v,w\in H$, the pointwise tensor $(v\otimes w)_{ij}(x):=v_i(x)w_j(x)$ defines an element of $K$, independent of the representatives, and
$$\|v\otimes w\|_K\le \|v\|_H\|w\|_H.$$
For any probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ and strongly measurable $U:\Omega\to H$ with $\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty$, both $U$ and $U\otimes U$ are strongly measurable Bochner-integrable maps into $H$ and $K$, respectively, and
$$\mathbb E\|U\otimes U\|_K=\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with its quotient norm, is complete. Equivalently, every Cauchy
sequence in the metric induced by that norm converges in $L^p(\mu)$.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere relative to $\mu$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The rationals embed densely in the reals), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $U$ is Bochner integrable, so $\bar u=\int_\Omega U\,d\mathbb P$ exists in the quotient space $H$ of [F1]. Subtracting the constant simple map $\bar u$ from the simple approximants in [F4] shows $Z:=U-\bar u$ is strongly measurable. Its second moment satisfies $\mathbb E\|Z\|_H^2\le2\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2+2\|\bar u\|_H^2<\infty$. [A1, A2, F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

On the product measure space of [F9], [F11] makes $|\widetilde U|^2$ product-measurable. Tonelli's theorem [F6] gives $\int_D\mathbb E|\widetilde U(\omega,x)|^2\,d\lambda=\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty$. Since $(\mathbb P\times\lambda)(\Omega\times D)=\lambda(D)<\infty$, Holder [F5] gives $\int_{\Omega\times D}|\widetilde U|\,d(\mathbb P\times\lambda)\le\lambda(D)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2)^{1/2}<\infty$. Fubini [F7] therefore makes the section expectation $m(x):=\mathbb E[\widetilde U(\omega,x)]$ measurable and defined for almost every $x$; set $m(x)=0$ on the exceptional null set. Tonelli [F6] and Holder's inequality on the probability space give $|m(x)|^2\le\mathbb E|\widetilde U(\omega,x)|^2$ almost everywhere, hence $m\in H$. For each $\psi\in H$, [F11] makes $\widetilde U(\omega,x)\cdot\psi(x)$ product-measurable, and its absolute integral is finite:
$$\mathbb E\int_D|\widetilde U\cdot\psi|\,d\lambda\le\mathbb E\|U\|_H\,\|\psi\|_H\le(\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2)^{1/2}\|\psi\|_H<\infty.$$
Fubini [F7] gives $S_\psi(m)=\mathbb E[S_\psi(U)]$. The map $S_\psi$ is bounded linear by [F2], so [F8] gives $\mathbb E[S_\psi(U)]=S_\psi(\bar u)$. Thus $S_\psi(m-\bar u)=0$ for every $\psi\in H$; taking $\psi=m-\bar u$ gives $\|m-\bar u\|_H^2=0$, hence $m=\bar u$ in $H$ and $\mathbb E[\widetilde U(\omega,x)-\bar u(x)]=0$ for almost every $x$. [A1, A2, F2, F5, F6, F7, F8, F10, step 1.1, algebra]
Preserve covariance integrability and additionally prove PSD for every finite vector on the common set of finite second moment.

Fix an admissible $\Phi$. By [F11], each component product $\widetilde U_i\widetilde U_j\Phi_{ij}$ is measurable, and the finite sum $(\widetilde U\otimes\widetilde U):\Phi$ is product-measurable on [F9]. Finite-dimensional Cauchy--Schwarz and the tensor norm identity in [F3] give
$$\mathbb E\int_D| (\widetilde U\otimes\widetilde U):\Phi |\,d\lambda\le\|\Phi\|_\infty\mathbb E\|U\otimes U\|_K=\|\Phi\|_\infty\mathbb E\|U\|_H^2<\infty.$$
Also, Holder [F5] on $\Omega\times D$ gives
$$\int_{\Omega\times D}|\bar u(x)|\,|\widetilde Z(\omega,x)|\,d(\mathbb P\times\lambda)\le\|\bar u\|_H\bigl(\mathbb E\|Z\|_H^2\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty,$$
so the expanded cross terms remain absolutely integrable after multiplication by the bounded $\Phi$. Fubini [F7] exchanges expectation and spatial integration. Expanding $\widetilde U=\bar u+\widetilde Z$ pointwise, the two cross terms have expectation zero for almost every $x$ by step 2.1; the constant term averages to itself since $\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$ by [F10], and the remaining random term is $R$. The deterministic tensor is integrable by Holder [F5], and $R$ is integrable by step 3.1, so the claimed identity follows. [A2, F3, F5, F7, F9, F10, F11, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, given] ∎

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $H$, and the finite-second-moment probability law $\mu$ be as in the Definition. For every $\psi\in H$, the integral defining $S_\psi(v)$ is finite and independent of the representatives of $v$ and $\psi$. The map $S_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ is linear and continuous, with
$$|S_\psi(v)|\le \|v\|_H\|\psi\|_H.$$
Its centered observable $f_\psi(v)=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi\,d\mu$ is Borel measurable and belongs to $L^2(\mu)$.

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a
$\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to $\phi$ ([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability
$\pi$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary
$P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose
shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. We take the
initial law to be $\pi$, which implies stationarity by
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]. Let
$f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$
be Borel with $\pi(f)=0$. Define
$\sigma_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$
only when the covariance series is absolutely convergent and the CLT is
established, as in
[[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Each of the following six conditions is sufficient for absolute convergence
of the covariance series and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be countably generated, let $P$ be a
$\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]], [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to $\phi$ ([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]) with invariant probability
$\pi$, and let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary
$P$-chain whose canonical left shift preserves its path law and whose
shift-invariant measurable events have probability zero or one. We take the
initial law to be $\pi$, which implies stationarity by
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]. Let
$f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$
be Borel with $\pi(f)=0$. Define
$\sigma_f^2=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$
only when the covariance series is absolutely convergent and the CLT is
established, as in
[[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Each of the following six conditions is sufficient for absolute convergence
of the covariance series and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2):$$

1. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>1$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   and $f$ is essentially bounded under $\pi$ (there is $B<\infty$ with
   $|f|\le B$ $\pi$-almost everywhere).
2. $P$ has polynomial total-variation rate of order $m>0$ with an integrable
   envelope ([[def-polynomial-ergodicity-with-integrable-rate-envelope]]),
   $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some $\delta>0$
   ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and
   $m\delta>2+\delta$.
3. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^{2+\delta}(\pi)$ for some
   $\delta>0$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
4. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and
   $\pi\bigl(f^2\log^+|f|\bigr)<\infty$, with
   $0\log^+0:=0$.
5. $P$ is geometrically ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]), reversible with respect to $\pi$ in the symmetric-flow sense ([[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]), and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
6. $P$ is uniformly ergodic ([[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]) and $f\in L^2(\pi)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

In case 4, the displayed logarithmic moment implies $f\in L^2(\pi)$: on $\{|f|\le e\}$ one has $f^2\le e^2$, and on $\{|f|>e\}$ one has $f^2\le f^2\log|f|$.

When $\sigma_f^2=0$, the zero-variance lemma
[[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]] gives the degenerate
normal limit from absolute covariance summability. Finite variance of $f$
alone is not one of the sufficient conditions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $P$ be a $\phi$-irreducible probability kernel ([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]) with invariant probability $\pi$ ([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]). The chain is **aperiodic** if there do not exist an integer $d\ge2$ and pairwise disjoint measurable sets $X_1,\ldots,X_d$ such that $\pi(X_1)>0$ and
$$P(x,X_{i+1})=1\quad(x\in X_i,\ 1\le i<d),\qquad P(x,X_1)=1\quad(x\in X_d).$$
Invariance then gives $\pi(X_i)>0$ for every $i$. The sets need not cover the full state space; the definition rules out any positive-mass cyclic part. Aperiodicity does not itself assert convergence.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability
kernel on it, meaning that $P(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$
and $x\mapsto P(x,A)$ is measurable for each $A\in\mathcal X$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure, that is a countably additive measure of total mass one
([[def-probability-measure]]). The product sigma-algebra
$\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$ is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The joint
flow measure of $(\pi,P)$ is the probability measure $\Lambda_{\pi,P}$ on
$(\mathsf X\times\mathsf X,\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X)$ given, for each
$C\in\mathcal X\otimes\mathcal X$, by

$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}(C):=\int_{\mathsf X}P(x,C_x)\,\pi(dx),\qquad C_x:=\{y\in\mathsf X:(x,y)\in C\}.$$

Existence, countable additivity, and the nonnegative iterated-integral identity
for this measure follow from
[[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. Let $\tau(x,y):=(y,x)$ be
the coordinate-swap map. It is measurable because the preimage of a measurable
rectangle $A\times B$ is $B\times A$ and such rectangles generate the product
sigma-algebra. Define the transpose measure by
$\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}(C):=\Lambda_{\pi,P}(\tau^{-1}(C))$.

The kernel $P$ is **reversible with respect to $\pi$** when
$$\Lambda_{\pi,P}=\Lambda_{\pi,P}^{\top}.$$
This definition uses equality of measures and requires no density, standard
Borel assumption, or prior assumption that $\pi$ is invariant.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

Here $T^{-1}E=\{x:T(x)\in E\}$ denotes an inverse image, whether or not $T$ is invertible. Neither completeness nor finiteness is implicit. The measure-space and measurable-map conventions are [[def-measure-space]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $Y=(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a process on a probability space whose finite-dimensional laws are invariant under common nonnegative time shifts; call this strict stationarity. For $j\ge0$, set $\mathcal F_j^-:=\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_j)$ and $\mathcal F_j^+:=\sigma(Y_j,Y_{j+1},\ldots)$. For $n\ge1$, define the **strong-mixing coefficient** by
$$\alpha_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}}|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|.$$

Define the **uniform-mixing coefficient** by
$$\phi_Y(n):=\sup_{j\ge0}\ \sup_{\substack{A\in\mathcal F_j^-\\\mathbb P(A)>0}}\ \sup_{B\in\mathcal F_{j+n}^+}|\mathbb P(B\mid A)-\mathbb P(B)|.$$

For square-integrable real random variables $U,V$ with positive variances, write
$$\operatorname{Corr}(U,V):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}}.$$
For each $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ consist of the triples $(j,U,V)$ such that $j\ge0$, $U,V$ are real and square-integrable, $U$ and $V$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_j^-$ and $\mathcal F_{j+n}^+$ respectively, and both have positive variance. Define the **maximal-correlation coefficient** by
$$\rho_Y(n):=\sup\Bigl(\{0\}\cup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)|:(j,U,V)\in\mathcal C_n\}\Bigr),$$
where square-integrability is in the sense of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Thus $\rho_Y(n)=0$ when there is no admissible pair, as for a constant process. The process is called strongly mixing, uniformly mixing, or rho-mixing, respectively, when the corresponding coefficient tends to zero. These coefficients are distinct conditions; no implication between them is included in this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad
f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

Let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$, $H$, and the finite-second-moment probability law $\mu$ be as in the Definition. For every $\psi\in H$, the integral defining $S_\psi(v)$ is finite and independent of the representatives of $v$ and $\psi$. The map $S_\psi:H\to\mathbb R$ is linear and continuous, with
$$|S_\psi(v)|\le \|v\|_H\|\psi\|_H.$$
Its centered observable $f_\psi(v)=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi\,d\mu$ is Borel measurable and belongs to $L^2(\mu)$.

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

derivations.claim: 1.1 For each scalar $x$, $S_\psi(V_x)=\int_D xe_1\cdot(e_1/\lambda(D))\,d\lambda=x\lambda(D)/\lambda(D)=x$. Thus the random-field sensor output $Y_n$ equals $X_n$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Independence of $\epsilon_{n+1}$ from the natural past and its stated law imply $\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n))=P(X_n,A)$ for every Borel $A$, with $P(x,\cdot)=N(\rho x,\eta^2)$. The stipulated stationary law $\nu$ is invariant in the sense of [F4]. [A1, A2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Stationarity and the recursion give $\mathbb E[X_{n+1}^2]=\rho^2\mathbb E[X_n^2]+\eta^2$, because $\epsilon_{n+1}$ is centered and independent of $X_n$. Thus $\gamma_0=\mathbb E[X_n^2]=\eta^2/(1-\rho^2)$. Iterating the recursion gives $X_k=\rho^kX_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\rho^{k-j}\epsilon_j$; the innovation sum is centered and independent of $X_0$, so [F5] yields $\gamma_k=\rho^k\gamma_0$ for every $k\ge0$. [A2, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Since $|\rho|<1$, [F6] gives $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|=\gamma_0\sum_{k\ge1}|\rho|^k<\infty$ and
$$\gamma_0+2\sum_{k\ge1}\gamma_k=\frac{\eta^2}{1-\rho^2}\left(1+\frac{2\rho}{1-\rho}\right)=\frac{\eta^2}{(1-\rho)^2}.$$
The last equality uses $1-\rho^2=(1-\rho)(1+\rho)$ and $|\rho|<1$, so $1+\rho>0$. [F6, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 The centered sum $S_n:=n^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}Y_j$ is normally distributed because the finite vector $(X_0,\ldots,X_{n-1})$ is jointly Gaussian. Expanding its variance and counting the $n-k$ pairs at lag $k$ gives
$$v_n:=\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\gamma_k.$$
[A2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 On the counting-measure space $\mathbb N$, the summands $\mathbf 1_{\{k<n\}}(1-k/n)\gamma_k$ converge pointwise to $\gamma_k$ and are dominated in absolute value by the summable sequence $|\gamma_k|$. By [F8], $v_n\to\gamma_0+2\sum_{k\ge1}\gamma_k=\eta^2/(1-\rho)^2=:v>0$. [F6, F8, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

3.3 Let $G$ have law $N(0,1)$. Since $S_n$ is centered normal with variance $v_n$, its law equals that of $\sqrt{v_n}G$. For every bounded continuous $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $h(\sqrt{v_n}G)\to h(\sqrt vG)$ pointwise and is bounded by $\|h\|_\infty$; [F8] gives convergence of expectations. By [F7], $S_n\Rightarrow N(0,v)$. The chain is stationary Markov, the covariance series is absolutely summable by step 3.1, and the CLT has now been proved, so [F9] identifies $v$ as its covariance long-run variance. [F7, F8, F9, step 3.1, step 4.1, given] ∎

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.
